title: Low‐Frequency Variability in Cross‐Channel Velocities Over the Northeast Channel; A 32 Year Census of Scotian Shelf Crossovers
content:
Abstract
Georges Bank (GB) is a highly productive shelf enclosing the southwestern side of the Gulf of Maine (GOM). The Northeast Channel (NEC) separates the region from the Scotian Shelf (SS). Typically, when the southward‐flowing water on the SS reaches the NEC, it flows right into the GOM, traveling around the GOM before reaching GB. Alternatively, events known as SS Crossovers can occur, in which water from the SS cuts directly across the NEC onto the southeastern edge of GB. These events can have significant ecosystem impacts because SS waters are physically and biologically distinct from those typically found on GB. In this work, we validate the use of satellite altimeter data to capture low‐frequency (>30‐day) changes in the cross‐NEC velocity. Then, using 32 years of satellite altimeter data, we created a long‐term census of SS crossover events. We find 4 periods with anomalous westward cross‐channel velocities in 1996, 1998, 2005, and 2024. During these 4 periods, surface water on the southern GB was approximately 0.7 psu fresher and 3° ${}^{\circ}$C colder than typical conditions. An investigation of potential forcing mechanisms finds that these anomalous cross‐channel velocities are likely generated by increased upstream velocities on the SS, with interannual variability linked to large‐scale changes in the North Atlantic circulation.

title: Quantifying and Comparing Diel Dynamics of Fish Communities Using eDNA Metabarcoding
content:
ABSTRACT
Many fish species show cyclical patterns in activity, such as migration and reproduction, in response to temporal environmental variations that are associated with daily, tidal and seasonal cycles. Short (e.g., hourly) timescale biological cycles, revealed by high temporal resolution occurrence patterns of organisms, provide important insights into behavioural and physiological ecology. Environmental DNA (eDNA) monitoring is an effective, non‐invasive tool for observing the occurrence patterns of multiple species simultaneously, and the sampling can be repeated at short intervals. However, applications of eDNA monitoring for examining relationships between fish diel patterns and fish habitat types, intraspecific variation in short‐term temporal occurrence patterns, as well as short‐term population dynamics in relation to environmental cycles across multiple fish species, remain limited. Here, we conducted quantitative eDNA metabarcoding analyses of coastal fish communities in northeastern Japan at 2‐h intervals and comprehensively explored short‐term temporal shifts in both fish populations and communities. The results show diel dynamics of various species within fish communities, which gives rise to distinct community distributions between day and night. In addition, there were populations whose eDNA dynamics were explained by the combination of daily and tidal cycles. Furthermore, short‐term temporal eDNA profiles suggested potential links between day‐night occurrence patterns of fish and their habitat types. These short‐term eDNA dynamics may also suggest that some species exhibit variability in short‐term temporal occurrence patterns. Such high‐frequency eDNA monitoring may facilitate comprehensive investigations into the activity patterns of diverse taxa, which leads to effective monitoring and management of various species.

title: A multistate Langevin diffusion for inferring behavior‐specific habitat selection and utilization distributions: Reply
Thermal regulation of ant colonies is driven by biological rhythms and acclimation
content:
Abstract
Activity in hot environments is physiologically costly for ectotherms. In social insect colonies, the division of labor may reduce the costs of physiological performance. Additional mechanisms may include plastic responses to thermal conditions and rhythmic investment into thermal tolerance. Here, we evaluate the extent to which static specialization, biological rhythms, and acclimation account for short‐term shifts in thermal performance using a pair of complementary experiments in the tropical ant Ectatomma ruidum. In the first experiment, we marked foraging workers at distinct time periods with differing temperatures, and then compared the thermal tolerance of these workers and non‐foragers with a time‐to‐failure knockdown assay. In the second experiment, we subdivided colonies into three laboratory nests under contrasting thermal regimes and performed the assay at daily thermal minima and maxima. We found thermal tolerance was governed both by acclimation and a daily rhythm. These plastic shifts in thermal tolerance were more substantial than differences among specialized workers. These colonies primarily responded to thermal challenges by flexible changes in thermal tolerance rather than the static differences associated with the division of labor. Our findings demonstrate how modular biological systems may demonstrate greater capacity for resilience to increasing variability in thermal challenges.

title: A statistical framework to identify gene-gene interactions underlying multiple dichotomous phenotypes from genotype data
content:
by Siru Wang, Xuhui Zhu, Yu Li, Gengjie Jia

Identifying gene-gene (G × G) interactions across multiple dichotomous phenotypes is challenging due to the extreme sparsity of SNP-derived interaction matrices and the reduced statistical power associated with binary outcomes. Existing G × G association methods are restricted to either single or multiple continuous phenotypes. Here we introduce GiMat (Gene Interaction and Multiple-phenotype Association Test), a statistical framework that extends multivariate kernel regression to model G × G interactions jointly across dichotomous phenotypes, while explicitly capturing homogeneous and heterogeneous interaction effects. Extensive simulations demonstrate that GiMat controls type I error conservatively and adapts power flexibly to different types of relationships between interaction effects and phenotypes. Applied to type 2 diabetes and hypertension comorbidity in the UK Biobank, GiMat identified four previously unreported G × G interaction pairs associated with both phenotypes. This scalable framework enables robust discovery of complex genetic interactions underlying multiple correlated phenotypes.

title: Aging out of the blue: Region-specific epigenetic clock calibration for a blue zone with the DNAm SuperLearner
content:
by Nolan Gunter, Andres Cardenas, Michael Kobor, Nicole Gladish, Julie MacIsaac, Kristy Dever, David Rehkopf, William Dow, Luis Rosero-Bixby, Alan Hubbard

Epigenetic clocks estimate biological age from DNA methylation patterns at CpG sites, providing robust predictions of mortality and morbidity risk. “Blue zones,” regions of exceptional longevity, offer a unique opportunity to investigate how biological aging diverges from chronological age. However, standard clocks are typically trained on large, heterogeneous datasets, reflecting average population trends rather than region-specific dynamics. Using data from the Costa Rican Longevity and Healthy Aging Study (CRELES), we profiled DNA methylation from residents of the Nicoya blue zone (n = 206) and a reference population in other parts of Costa Rica (n = 875). We propose training a SuperLearner, an ensemble machine learning approach, on the non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans to optimize predictive performance across existing clocks and flexible machine learners. By its Oracle property, the SuperLearner’s weighted combination of algorithms performs asymptotically as well as the best possible combination of the candidate predictors. We then used this trained model to construct a calibrated hypothesis test comparing Epigenetic Age Acceleration (EAA) distributions between the blue zone region and the reference population. Before calibration or covariate adjustment, estimates for Nicoyans depended heavily on the chosen clock. The SuperLearner placed them about three years younger on average (R¯1=−3.05,95% CI [−3.64,−2.46]), whereas DNAmFitAge placed them almost four years older (R¯1=3.59,95% CI [3.02,4.17]). Mean calibration to non-Nicoyan Costa Ricans made estimates consistent across clocks, with an estimated EAA advantage to approximately two years (Δ^=−1.96,95% CI [−2.56,−1.37]). After age-stratified calibration within 10-year age groups, only a small EAA advantage (Δ^=−0.35,95% CI [−0.64,−0.05]) remained, concentrated among the oldest participants. This approach provides a robust and reproducible framework for estimating longevity in distinct regions when a relevant reference population is available.

title: Storing long-lived memories via molecular error correction: A minimal mathematical model of Crick’s memory switch
content:
by John J. Vastola, Tejas Ramdas, Samuel J. Gershman

Cells store information in part by attaching molecular marks to proteins and DNA. But because marks can be randomly removed (e.g., due to ambient phosphatase activity) and added (e.g., due to ambient kinase activity), information encoding may be poor, and in the worst case marks may only store information on the time scale of molecular turnover. We identify a high-level strategy cells use to maintain encoding fidelity beyond the time scale of turnover—which we call molecular error correction—and find that it closely resembles an underexplored theoretical proposal by Francis Crick. To assess the effectiveness of molecular error correction, we construct and analyze several minimal mathematical models of molecular memory switches. We find that Crick-like error correction provides an efficient way to improve the lifetime of stored memories, especially compared to redundantly encoding information using a large number of molecules, but that it can yield false positives (and hence low information fidelity) when there is ambient marking activity; given these two competing concerns, the optimal level of error correction is moderate rather than arbitrarily high. We also find that combining error correction with redundant encoding can efficiently and robustly produce memories that last between ten and one hundred times longer than the turnover time scale. Our work provides insight regarding how to model and interrogate noisy molecular memory systems, suggests that error correction is a design principle of molecular memory, and quantitatively connects error correction to observable memory time scales.

title: Radiopharmaceutical therapy for metastatic prostate cancer: Insights from mechanistic modeling and in silico trials
content:
by Matteo Italia, Silvia Bordel-Vozmediano, José García Otero, Gabriel F. Calvo, Víctor M. Pérez-García

Radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has rapidly evolved into a key precision-oncology modality, with radioligands now approved or in late-stage development for multiple solid tumors, including neuroendocrine and prostate cancers. RPT with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA (Prostate-Specific Membrane Antigen) has recently been approved as a life-prolonging treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but its clinical use still relies on nonpersonalized, empirically chosen fixed schedules. Here, we develop a mechanistic, patient-personalizable mathematical model simulating mCRPC response and organ-at-risk toxicity during [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT. The model integrates tumor growth dynamics, radiobiological response, and organ-resolved pharmacokinetics inferred from mass data and standardized uptake values obtained from positron emission tomography studies. Parameters were derived from the literature, although the framework allows personalization by fitting to patient-specific data, such as imaging and prostate-specific antigen levels. Analytical threshold analysis identified a critical activity scale governing net tumor control, while simulations of a representative virtual patient (VP) illustrated the model’s coupled tumor and activity dynamics. Global sensitivity analysis identified tumor growth, uptake, and radiosensitivity parameters as key drivers of interpatient variability. Using VP cohorts generated via stochastic parameter sampling, we conducted in silico trials and benchmarked the model against published dosimetry and survival data for [177Lu]Lu-PSMA trials. Convergence testing supported the use of cohorts of 500 VPs for stable population-level estimates. We then explored dosing and scheduling strategies to quantify efficacy–toxicity trade-offs. Consolidated regimens with fewer, higher-activity injections improved overall survival (OS) in silico but increased toxicity, especially in kidneys. Cycle length had a weaker influence on OS within a 2–9 week window, while it clearly affected toxicity, whereas excessive delays (> 12 weeks) markedly reduced efficacy. These methodological findings illustrate how mechanistic modeling and in silico trials can inform the design and personalization of RPT regimens.

title: Migration as a key influence on ungulate eco-evolutionary history
content:
by Gustavo Burin

Species can overcome resource limitations by migrating to more favourable areas. A new study in PLOS Biology shows that migration has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, that likely led to changes in ecosystem functioning. Species can overcome environmental limitations by migrating to more favorable areas. This Primer explores a new study in PLOS Biology showing that this behavior has an important effect on the diversification dynamics of ungulates, which in turn likely led to changes in ecosystem properties and functioning.

title: An indirect wing steering muscle stabilizes flight by regulating wing pitch angle in Drosophila
content:
by Han Kheng Teoh, Debojyoti Biswas, Haoru Li, Abby Leung, B. Kemper Ludlow, Samuel C. Whitehead, Erica Ehrhardt, Michael Dickinson, Tsevi Beatus, Noah J. Cowan, Itai Cohen

Flapping flight is inherently unstable, requiring Drosophila to fine-tune their wing motions on a milliseconds timescale. Pioneering studies have shown that the direct steering muscles, which attach to the wing hinge, are important for generating these rapid flight reflexes. Recent connectome data, however, reveal that indirect steering muscles or tension muscles, which alter the mechanics of the thorax, receive some of the same synaptic inputs from the sensory apparatus as the direct steering muscles. This discovery suggests that the indirect steering muscles may also be important for flight control. Here, we show that the indirect tergopleural muscles indeed contribute substantially to stabilization, particularly for large pitch perturbations. We find that for small perturbations (less than 1,000 °/s), flies modulate their wing stroke amplitude to generate lift-based corrective torques, a strategy that has been previously documented. For larger perturbations, however, we observe that Drosophila engage an additional wing degree of freedom—the wing pitch angle—to leverage additional lift and drag forces during the corrective maneuver. Quasi-steady aerodynamic simulations reveal that this strategy minimizes power consumption, anaolgous to how some mammals (including humans) adjust their steady-state gaits in a near energy-optimal manner. Using optogenetics and a control theory framework, we demonstrate that the tergopleural muscle is activated by a proportional gain component of a nonlinear proportional-integral controller responsible for determining the wing pitch angle during large perturbations. A simplified torsional spring model for the wing hinge captures the changes in the wing pitch dynamics observed during correction maneuvers by using the tergopleural muscle to adjust the rest angle of the wing. These findings provide a striking example of reflex strategy selection in time-critical behaviors and underscore the vital role of indirect steering muscles in flight stabilization.

title: The importance of deep time from Hutton to Earth system science
content:

Modern observations sample only a brief interval of Earth history, limiting tests of Earth system behaviour beyond present conditions. Integrating deep-time evidence with observations and Earth system model results can extend empirical testing across a much wider range of environmental conditions.

title: Rhodopsin 7 is an ancestral non-canonical photoreceptor that shapes light-responsive behavior
content: Animals rely on light not only for vision but also to adapt behavior to their environment through non-image-forming pathways. In Drosophila, most rhodopsins mediate retinal image formation, but Rhodopsin 7 (RH7) is widely expressed in the brain and optic lobe, acting as a non-canonical light sensor reminiscent of mammalian melanopsin. We combined expression mapping, behavioral assays, and phylogenetic comparisons to investigate its function. RH7 detects temporal changes in luminance, guiding rapid behavioral responses, and regulating daily activity patterns. Flies lacking RH7 are less active during the dark phase, while strains with constitutively active RH7 show increased activity. Phylogenetic analyses suggest that RH7 is an ancient rhodopsin present across panarthropods, representing an intermediate between G protein–coupled receptors and specialized rhodopsins, highlighting a key step in the evolution of non-visual light perception. These findings show that RH7 functions as a melanopsin-like sensor, shaping behavior, and illuminating the origins of light detection.

title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels
content: Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse’s contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

title: Correction: Uncovering the electrical synapse proteome in retinal neurons via in vivo proximity labeling
Lower Core Pressure From a Three‐Dimensional Model of Earth's Internal Stress
content:
Abstract
Earth's iron core drives many internal and external processes. Pressure is a primary variable controlling its physical state and dynamic behavior, yet deep‐Earth pressure cannot be measured directly and has primarily been estimated assuming hydrostatic equilibrium (AHE). Meanwhile, growing evidence suggests that Earth's internal stress may extend beyond hydrostatic conditions. Here, we develop a three‐dimensional model (TDM) to determine Earth's internal stress without prescribing a particular stress state. Our TDM yields pressures 86.9 GPa lower than estimates derived by AHE throughout the outer core. In the inner core, the pressure reduction increases from 85.7 GPa at the inner core boundary to 90.6 GPa at Earth's center. The lower pressures calculated from TDM reconcile seismologically inferred core densities with high‐pressure experimental densities, largely resolving the long‐recognized density discrepancy.

Legacy effects and recovery potential of carbonate budgets on Seychelles coral reefs
content:
Abstract
Coral reef carbonate budgets are fundamental indicators of ecosystem function, underpinning framework accretion and reef growth. Although spatial assessments and short‐term studies exist, multi‐decadal evaluations of net budget states spanning repeated disturbance events remain rare. We analyzed a 31‐year dataset (1994–2025) from reef sites across the inner Seychelles to quantify long‐term coral and gross carbonate production and gross (biological) erosion, and net budget state trends (kg CaCO3 m−2 yr−1) across four thermal stress events (1998, 2010, 2016, 2024). Reefs previously classified as ecologically “recovered” to hard coral‐dominated, or “regime‐shifted” to macroalgal‐dominated states following the 1998 mass bleaching displayed contrasting multi‐decadal net budget trajectories. Coral production rates declined sharply at all sites after 1998, with regime‐shifted reefs exhibiting persistently negative or near‐zero net budgets. In contrast, recovering reefs showed rapid increases in coral production and net budgets until 2014, before being reset by the 2016 bleaching event, which reduced coral production by approximately 50% and drove budgets close to zero. Gross erosion varied comparatively little through time and among site groupings, despite transient post‐bleaching increases in parrotfish erosion and a recent sea urchin mass‐mortality event. Consequently, net budget dynamics were primarily driven by changes in coral production, particularly fluctuations in branching Acropora and Pocillopora. Higher pre‐bleaching dominance of these fast‐growing taxa amplified subsequent declines, implying a legacy effect on magnitudes of change and a trade‐off between high productivity and thermal vulnerability. By 2025, several reefs remain in low or neutral net budget states, raising concerns for framework persistence under future thermal stress.

title: Microplastic carbon turns slowly into essential biomolecules in artificial mesocosms
content:
Abstract
Plastic litter is a global concern, yet its biochemical fate and contribution to aquatic carbon cycling under environmentally realistic conditions remain poorly understood. Previous laboratory studies have demonstrated the incorporation of microplastic‐derived carbon into freshwater food webs, but it is unclear whether these processes also occur in more natural settings. Here, we evaluated whether polyethylene microplastic (PE‐MP) carbon can be incorporated into a Baltic rock‐pool food web under field‐mesocosm conditions using 13C‐enriched PE and stable‐isotope analyses. Using 13C‐enriched PE‐MPs at an environmentally relevant concentration, we were able to distinguish PE‐MP effects from seasonal variation and trace plastic‐derived carbon into dissolved inorganic carbon, microbial membrane lipids, and amino acids. Bacterial (16:1ω7 and 18:1ω7) and algal (18:3ω3) fatty acids were more 13C‐enriched in treatment mesocosms than in controls, demonstrating microbial utilization of polyethylene‐derived carbon. Microbes further incorporated plastic‐derived carbon into essential and non‐essential amino acids. This carbon was subsequently transferred to the dominant zooplankter, Daphnia magna, where it was detected in membrane lipids, amino acids, and resting eggs (ephippia). Based on carbon‐incorporation rates, complete degradation of PE‐MPs was estimated to be 68–200 yr, depending on temperature and microbial community composition. However, these estimates are based on pure polyethylene and may differ for commercial plastics due to differences in additives and morphology. Our results demonstrate that previously identified pathways of microplastic‐carbon assimilation and trophic transfer also occur under field conditions, resulting in the incorporation of plastic‐derived carbon into aquatic food webs.

title: Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and remodel host-cell metabolism
content: Flaviviruses reprogram host-cell metabolism to support viral replication. In previous work, we showed that Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and were predicted to interact with viral enzymes. Here, we investigated whether S01, a purified solid from Solanum ovalifolium containing predominantly two characterized spirostane saponins, also modulates host-cell metabolism in association with reduced permissiveness to dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2). We performed untargeted GC-QTOF-MS metabolomics in Vero cells under four conditions, including untreated control, S01 treatment, DENV-2 infection, and DENV-2 infection with S01 treatment. Quality-control samples clustered tightly, supporting analytical reproducibility. Principal component analysis revealed separation among experimental groups, and PERMANOVA confirmed significant global metabolic differences (F = 27.567, R{superscript 2} = 0.827, p = 0.001).  S01 also retained strong antiviral activity, producing 99.9% inhibition under the metabolomics conditions. DENV-2 infection was associated with alterations metabolites related to amino acid, carbohydrate, lipid, and sphingolipid metabolism. Pathway analysis highlighted glutamate metabolism, arginine and proline metabolism, glycolysis-related pathways, fatty-acid oxidation and carnitine-associated metabolism, phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, and sphingolipid metabolism. In uninfected cells, S01 induced a distinct metabolic profile (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.951, Q{superscript 2} = 0.851; permutation p = 0.002), characterized by increased carbohydrate-related metabolites, including the unresolved Talose/D-glucose feature, gluconic acid, 2-keto-L-gulonic acid, and D-mannitol, together with decreased abundance of selected lipid-related metabolites. During infection, S01 induced a distinct metabolic (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.928, Q{superscript 2} = 0.841), characterized by lower abundance of several fatty-acid-related and organic-acid metabolites and higher abundance of carbohydrate-related metabolites, while modifying selected DENV-2-associated metabolic alterations. These findings associate S01 antiviral activity with substantial remodeling of host-cell metabolism. Together with previous docking predictions of interactions with viral targets, the results support a model in which the antiviral activity of Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins may involve complementary effects on viral and host-associated processes.

title: A normalization strategy for extreme proteome regulation reveals distinct targets of eIF4A1/2 and their inhibitor silvestrol
content: Cells rapidly adjust protein synthesis in response to stress, signalling and drugs, often converging on the cell's translation machinery affecting the synthesis of multiple proteins simultaneously. Nascent proteome analysis, combining pulsed SILAC labelling with enrichment of newly synthesized proteins (NSPs), can measure these changes proteome-wide. However, quantitative proteomics relies on normalization methods that assume most proteins remain unchanged. When protein synthesis shifts globally, this assumption fails: normalization then erases the biological effect, whereas omitting it leads to misinterpretation of data. Since no approach has so far reliably preserved global changes in protein synthesis, we developed labelled protein ratio (LPR) normalization, which uses the ratio of newly synthesized to pre-existing protein in the global proteome as an internal scaling factor. Two SILAC benchmarks showed that this factor is accurate down to a few percent of labelled protein and recovers defined global differences, whereas twelve established normalization methods did not. Applied to cycloheximide treatment, LPR normalization revealed a 57% decrease in synthesis, which median normalization reported as balanced up- and down-regulation with spurious increases in multiple proteins. After depletion of the core translation initiation factor eIF4A1, LPR normalization uncovered a broad translational repression that median normalization largely masked, while eIF4A inhibition with silvestrol showed a divergent pattern, suggesting secondary effects. LPR normalization thus provides a general strategy for quantifying global changes in protein synthesis.

title: Persistent DNA damage reprograms the cutaneous microenvironment into a stress-responsive immunometabolic pro-pigmentary niche
content: Chronic ultraviolet (UV) exposure induces progressive pigmentary remodeling of the skin, yet how persistent DNA damage influences tissue-level responses remains poorly understood. Xeroderma pigmentosum complementation group C (XP-C), characterized by defective global genome nucleotide excision repair, provides a model to investigate these processes. Here, integrating chronic UVB irradiation of Xpc-deficient mice with spatial transcriptomics, multi-omics profiling, and functional analyses, we identify a coordinated multicellular response associated with persistent hyperpigmentation. UVB-exposed Xpc-deficient skin exhibited increased eumelanin accumulation, altered melanosome organization, enhanced melanosome transfer to keratinocytes, and regional melanocyte expansion. Proteomic, metabolomic, and kinomic analyses revealed coordinated alterations in inflammatory, cytoskeletal, redox, metabolic, and pigmentation-associated programs. Spatial transcriptomics further identified distinct keratinocyte states and inflammatory immune niches enriched in hyperpigmented regions, coinciding with increased melanocyte abundance and DNA damage. These findings suggest that pigmentary remodeling occurs within a spatially organized, stress-responsive immunometabolic tissue environment rather than reflecting melanocyte-intrinsic alterations alone. Analyses of human XP-C skin and XPC-deficient primary human melanocytes revealed overlapping pigmentation-associated, inflammatory, and cytoskeletal alterations, supporting the relevance of these observations to human disease. Together, our findings reveal a previously underappreciated relationship between persistent DNA damage and spatially coordinated multicellular remodeling, providing a framework for understanding how defective genome maintenance is associated with chronic pigmentary changes and altered tissue homeostasis. These findings may also offer insights into the mechanisms underlying common acquired hyperpigmentary disorders.

title: Gene network topologies for heterogeneity restoration during self-renewal
content: The ability for a subset of cells to establish a heterogeneous cell population with multi-lineage competency is crucial for the self-renewal capacity of tissues and organs. Restoration of heterogeneous gene expression patterns has been observed in pluripotent and multi-potent stem cells, and the heterogeneity restoration can influence the potential of differentiation into multiple cell types. Similarly, cancer cells can acquire the capacity to establish non-genetic heterogeneity that plays a role in cancer progression and resistance to therapeutics. Specific models of gene regulatory networks have been proposed to explain heterogeneity restoration. However, due to the lack of systematic analysis, it is unclear which network topologies are more efficient for this multicellular function, and what intrinsic and extrinsic factors can determine the optimal choice of network topology. In this work, we use mathematical models describing gene expression of single cells and their underlying population dynamics to examine the influence of network topology on the recovery of multimodal expression patterns originating from a homogeneous population. We found that feedback loops are a key factor contributing to heterogeneity restoration. Negative and positive feedback loops support the existence of heterogeneity restoration, but only positive feedback can accelerate the process with low cost of single-cell-level variations of expression. Furthermore, networks with mixed feedback were the most robust ones for heterogeneity restoration with respect to changes in both kinetic rate constants and noise levels. Using experimentally validated network databases, we showed that genes involved in feedback loops are enriched with functions related to cell fate decisions, and we identified examples of realistic gene regulatory networks cell fate dynamics. Our results suggest multiple potential evolutionary paths towards gene circuits governing heterogeneity restoration and key factors contributing to the dynamics of this process. We expect that this systematic study will enable future discoveries of new gene regulatory networks governing progenitor and cancer cell dynamics as well as therapeutic strategies targeting heterogeneity-enabling circuits.

title: HyperGenie: A method for predicting enzymatic gene essentiality using hypergraph neural networks and genome-scale metabolic models
content: Identifying essential genes in bacteria is crucial for drug discovery and synthetic biology. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) evaluated via flux balance analysis remain standard, yet they rely on the often-invalid premise that mutant strains optimize for maximum growth. Recent machine learning approaches circumvent this limitation using random forests or graph neural networks on mass flow graphs (MFGs). However, data-driven tools like random forests discard network topology, while graph-based tools like MFGs decompose multi-component biochemical reactions into pairwise interactions, misrepresenting complex stoichiometry and limiting interpretability. Furthermore, existing methods remain largely uncharacterised in data-scarce regimes and cross-environmental conditions. Here, we introduce HyperGenie, a framework that integrates genome-scale metabolic models with directed hypergraph neural networks by representing metabolites as nodes and reactions as hyperedges. Operating directly on wild-type flux features, HyperGenie eliminates post-knockout optimality assumptions, achieves a 13% PR-AUC improvement over prior objective-dependent methods, and matches computationally demanding, state-of-the-art flux-sampling baselines. Using HyperGenie to guide targeted growth curve assays, we identified latent essentiality misannotations across three genes in the benchmark iML1515 dataset, which we then reconciled and validated experimentally via PCR. In data-scarce regimes, HyperGenie retained robust predictive performance (> 90% PR-AUC) when trained on as little as 40% of the data. To isolate the value of hypergraph message passing, we benchmarked HyperGenie against an independent-reaction multilayer perceptron (MLPGenie) across diverse nutrient environments and uptake rates, where HyperGenie's hypergraph inductive bias yielded consistent accuracy gains (> 2% in glucose; > 4% across six alternative carbon sources). Notably, HyperGenie exhibits robust zero-shot cross-nutrient generalization, accurately forecasting gain-of-essentiality phenotypes on novel carbon sources, though loss-of-essentiality remains challenging. Finally, coupling hypergraph representations with SHAP attribution provides actionable mechanistic insights into metabolic rewiring, establishing a data-efficient, interpretable platform for discovering novel antibiotic targets.

title: PYTHOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION AND ANTIMICROBIAL ACTIVITY OF LEPIDIUM SATIVUM SEED EXTRACTS AGAINST SELECTED HUMAN PATHOGENS.
content: This study evaluates the antimicrobial activity of Lepidium sativum (Garden Cress) seed extracts against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Fusarium oxysporum, and Candida albicans using methanol and acetone as solvents. The antimicrobial effects were assessed through the zone of inhibition and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) using serial dilution. The methanol extract exhibited the highest inhibition zones, measuring 23.6 mm for S. aureus and 21.5 mm for E. coli, while the acetone extract showed 22.9 mm and 18.3 mm, respectively. C. albicans exhibited moderate susceptibility, with inhibition zones of 16.2 mm (methanol) and 14.8 mm (acetone), whereas F. oxysporum showed weaker inhibition at 12.4 mm and 10.7 mm, respectively. MIC values ranged from 10-1 to 10-4 dilutions, with methanol extracts maintaining higher efficacy at lower concentrations. These findings validate Lepidium sativum as a potential natural antimicrobial agent, particularly against gram-positive bacteria, and suggest further exploration of its bioactive compounds for pharmaceutical applications.

title: Cumulative antibiograms: effects of isolate selection and stratification order on susceptibility estimates and resistance representation
content: Cumulative antibiograms depend on how isolates are selected and how data are stratified. Different selection strategies may affect both the number of isolates included and the susceptibility estimates reported. We retrospectively analyzed routine microbiology records from a tertiary-care hospital in Barcelona, Spain (2022-2025). Within each patient-organism-calendar-year unit, we compared three isolate-selection strategies: first-isolate, resistance-phenotype, and susceptibility-profile. We assessed the number of isolates retained, susceptibility at standard or increased exposure, the identification of resistance-phenotype profiles, and the effect of de-duplication before versus after stratification. Annual differences in susceptibility were estimated using paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptibility-profile selection retained 16.9% more isolates than first-isolate selection, with differences exceeding 5 percentage points in 10 of 44 annual antimicrobial comparisons. No annual susceptibility differences exceeding this threshold were observed for the other species. Resistance-phenotype and susceptibility-profile selection criteria identified 468 MDR and 278 XDR P. aeruginosa isolates. Of these, 90 (19.2%) of the MDR and 53 (19.1%) of the XDR isolates were not captured by first-isolate selection. In the broader stratification dataset, stratification-first processing increased first-isolate retention by 21.2% for blood specimens and 11.2% for inpatients. These findings show that modest changes in cumulative susceptibility can coexist with incomplete representation of resistant phenotypes. In conclusion, phenotype- and AST-profile-based selection capture additional resistance information beyond first-isolate selection, despite modest differences in cumulative susceptibility. Clinical validation is needed before their use to guide empirical therapy.

title: Pioneering Hybrid Genome Assemblies of Fusarium graminearum and Fusarium avenaceum from Indian Wheat: Insights into Virulence Frameworks and Genome Evolution
content: Fusarium head blight (FHB), primarily caused by various species of Fusarium, is a destructive disease of wheat that reduces yield and contaminates grain with mycotoxins. The present study reports high-quality hybrid genome assemblies for two Indian wheat isolates, Fusarium graminearum strain TNW1 and Fusarium avenaceum strain DMW8, representing the first genome-scale comparative study of FHB associated Fusarium isolates infectious on wheat from India. Both Indian isolates retained conserved Fusarium secondary metabolite clusters, including aurofusarin, chrysogine, clavaric acid, koraiol, orcinol/orsellinic acid, and oxyjavanicin, while exhibiting distinct species-associated biosynthetic profiles. TNW1 contained zearalenone and DON-related biosynthetic clusters, whereas DMW8 contained beauvericin and other species -associated clusters, highlighting differences in predicted biosynthetic potential between the two Fusarium species. Notably, both genomes showed relatively low transposable-element (TE) content compared with their respective species groups, with TEs occupying 0.96% of the TNW1 genome and 1.55% of the DMW8 genome. RIP-associated genomic coverage was also comparatively low, at 20.01% and 22.38%, respectively. TE insertion analysis identified predominantly reference-associated insertions, with two candidate non-reference insertions detected in DMW8. Gene-family analyses revealed greater duplication and expansion contraction dynamics in DMW8 than in TNW1. Together, these findings highlight differences in predicted genomic features, secondary metabolite biosynthetic potential, and gene family composition between the two Indian isolates, providing genomic resources for future investigations of Fusarium biology and wheat pathogen interactions.

title: How good a predictor the in vitro antibiogram is, of in vivo antibiotic efficacy? An in vitro - in vivo integrated approach
content: Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing, particularly the disc diffusion assay (DDA), provides a convenient means of assessing bacterial susceptibility to antibiotics. However, its ability to predict antibiotic efficacy in an infected host remains uncertain. This study investigated the relationship between DDA-derived inhibition zones and host-protective antibiotic activity using Caenorhabditis elegans infection models involving three bacterial pathogens: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Clostridioides difficile. A total of 42 antibiotics were evaluated through DDA, while a separate panel of 75 antibiotics was screened using an automated C. elegans infection assay. Twenty-six antibiotics common to both panels were selected for comparative analysis. Gnotobiotic L3-L4 stage worms were challenged with individual pathogens in the presence of each antibiotic at a fixed concentration of 9.6 microgram/mL. Worm activity was quantified at 24, 48, and 72 h using an automated worm tracker system, with appropriate health, infection, vehicle, and antibiotic-toxicity controls. Overall, DDA-derived zone of inhibition (ZOI) diameters showed weak-to-moderate, pathogen- and time-dependent correlations with worm activity. At 24 h, Pearson's correlation coefficients ranged from -0.20 to 0.31 across the three pathogen-host systems, while at 48 h they ranged from -0.009 to 0.49. Notably, antibiotic rankings based on DDA and host-protective activity differed considerably. For example, against C. difficile, imipenem produced the largest inhibition zone (41 mm) but failed to protect worms at 24 and 48 h, whereas tobramycin, despite producing a smaller inhibition zone (26 mm), exhibited the highest early worm activity. Similar discrepancies were observed with the other pathogens. These findings demonstrate that DDA-derived susceptibility profiles do not consistently predict antibiotic-mediated protection in an infected host. The C. elegans model may therefore serve as a complementary whole-organism screening platform, providing additional functional information for prioritizing antimicrobial agents beyond conventional in vitro susceptibility testing.

title: Intracellular spirochete integrates into a chemosynthetic micro-consortium of a deep-sea vent mussel
content: Animal-microbe interactions comprise a diverse functional landscape, spanning pathogenic to mutualistic outcomes across extracellular and intracellular niches. Within this context, spirochetes are predominantly documented as extracellular associates or transient pathogens, leaving stable, functional endosymbiosis within animal cells unverified. Here, we report the discovery of an intracellular consortium comprising a spirochete and a primary sulfur-oxidizing bacterium within gill bacteriocytes of the deep-sea hydrothermal vent mussel Gigantidas horikoshii. Combining three-dimensional ultrastructural imaging, spatial histology, and multi-omics analyses, we characterize the intracellular spatial architecture and metabolic integration of this system. Both bacteria co-reside within a closed, membrane-bound network of interconnected chambers, where the spirochete is distributed across compartments and occasionally extends across host cell boundaries. Multi-omics profiling uncovers metabolic cooperation between the two bacteria: while the sulfur-oxidizing bacterium provides autotrophic primary production, the spirochete actively transcribes pathways for reactive oxygen species scavenging and organic acid assimilation, likely mitigating localized oxidative stress and acidosis. Coupled with its motility machinery and an expanded repertoire of host-interaction factors, these physiological traits suggest that the spirochete acts as an active stabilizer of the shared intracellular microenvironment. Together, these findings reveal that spirochetes can establish a stable, functional micro-consortium with chemosynthetic bacteria within animal cells, refining the recognized landscape of animal-microbe interactions and illuminating mechanisms linking mutualistic endosymbiosis and intracellular infections.

title: Effect of neuB deletion on biofilm formation and extracellular electron transfer in Geobacter sulfurreducens
content: The extracellular matrix of Geobacter sulfurreducens biofilms is primarily composed of proteins and exopolysaccharides. The extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) matrix provides the structural scaffold necessary to facilitate extracellular electron transfer (EET); however, the specific role of its carbohydrate components remains unexplored. Sialic acids are a class of carbohydrate derivates that can modulate extracellular matrix stability in bacteria. N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac), the most common sialic acid, is primarily synthesized by NeuB. We hypothesized that the neuB gene homolog in G. sulfurreducens (gsu1970), putatively involved in Neu5Ac synthesis, plays a key role in EPS organization and EET performance. Deletion of neuB reduced insoluble Fe(III) oxide reduction by approximately 91%. Furthermore, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) revealed that the {Delta}neuB strain formed significantly less dense EPS matrices on both hematite and fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) electrodes. Interestingly, bioelectrochemical analysis of FTO anodes showed that the mutant produced a 3-fold higher current density and exhibited a more negative open-circuit potential than the wild-type strain. It is important to mention that this enhanced performance on FTO is linked to a significant upregulation of omcS, however, more specific experiments need to be performed to establish a definitive causal relationship between omcS transcription levels and the observed bioelectrochemical enhancement. This transcriptional change was not observed during growth on hematite. Our results suggest that neuB expression contributes to maintaining the structural integrity of the WGA-reactive glycoconjugates within the EPS matrix during insoluble iron reduction. Conversely, its absence is associated with a compensatory upregulation of omcS on FTO electrodes. Overall, this study highlights the potential importance of putative sialic acids-related biosynthetic pathways in Desulfuromonadia, showing that alteration of EPS carbohydrate biosynthetic genes can markedly influence both iron reduction and the performance of electroactive biofilms behavior.

title: A metacommunity of complex microbial communities shows high spatial synchrony, ecological memory, gradual succession and invasion resistance
content: Complex microbial communities are increasingly applied in biotechnological and health-related environments, yet maintaining their diversity and relative community composition over extended periods remains challenging. While dispersal can counteract the divergence of spatially separated communities, it remains unclear whether controlled mass transfer can sustain compositional synchrony in highly diverse communities over extended periods, whether this synchrony persist after dispersal is interrupted, and how robust such communities are to invasion. Here, we investigate these questions using a loop-design reactor (LDR) comprising five local wastewater microbial communities connected by controlled mass transfer. The experiment covered multiple rounds of alternating mass transfer and insular phases over a time frame of 318 days, different mass transfer intensities, and the introduction of defined microbial invaders. Community dynamics were monitored at a high temporal resolution by single-cell flow cytometry and complemented by metagenomic analyses of selected samples to characterize taxonomic compositions and functional potential. A Bray-Curtis-based Synchrony Index revealed that controlled mass transfer established high compositional synchrony among five local communities, which persisted for more than 150 generations. Although the community structures underwent gradual succession, the local communities remained synchronized, demonstrating parallel rather than divergent temporal trajectories. Interruption of dispersal initially promote divergence, whereas during later insular phases high compositional similarity persisted in the absence of mass transfer, consistent with ecological memory. Introduced microbial species failed to establish within resident communities, indicating high invasion resistance. Community functional potential remained largely stable throughout the experiment, although phosphorus accumulation failed during phases of high mass transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled mass transfer can maintain long-term spatial synchrony of complex microbial communities while allowing gradual community succession. Repeated connectivity promoted compositional similarity beyond periods of active dispersal while maintaining invasion resistance and functional stability, highlighting controlled dispersal as a promising community-level strategy for managing complex microbial communities.

title: LuxS Inactivation Increases Antibiotic Susceptibility and Impairs Genetic Competence in Streptococcus pneumoniae
content: The LuxS enzyme participates in bacterial metabolism and produces the precursor of autoinducer-2 (AI-2), a signaling molecule implicated in bacterial stress responses and genetic competence. Although LuxS/AI-2 has been associated with antibiotic responses in other streptococci, its contribution to antibiotic susceptibility in Streptococcus pneumoniae remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of LuxS in pneumococcal survival during exposure to erythromycin and ampicillin and examined whether supplementation with 4,5-dihydroxy-2,3-pentanedione (DPD), the precursor of AI-2, could alleviate the effects of luxS inactivation. The {Delta}luxS mutant exhibited significantly greater reductions in viable cell counts than the wild type following antibiotic exposure, even after accounting for differences in baseline growth. Supplementation with 50 nM DPD significantly improved mutant survival during exposure to both antibiotics. We further investigated the contribution of LuxS/AI-2 to genetic competence, a phenotype previously associated with luxS inactivation. The mutant exhibited reduced transformation efficiency, which was significantly improved by DPD supplementation, although recovery remained partial. Together, these findings provide evidence that LuxS contributes to pneumococcal survival during antibiotic exposure and demonstrate that exogenous DPD can partially compensate for the effects of luxS inactivation on antibiotic responses and genetic transformation. These results extend our understanding of LuxS/AI-2-associated phenotypes in S. pneumoniae.

title: Reconstitution in JCVI-syn3B suggests the roles of the Spiroplasma Fibril protein (Sfibril) in swimming
content: Spiroplasma, wall-less helical bacteria of the class Mollicutes, swim without flagella by shifting the handedness of their helical body. This motility is driven by an internal ribbon composed of actin-superfamily MreB proteins (SMreB) and the Spiroplasma-specific Fibril protein (Sfibril), which accounts for nearly half of the ribbon mass. However, because helical shape and swimming have been reconstituted with SMreBs alone, the role of Sfibril has remained unclear. Here, we expressed Fibril from Spiroplasma eriocheiris under its native promoter in the minimal synthetic bacterium JCVI-syn3B (syn3), in which swimming had been reconstituted with SMreB proteins, and analyzed cell morphology and swimming. Sfibril formed filaments with chained ring units in syn3 cells and, by itself, induced cell elongation and left-handed helical shape. Elongated cells expressing Sfibril recovered their length after hypo-osmotic shock, indicating that Sfibril confers morphological robustness. In cells expressing SMreB4 and SMreB5 from Spiroplasma, Sfibril increased the fraction of helical and motile cells, extended the distance of continuous kink propagation, reduced cell bending, and increased traveling distance. In addition, Sfibril altered the handedness of SMreB5-driven helices from exclusively right-handed to a mixture of right- and left-handed. These results suggest that Sfibril is not essential for helicity shift but stabilizes the cell body and supports efficient, processive helicity shifts.

title: Charting the Expansive Outer Membrane β-Barrel Landscape in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
content: Outer-membrane beta-barrel (OMBB) proteins are central to Gram-negative bacterial physiology, mediating nutrient acquisition and secretion while shaping host interactions and antimicrobial permeability. Yet tools to catalog the diversity and functional potential of the OMBB proteome in these bacteria remain incompletely defined. Here, we combine proteome-scale structure prediction analysis and experimental validation to systematically map the OMBB proteome of the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We identify 105 proteins containing predicted OMBB domains with 8-26 beta-strands, substantially expanding the repertoire across major structural classes and revealing previously unrecognised domain architectures. Comparison with experimentally defined structures shows that prediction accurately captures global barrel architecture but systematically overestimates beta-strand continuity and underrepresents flexible extracellular loops, key determinants of molecular recognition. We then defined the cryo-EM structures of PA2590 and PA3535 (EprS), confirming their predicted functions as a TonB-dependent transporter and an autotransporter, respectively. Using structural prediction, we also identified the phospholipase A1-like activity in the uncharacterized autotransporter PA4579, linking a predicted catalytic site to function. Together, our findings expand the structural and functional landscape of the P. aeruginosa OMBB proteome and establish a generalizable framework for converting proteome-scale structural predictions into experimentally testable mechanisms, enabling discovery of functions hidden within poorly annotated outer-membrane proteomes.

title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
content: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

title: Compartment-associated filtering and environmental gradients shape fungal communities in arid Artemisia species
content: Plant-associated fungal communities are shaped by interactions among host, environmental conditions, and compartment-specific filtering processes, yet the relative importance of these drivers remains poorly understood in arid and semi-arid ecosystems. We investigated fungal communities associated with three Artemisia species (Artemisia herba-alba Asso., Artemisia mesatlantica Maire and Artemisia negrei L.), including Moroccan endemics, across bulk soil, rhizosphere, root, and shoot compartments using ITS amplicon sequencing, culture-dependent isolation, and ecological analyses. Fungal community composition differed significantly among compartments (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.08, P = 0.012), whereas alpha diversity showed limited variation. Taxonomic profiles revealed compartment-associated shifts, with recurrent fungal genera concentrated in belowground compartments and a higher proportion of unclassified taxa in shoots. Core microbiome analyses identified overlapping fungal taxa between rhizosphere and root communities. Soil physicochemical gradients were associated with fungal community composition, and structural equation modeling indicated significant associations with both environmental variables and plant compartments. Source-tracking analysis attributed approximately 99.4% of root community composition to rhizosphere sources, whereas shoot communities showed contributions from both roots (60%) and the rhizosphere (39%). Culture-dependent isolation recovered 21 fungal isolates, with five genera shared between cultivation and sequencing datasets. Together, these findings reveal compartment-associated fungal community restructuring along the soil?plant continuum and highlight the complementary contributions of environmental conditions, plant-associated habitats, and cultivation-based characterization to understanding fungal microbiomes in arid ecosystems.

title: Host HSP90 mimicry by a parasite effector triggers mitochondrial membrane shedding
content: The outer mitochondrial membrane mediates critical host defenses against intracellular pathogens. How microbes manipulate this compartment remains poorly understood. Here, we found that the human parasite Toxoplasma gondii remodels host mitochondrial membranes through molecular mimicry of HSP90 chaperones. Cryo-electron microscopy analyses showed that the parasite effector TgMAF1 binds the same specialized clamp domain of the mitochondrial import receptor TOM70 as chaperones of the HSP70/90 family. Biochemical and comparative genomics analyses demonstrate that this mimicry arose through the neofunctionalization of the TgMAF1 C-terminus from an ancestral paralog incapable of TOM70 binding. In molecular dynamics simulations, complexed TgMAF1-TOM70 triggered the formation of higher order assemblies that induced local membrane curvature. These findings uncover a previously unknown host subversion strategy and establish molecular mimicry of a chaperone as a mechanism for pathogen-driven remodeling of the host OMM.

title: Tissue-specific genomic and transcriptomic dynamics of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in the Pacific oyster Magallana gigas revealed by long-read sequencing
content: Ostreid herpesvirus 1 (OsHV-1) causes recurrent mass mortality of juvenile Pacific oysters (Magallana gigas) worldwide, yet its lytic cycle remains poorly characterized in vivo. In the absence of a permissive cell line, most studies have relied on intramuscular injection, which bypasses the natural route of infection, or on primary haemocyte cultures, which cannot capture tissue-level host-virus interactions. In addition, gene expression studies have relied on short-read sequencing, which fragments transcription units and cannot resolve complex transcriptional architectures. Long-read sequencing has recently revealed abundant overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts in other herpesviruses, but whether OsHV-1 shares this complexity, and how its transcriptional program varies across host tissues during natural infection, remains unknown. Here, we exposed naive oysters to OsHV-1 by bath exposure and combined long-read genomic and transcriptomic sequencing of gills, mantle, digestive gland and adductor muscle at increasing levels of infection. OsHV-1 genomes were assembled directly from infected tissues, and intra-host viral diversity was structured by host rather than tissue. We identified 410 unspliced viral transcripts, including overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts. The viral transcriptional program was largely conserved across tissues and resembled that previously described in haemocytes in vitro. In the host, infection triggered a response shared by all tissues, but earlier and stronger in the gills and mantle. Together, these results provide the first long-read view of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in its natural host.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterisation of Penicillium melinii, a plant growth-promoting root endophyte that remains effective under salt stress
content: Penicillium melinii isolate 2 is a root endophyte of Arabidopsis thaliana that promotes the growth of different plant species, but the genetic basis of this activity remains unknown. Here we combined Oxford Nanopore long reads and Illumina short reads to obtain a high-quality, near-chromosome-level assembly of 29.39 Mb in six nuclear scaffolds, two of them telomere-capped at both ends (97.6% complete BUSCOs), together with, to our knowledge, the first complete mitochondrial genome reported for the species (26,730 bp). Annotation predicted 9,566 protein-coding genes. Compared with two other plant growth-promoting Penicillium species, P. bilaiae and P. citrinum, the isolate encodes fewer carbohydrate-active enzymes, biosynthetic gene clusters and candidate effectors, pointing to an overall reduction of the secreted repertoire. In vitro, the isolate grew significantly above the control on 63 of 95 carbon sources, mainly carbohydrates, and was positive for 7 of 11 plant growth-promoting traits: siderophore production, phosphate and zinc solubilisation, ammonia release, and urease, proteolytic and lipolytic activities. Radial growth was unaffected by NaCl up to 150 mM and persisted at 1 M, whereas conidiation was more salt-sensitive. On medium containing 100 mM NaCl, inoculation increased Arabidopsis shoot fresh weight and root system growth. Genome mining identified candidate genes for these traits. Together, these results provide a genomic and phenotypic basis for evaluating P. melinii isolate 2 as an inoculant for saline soils and identify candidate determinants for functional validation.

title: Defining host factors required for dengue virus NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability and endothelial glycocalyx layer disruption
content: Dengue virus (DENV) is a mosquito-borne positive-sense RNA virus belonging to the Flaviviridae family that poses a significant threat to global health. Clinical manifestations of DENV infection range from febrile to severe disease characterized by vascular leakage. The secreted DENV nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) contributes to endothelial dysfunction through interactions with endothelial cells, leading to disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx and intercellular junction complexes (IJC). However, host factors required for NS1-triggered endothelial dysfunction are not well understood. It is also unclear if NS1 highjacks different host factors and signaling pathways for glycocalyx and IJC disruption. To address these questions, we used a targeted genetic approach to identify host factors required either for NS1-triggered endothelial glycocalyx layer (EGL) disruption, as assessed by immunofluorescence assays, or for IJC disruption, as measured by transendothelial electrical resistance. After demonstrating the decoupled nature of EGL and IJC disruption in our models, we genetically depleted host factors with known roles in regulating endothelial barrier function and/or involvement in NS1 pathogenesis, including heparanase, cathepsin L, sialidases, and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and {beta}-catenin signaling pathways. Our results reveal a complex genetic landscape where NS1-induced disruption of EGL and IJCs involves both unique and shared host factors. Further, our data identify a direct role for {beta}-catenin in NS1-induced endothelial dysfunction in vitro and in vivo. Overall, this work advances understanding of host factors required for DENV NS1-triggered endothelial dysfunction, revealing distinct intracellular pathways that are highjacked by NS1 to modulate barrier function, thus providing new insights into dengue-associated vascular leak.

title: Genomic reassessment of Enterobacter species and subspecies
content: Enterobacter species are opportunistic pathogens whose identification is complicated by closely related lineages and changing species nomenclature. We reassessed 1,074 public genomes using average nucleotide identity (ANI), type-strain comparisons and phylogenies based on conserved markers, genome alignments and k-mers. Among 1,070 genomes included in the classification comparison, 123 changed species or subspecies membership relative to NCBI labels, 499 changed names following revisions to species boundaries or ranks, and 69 previously unnamed genomes received species assignments. The oharae, steigerwaltii, xiangfangensis and hoffmannii lineages formed an expanded Enterobacter xiangfangensis, separate from the lineage containing the E. hormaechei type. We propose five transferred combinations: E. xiangfangensis subsp. oharae comb. nov., E. xiangfangensis subsp. steigerwaltii comb. nov., E. xiangfangensis subsp. hoffmannii comb. nov., E. roggenkampii subsp. quasiroggenkampii comb. nov. and E. chengduensis subsp. rongchengensis comb. nov. We also describe the corresponding type subspecies, E. xiangfangensis subsp. xiangfangensis comb. nov., E. roggenkampii subsp. roggenkampii comb. nov. and E. chengduensis subsp. chengduensis comb. nov., and emend the descriptions of E. xiangfangensis and E. hormaechei. E. dykesii and E. quasimori are treated as later heterotypic synonyms of E. asburiae and E. mori, respectively. Within E. xiangfangensis subsp. hoffmannii, we define 25 genomic groups (genomovars) at 99.5% ANI. Conflicting tree relationships leave the position of E. ludwigii and the branching order of the hoffmannii-associated types unresolved. We developed Pterobacter to apply the revised classifications to assemblies, using alignment-based ANI near the species boundary and withholding assignments when the reference evidence is insufficient.

title: In vivo crosslinking and cryo-EM analyses suggest a revised model of conjugative pilus biogenesis
content: Bacterial conjugation requires elaboration of a conjugative pilus by membrane-embedded transport machineries known as Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SSs). Recent structural findings suggested a model of conjugative pilus biogenesis in which the pilus is assembled from the VirB6-base of the T4SS Stalk, while the VirB5-apex is projected at the pilus tip. In this study, we show that in vivo crosslinking of these two Stalk segments within the R388 T4SS has only a modest effect on conjugative transfer efficiency, inconsistent with them separating during pilus elaboration. Combined with cryo-electron microscopy analyses of the homologous pKM101 T4SS, this leads us to propose a revised model, in which the sixfold-symmetrical inner membrane complex of the T4SS serves directly as a base for assembly of the fivefold-symmetrical pilus. The resulting symmetry mismatch is resolved by the sequential incorporation of pilus subunits at a continuously repositioning gap at the base of the nascent pilus. This revised model answers the long-standing question of how T4SSs accommodate a central symmetry mismatch during a crucial process of bacterial conjugation underpinning horizontal gene transfer.

title: Modular evolution and functional divergence of the Pseudomonas Fit toxin locus
content: The insecticidal Fit toxin is well known for its role in insect interactions in plant-associated Pseudomonas. However, its presence in non-entomopathogenic Pseudomonas, including the marine fish pathogen Pseudomonas baetica, raises questions about its evolutionary history and functional diversification. Here, we investigate the fit locus across the Pseudomonas fluorescens species complex using comparative genomic, structural, and functional approaches. Phylogenomic analyses support several ancient acquisitions of the fit gene cluster, followed by Pseudomonas subgroup-specific chromosomal integration and diversification of the toxin FitD and the sensor kinase FitF. Although P. baetica carries a fit operon, it showed no oral toxicity toward insect larvae. This lack of toxicity is associated with resistance to gut colonization by the commensal Enterobacter sp. Direct hemolymph injection also failed to reveal toxicity and the Fit activity in P. baetica is limited by the absence of fit promoter activation in insect hemolymph. Finally, in a zebrafish model, FitD is dispensable for P. baetica, which causes severe systemic infection through other virulence mechanisms. Nonetheless, FitD contributes to the virulence of P. protegens CHA0 in zebrafish, thereby extending its effects from insects to vertebrate hosts. Together, these findings highlight the evolutionary and regulatory plasticity of the fit locus and show how an ancestral toxin system can acquire different functional roles in bacteria adapted to distinct ecological niches.

title: Microbial communities do not drive chronic Quercus spp. decline but exacerbate tree weakening: a multi kingdom soil root continuum study in Chantilly forest
content: In European forests, several species of Quercus spp. are currently subject to major declines, defined as a slow deterioration of the tree caused by the interaction of abiotic and biotic factors, in which drought often plays an important role. The decline of holobionts, like oak trees, may have consequences that extend beyond the tree physiology. To better understand the interactions between chronic oak decline and oak associated microbial communities and their functional consequences, we analysed the bacterial, fungal and oomycetes communities in the bulk soil, the rhizosphere and the roots of pairs of declining and non-declining oaks in the Chantilly forest (France) by a metabarcoding approach. Chosen pairs of oaks were distributed on contrasted soil types to determine the influence of soil properties on the tree-microbe interactions during decline. Rhizospheric soil microbial enzymatic activities were also measured to assess the effect of oak decline on microbial-driven nutrient cycling activities. We observed a differential response of microbial communities to decline as a function of the kingdom. Bacteria were more sensitive to oak decline, particularly in the bulk soil and on podzol soil. By contrast, the composition of fungal communities was overall little impacted by oak decline, no matter the soil type, but their functional abilities may be partly impaired. Laccase and chitinase activities were reduced in the rhizospheric soil of declining oaks growing on brunisol and luvisol. Furthermore, the proportion of ectomycorrhizal fungi with high biomass exploration types were reduced by half in the roots of declining trees while the pathogenic Phytophthora cactorum and P. plurivora were more frequent. Altogether, our data suggest that chronic oak decline affects directly and indirectly the composition and functional abilities of oak associated microbial communities in a soil dependent manner.

title: A host-pathogen tug-of-war over migrasome biogenesis in Vibrio cholerae infection
content: Migrasomes are extracellular organelles implicated in cell communication and immune signaling, yet their induction by bacterial toxins and functional consequences during infection remains unknown. Here, we show that Vibrio cholerae infection induces non-canonical migracytosis in multiple cell types through the MARTX toxin. The actin cross-linking domain (ACD) promotes cell contraction and retraction fiber formation, while the /{beta}-hydrolase domain (ABH) collaborates with actin-polymerization machinery to support migrasome maturation. The Rho inactivation domain (RID) covalently modifies multiple Rho/Ras GTPases, and its absence yields oversized membrane blebs (large vesicles) enriched in endoplasmic reticulum, lipid droplets, and pro-inflammatory chemokines compared with wild-type migrasomes. In an infant mouse model, RID-deficient V. cholerae exhibits impaired intestinal colonization and elevated host chemokine transcription. These findings establish that MARTX-driven migrasome formation is not merely a byproduct of cytoskeleton damage, but represents a coordinated, domain-specific reprogramming of host membrane dynamics with implications for host-pathogen interplay.

title: Barley malting for beer production - Impact of temperature on the barley-associated microbiome, malt quality and energy expenditure.
content: Malt production is an energy-intensive process, and elevated germination temperatures have been proposed to shorten it and thereby lower the energy demand. However, the effect of elevated temperatures on the barley-associated microbiome remains unexplored. Using a multi-metaomics approach, we explored microbial composition and function in four barley varieties malted at pilot scale under standard industrial conditions (IMR) and an accelerated regime using higher temperatures (AMR). AMR yielded malts with excellent friability, resulting in adequate wort viscosity and saccharification times despite lower amylase and beta-glucanase activities, with no effect on proteolysis modulation. AMR substantially shifted microbial community composition. Fungi, notably Alternaria alternata, contributed xylan- and beta-glucan-degrading enzymes, whereas abundant detection of the strong biofilm former Pseudomonas coincided with impaired wort filtration. Electrical energy use was lowered in AMR by approximately 5-9%, mainly through lower humidification and cooling demand. Malting with increased temperatures thus promises high-quality malt with time and energy savings, provided that the malting microbiome is monitored and controlled.

title: Agricultural Management Restructures the Functional Composition of Soil Fungal Communities Across Tropical Landscapes
content: Soil fungal communities regulate key ecosystem processes, yet the extent to which agricultural management restructures fungal diversity across tropical landscapes remains poorly understood. We characterized fungal communities in 124 soil samples collected from natural vegetation, organic farms, and non-organic farms across four Honduran departments using internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2) and small-subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU) metabarcoding. Land use was associated with Bray-Curtis community composition after adjusting for geography, sequencing run, and read depth (ITS2 R2 = 0.06, SSU R2 = 0.05, both P < 0.001). Community dissimilarity increased with geographic distance within each land-use category (pooled Mantel r = 0.30 for ITS2 and 0.19 for SSU), and land-use categories shared 2.0-7.1 times as many fungal features as expected (all adjusted P < 0.001). For ITS2, total richness in non-organic soils was 18% lower than in natural soils and 25% lower than in organic soils. Across both markers, land-use restricted richness was 58-85% lower in non-organic soils than in natural and organic soils. In addition, symbiotrophs in non-organic soils were 18-20% of that in natural soils, while saprotroph and pathotroph responses varied by marker. Together, these findings demonstrate that agricultural management is associated with changes in fungal diversity, occupancy, and predicted trophic composition without eliminating the geographic structure or extensive taxonomic overlap of regional communities.

title: The dynamic expressome of Pseudomonas putida: condition-dependent remodelling of the RNA polymerase interactome
content: As in many bacteria, the 2{beta}{beta}'{omega} core RNA polymerase (RNAP) of Pseudomonas putida interacts in vivo with sigma factors, transcriptional regulators and auxiliary proteins whose relative abundance varies with the physiological state. Here, we used an in vivo immunocapture approach to examine condition-dependent changes in the RNAP interactome of P. putida KT2440. His-, Myc- and E-tags were separately introduced at the C-terminus of RpoC ({beta}'), a permissive, surface-exposed site accessible to cognate antibodies. Myc-tagged RNAP complexes were immunocaptured with magnetic beads and analyzed by LC-ESI-MS/MS and computational methods. The results revealed condition-dependent association of the RNAP core (RpoA, RpoB, RpoC and RpoZ) with distinct pools of sigma factors, as well as ribosomal proteins, RNA-processing factors and metabolic enzymes. Nutrient starvation, nutrient-rich growth and high temperature altered the composition and relative representation of RNAP-associated proteins. Despite the limited physiological conditions examined, our results support a model in which RNAP acts as a dynamic organizational hub of the bacterial expressome, integrating transcription with translation, RNA maturation and central metabolism.

title: Taxogenomic resolution of the 16SrIII (X-disease) group: elevation of Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni-related strains to species rank and proposal of three novel Candidatus species Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov., Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov. and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov.
content: Alongside the proposal of the taxon Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni for 16SrIII (X-Disease) group, the designation Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni-related strains was proposed for strains that were closely related to the taxon based on multilocus sequence characterization. However, recent genome-based studies have created taxonomic ambiguity by either assigning related strains directly to the taxon Ca. P. pruni or separating them into more than one genomic cluster without formal taxonomic classification or proposing new taxon for new divergent strains. In this study, we sequenced genomes of the pecan bunchy top phytoplasma (PBT), previously designated a Ca. P. pruni-related strain, initially to confirm the pathogen in an Oklahoma pecan orchard. Phylogenomic comparisons with previously sequenced Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni strains revealed four well-supported taxonomic groups based on average nucleotide identity, digital DNA-DNA hybridization, and phylogenetic analyses, with different host ecologies consistent with International Research Programme on Comparative Mycoplasmology (IRPCM) guidelines for assigning new taxon. Accordingly, we propose a reclassification of Ca.
