P. pruni and related strains into four species: Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni, representing the taxon associated with X-disease phytoplasma; three proposed new Candidatus species including Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov, Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov. The study provides comparative-genomic insights into these taxonomic groups that support their evolution.

title: Three novel deep-branching orphan protist lineages from the marine rare biosphere
content: Metabarcoding has transformed our view of marine protist communities, yet many sequences in environmental surveys are not assigned confident taxonomic identity. These taxonomically ambiguous sequences may include lineages that are not within any known eukaryotic supergroup, which we refer to here as orphan lineages. These orphan lineages matter beyond taxonomy-based community analyses, because they can help us understand early eukaryotic evolution. Here we used phylogenetic inferences and sequence similarity networks (SSNs) of long-read metabarcoding data of the ribosomal operon (18S-28S rDNA) to identify three novel phylum-level orphan lineages. We designate these lineages Deep Orphan Lineages 1-3 (DEEPOLs) and show that they are exclusively marine and part of the rare biosphere, yet ecologically distinct: DEEPOL1 is a cosmopolitan generalist, DEEPOL2 a conditionally rare lineage capable of local polar blooms, and DEEPOL3 a non-polar lineage with a tendency toward the dark ocean. For DEEPOL2, lineage-specific digital PCR (dPCR) combined with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) provides the first in situ visualization of these cells, revealing small, flagellated, and morphologically inconspicuous protists. Together, our results show that substantial diversity remains hidden among rare lineages, and that long-read sequencing combined with targeted molecular and microscopy approaches offers a first step toward linking orphan sequences to organisms and their evolution and ecological roles.

title: Single-cell genomics reveals genomic and functional differentiation between freshwater and saline Achromatium populations.
content: Giant sulfur bacteria of the genus Achromatium reportedly contain extensive genomic diversity within individual cells. Most genomic data (35 assemblies) come from freshwater populations obtained from Lake Stechlin, Germany, alongside four single-cell genomes from a salt marsh and saline mineral springs. Here, we characterize marine Achromatium from mangrove sediments in Guadeloupe and compare them with freshwater and saline references. Microscopy, elemental mapping, and Raman spectroscopy revealed calcium-rich inclusions, and intracellular elemental sulfur as previously described for this genus. Scanning electron microscopy revealed two cell-size morphotypes. We generated eleven single-cell, four mixed-cell, and two metagenomic binned assemblies from Guadeloupe mangrove. Divergent copies of conserved marker genes revealed extensive intracellular genomic diversity in individual cells of both morphotypes. Multigene phylogenies provided separation between freshwater references and most genomes from saline environments, including the Guadeloupe population. Gene presence-absence analyses further revealed differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe and Stechlin cells across five functional annotation categories including PFAM, KEGG Orthologs, and CAZymes. Differences in genes associated with osmotic regulation, ion transport, carbohydrate degradation, and secretion systems suggest variation in functional potential related to environmental adaptation, interactions and resource utilization. No significant differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe morphotypes were found. Together, these marine genomes reveal genomic and functional differentiation from freshwater populations and suggest that intracellular diversity does not erase freshwater/saline population boundaries.

title: Depolymerases unmask a conserved receptor to enable phage control of capsulated Acinetobacter baumannii
content: We characterized bacteriophage Abs1 that infects clinical Acinetobacter baumannii isolates via the highly prevalent and conserved outer-membrane protein receptor, OprC. However, phage Abs1 is unable to infect capsulated A. baumannii strains as the capsule prevents phage access to its underlying receptor. To circumvent this, we combined phage Abs1 with recombinant depolymerases targeting the major A. baumannii capsule types. In a murine bacteremia model, this combination significantly reduced bacterial burden caused by diverse, capsulated A. baumannii strains.

title: Choosing between Glycolysis and Cholera: identifying glycolipid- and enzyme-based markers of extracellular vesicles in non-model organisms
content: The lack of universal markers for extracellular vesicles (EVs) is delaying progress in the field, especially research using non-model organisms. To develop effective options for the detection of EVs, we explored glycolipid-based and protein-based markers. In this study, we show that cholera toxin subunit B (CTxb), which targets the glycosphingolipid GM1 in vertebrates, also binds to EVs from various non-model organisms enabling detection. However, whilst CTxb selectively detect EVs from cell culture and parasite media, it is unsuitable for complex biofluids, such as serum and plasma due to cross-reactivity with high- and low-density lipoproteins. Additionally, we show that the universally conserved glycolytic enzyme enolase is found in EVs from phylogenetically distant species. Multiple highly conserved regions exist across human and several representative non-model organism orthologues, enabling detection of EVs from non-model organism using antibodies against human enolase. Furthermore, the conserved enzymatic activity of enolase enables detection of EVs using an enzymatic assay. Together CTxb and enolase provide a tandem approach for detection of EVs from non-model organisms by targeting different, conserved components of EVs.

title: Enhancing violacein production in an Antarctic bacterial strain: New opportunities for biomedical use
content: Violacein is a valuable bioactive metabolite produced by diverse bacteria, including the Antarctic isolate Janthinobacterium sp. UV13. Despite its broad therapeutic potential, large-scale production in native producers is hindered by low yields and the concurrent synthesis of exopolysaccharides, which increases downstream processing complexity and costs. This study employed a sequential statistical approach to optimize culture parameters, enhancing violacein productivity while minimizing exopolysaccharides production in UV13. The methodology included carbon and nitrogen source screening, a Plackett Burman design and a concentration response optimization, followed by chemical inducers evaluation. Results demonstrated that sucrose was an effective carbon source (violacein yield: 32.75 mg/L). Inorganic nitrogen significantly favored violacein synthesis (yield: 28 mg/L, p < 0.05) over organic alternatives which reduced violacein yields 3.4 to 4.2 fold. A single factor central composite design of ammonium sulfate concentration yielded a formulation producing 75.8 mg/L of violacein with an exopolysaccharide titer of 0.91 mg/L. Furthermore, tryptophan was the better inducer, increasing violacein production 2.2 fold (p < 0.05) while simultaneously decreasing exopolysaccharides formation 4.5 fold. The new formulated medium significantly outperformed previously reported conditions, demonstrating that parameter manipulation unlocks UV13 biosynthetic potential for scalable violacein production.

title: Decline and extirpation of birds in a tropical Asian grassland ecosystem over the past century
content: Grasslands are facing unprecedented habitat loss due to settler-driven agriculture during colonial expansion, conversion to tree plantations, misclassification as wastelands, absorption into megadevelopment projects, and insufficient response to climate change. Globally, grassland birds have faced the steepest declines, with many formerly common species facing rapid decline, losing much of their original ranges. In South Asia, our knowledge of how these land-use changes in grasslands have affected birds remain scant. Natural history collections and archives are vital resources to identify historical baselines for conducting a resurvey and identifying trends in long-term biodiversity response. Yet such historical data remain insufficient in tropical regions. In this study, by compiling an unprecedented dataset of ornithological surveys from the 1900s using a diverse set of historical data, we conducted a 3-year resurvey in an Eastern Himalayan grassland first surveyed by British Ornithologist Herbert Stevens. We surveyed nine historical localities. Using a recently developed Bayesian method to calibrate modern surveys with historical museum data, we found a 70.5% decline in grassland specialist birds. We also report the local extirpation of four endemic species of grassland birds. Open habitat raptors showed a 74.9% decline, while generalist species showed an increase of 23.5% and wetland birds showed a marginal increase of 2.64%. By quantifying functional distinctiveness, a measure of morphological diversity, we find that loss of grassland species does not impact morphological and functional diversity in modern assemblage. We also find that most resurvey localities have a high number of invasive species that have completely altered these communities. Grassland specialist birds of South Asia are highly range-restricted and have specific habitat requirements; the lack of intact tall grass communities in concert with site-level disturbance pressures from grazing, conversion and fire have likely contributed to their local extirpation. Our study serves as one of the first efforts to resurvey wet grasslands of South Asia and document local-level extirpation. We also highlight the importance of museum-based research to document long-term changes for urgent conservation attention.

title: Effects of drying and milling treatments on estimates of foliar functional traits with VSWIR spectroscopy
content: Spectroscopy of dried, ground foliage is a cost-efficient measurement to estimate leaf biochemical traits in agricultural and ecological research. Drying removes water that obscures biochemical absorption features, and milling homogenizes samples, yet how drying and milling methods affect spectra and trait predictions is understudied. We compared two drying methods (oven-drying; flash-freezing then freeze-drying) and three milling methods (coarse and fine rotary milling; ball milling) using 61 individuals of 11 broadleaf and needle- or scale-leaved woody species. Mean reflectance differences between milling treatments ranged 1.7-4.6% across the full spectrum and were largest between fine and coarse rotary milling. Freeze-dried samples had on average 7.2% higher reflectance than oven-dried samples, with larger differences in broadleaf species. Bayesian ANOVAs of spectrally predicted nitrogen and calcium demonstrated that drying had the largest effect, and that fine and ball milling also shifted predictions relative to coarse milling, but all treatment effects were smaller than interspecific variation. Although the partial least squares regression models were trained on oven-dried material, freeze-dried and more finely milled samples had lower prediction error (NRMSE) than oven-dried samples. Our finding emphasize that sample processing methods should be carefully documented for studies measuring traits from foliar spectroscopy.

title: Cryptic viruses shape trophic networks after biological invasions
content: Biological invasions restructure ecological communities by bringing previously isolated organisms into contact, but the viral flow within the trophic network and its consequences have not been established. Here, we show viral exchange following the introduction of a parasitoid wasp released for classical biological control in citrus. Within a few years, viruses spread bidirectionally between native and exotic host-parasitoid trophic chains and reached a generalist hyperparasitoid at the fourth trophic level. Cohabitation and multiparasitism, two ubiquitous interactions between the two trophic chains, were sufficient for viruses to be transferred between species and maintained transgenerationally. A virus acquired by the introduced parasitoid increased its offspring production by 30%. Our results identify cryptic viruses as an overlooked dimension of biological invasions, reshaping trophic networks and the outcome of the species we deliberately introduce.

title: Will they survive? The critical status of Asiatic cheetahs in Iran
content: The Asiatic cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus), once widespread, now survives only in Iran, with its population nearing extinction. In this study, we synthesised 13 years (2012 to 2024) of monitoring data to assess demographic and spatial patterns of this critically endangered subspecies in Iran. Using extensive camera trap surveys across eight reserves, supplemented by published records of cheetah occurrences on social media, we identified 24 adult cheetahs in the Northern and Southern Landscapes. No reproduction or new individuals have been recorded in the Southern Landscape for over a decade, while the Northern Landscape supports the remaining population, likely fewer than 30 adult individuals. From 2012 to 2024, at least 38 cubs were born from eight females in the Northern Landscape, with 74.1% surviving their first year. The absence of any newly detected adults throughout the 13-year study period suggests that long-term individual-based monitoring has likely captured the entire known adult population. Asiatic cheetahs show high mobility, often crossing unprotected communal lands and a major highway, increasing mortality risks. Camera traps enabled us to effectively identify individuals but are limited for tracking fine-scale movements, underscoring the need for satellite telemetry. Roadside fencing, wildlife underpasses, habitat protection, community-based land management, and stronger anti-trafficking measures are critical to enhance survival. Genetic risks, including low population size and inbreeding, further threaten viability. These findings inform conservation strategies for endangered carnivores in arid ecosystems. Keywords: arid environment, camera trap, illegal wildlife trade, population viability, small population

title: Community responses outweigh species-level plasticity in shaping future marine forests
content: Anthropogenic ocean warming (OW) and acidification (OA) are progressively reshaping marine ecosystems, yet ecosystem-level evidence remains limited. Marine forests are foundational ecosystems that support highly productive and diverse communities. Understanding how macroalgal communities will assemble, perform and persist in future ocean conditions requires integrated evidence capturing concurrent shifts in primary productivity, species interactions, and associated macroalgal community responses. Here, we provide a multi-level approach combining laboratory experiments with field surveys to assess how Mediterranean marine macroalgal forests will respond to future warming and acidification. We used local populations from natural CO2; vents in Panarea (Aeolian Islands, Italy) and present-day pH conditions of the emblematic forest-forming species Ericaria balearica to quantify multi-level responses to future climate drivers. Specifically, we crossed temperature (present day, T+2 C, T+4 C), pH (present day pHT ~ 7.9, low pHT ~7.6), and origin population (ambient vs CO2 vents) in laboratory experiments, where we measured changes in Ericaria biomass and metabolism, as well as herbivory by the sea urchin Paracentrotus lividus. We also assessed in situ community structure by quantifying species-specific percent cover and biomass along a pH gradient. In natural CO2 vents, E. balearica biomass was greater than at ambient sites, and associated macroalgal community composition differed between pH zones. In the laboratory, across the simulated spring-summer warming period, E. balerarica biomass declined similarly in all treatments with no important effect of pH; a marginal signal suggested that vent-origin individuals retained more biomass only under present-day temperature. Sea urchin consumption was reduced under low pH and showed a weaker response to temperature. Overall, we found no clear direct impact of OWxOA on E. balearica performance but significant influence of OA on herbivory and the associated macroalgal community, indicating that ecological processes outweigh the effects at the individual or population level.

title: Resource enrichment and utilization underlie widely observed production and biomass scaling relationships
content: Broadly observed trophic scaling patterns relate the biomass of predators to the biomass of prey, and biomass to productivity. The consistency with which these patterns are observed suggests the existence of governing principles that apply across ecosystems. We present a model for the trophic interaction between phytoplankton and zooplankton that produces the scaling patterns as an emergent property of resource enrichment without invoking the influence of phenotypic or genotypic diversity on system structure. Using formulations with broad empirical support, the model incorporates processes that are common to all ecosystems: resource enrichment, feeding, growth, maintenance, and mortality. Thus, our interpretation of widely observed scaling relationships provides constraints for models that quantify the coupling between ecosystem structure and elemental cycles across terrestrial and aquatic environments.

title: Microeukaryotic indicators of freshwater ecosystem condition from a national river monitoring network
content: Microeukaryotes are a diverse and functionally important component of river biofilms, including primary producers, consumers, decomposers, and parasites and symbionts. However, their diversity is likely underestimated, and their composition, environmental drivers, and seasonal dynamics have rarely been studied at large spatial scales. Microbiological monitoring of freshwater ecosystems has historically focused almost entirely on diatoms, so the potential of the wider microbial community as indicators of river condition is unknown. Here, we used 18S rRNA gene metabarcoding of more than 1,600 biofilm samples from 700 sites across England's River Surveillance Network. We show that communities were dominated by diatoms, chlorophytes, ciliates, and fungi, and shifted from phototroph-dominated biofilms in spring towards more diverse, heterotroph-rich biofilms in autumn. Community turnover was driven by water chemistry rather than geographic distance, with alkalinity, DO, temperature, and nitrate-N among the strongest drivers of composition. Co-occurrence networks resolved assemblages of taxa with shared environmental responses, and threshold indicator taxa analysis identified ASV-level indicators of water chemistry gradients. Community change points along these gradients closely matched those reported for bacteria from the same biofilms, and several taxa declined at lower concentrations than the community as a whole, offering potential early warning of change. These findings show that the microeukaryotic community tracks water chemistry consistently across a national river network and can provide a taxonomically broad set of sensitive and interpretable indicators of river condition that complement diatom-based monitoring and emerging bacterial approaches.

title: A unifying framework for structured population dynamics in modern coexistence theory
content: Variation within populations is ubiquitous in nature, yet many models and frameworks in community ecology assume that all individuals within a population interact with the community identically. Modern coexistence theory is no exception; however, several subfields of ecology have independently been integrating coexistence theory, each asking the same underlying question: how do structured population dynamics shape coexistence outcomes? Here, I propose a unifying framework for integrating population variation into modern coexistence theory that is applicable across all fields of ecology. The application of this framework is presented in three case studies: niche overlap and fitness differences between influenza substrains, mutual invasibility between competing perennial plants, and fluctuation-dependent invasion outcomes in apparently competing prey with a foraging-predation risk tradeoff. Together, these examples illustrate the framework's broad applicability, power to resolve the interaction between population and community level processes, and its potential to reveal novel ecological phenomena.

title: Synergistic mechanistic and deep learning approaches for modeling insect thermal responses and geographic distributions
content: Aim The Hutchinsonian shortfall, the lack of knowledge about species' abiotic tolerance, limits our understanding of species responses to environmental change and consequently also the outlining of their distribution in space and time. Such environmental tolerance is commonly inferred with two distinct approaches: i) trait performance studies, which use lab experiments to model species' functional responses, often overlooking real-world complexity, and ii) species distribution models, which infer environmental suitability from occurrence data, but offer limited causal insights. In this paper, we argue that these two strategies bring complementary information that can be integrated to estimate species-environment relationships more robustly and accurately map species distributions. Location Global scale Time period 2000-2019 Major taxa studied Given their exceptional diversity and climatic sensitivity, insects provide a powerful system for studying these responses. We selected key insect species representing i) disease vectors: the yellow fever (Aedes aegypti) and Asian tiger (Aedes albopictus) mosquitoes; ii) agricultural pests: the cotton bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) and the fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda); and iii) biocontrol agents: the green lacewing (Chrysoperla carnea) and the 14-spotted ladybug (Propylea quatuordecimpunctata). Methods We compared predicted insect thermal suitability and distributions derived from two complementary methodological approaches: mechanistic models based on experimentally derived thermal responses of ecological rates, and deep learning-based species distribution models based on occurrence data. We further tested hybrid frameworks integrating mechanistic and correlational information through model ensembling, mechanistic regularization, and mechanistically informed deep learning. We assessed the efficacy of these methods under increasing data scarcity by progressively removing up to 80% of species occurrence records using three strategies: removal from the warmest or coldest parts of species' thermal ranges, removal from the least-sampled locations based on geographic sampling bias, and random removal as a baseline. Results Our findings highlight that occurrence-derived thermal suitability closely reproduces the observed distributions of insects. Compared to the mechanistic estimates, these thermal response curves are consistently shifted towards lower temperatures, potentially reflecting niche underfilling. However, when challenged with progressive data removal, correlative methods fail to extrapolate reliably in data-deficient regimes, where mechanistic knowledge becomes increasingly more crucial. Hybrid approaches in turn leveraged complementary information, improving predictive performance and reducing the sensitivity of environmental suitability estimates to sampling biases. Main conclusions Ultimately, we show how the synergistic integration of experimental ecology with observational biogeography can lead to more accurate and ecologically robust predictions for species distributions and their environmental responses to climatic changes.

title: Quantifying floral rewards: Comparative evaluation of nectar extraction techniques
content: 1.) Nectar is a crucial resource for a wide range of insect species and one of the driving forces shaping plant-pollinator interactions. Flowers have evolved diverse strategies to restrict nectar access, ensuring only beneficial flower visits resulting in successful pollination. This range of adaptations, often morphological, makes it difficult for researchers to collect nectar in a standardised manner. In this study, we compare common methods used for nectar extraction, with a focus on applicability across several plant families 2.) We assessed pre-treatment methods widely used before nectar extraction, such as pollinator exclusion by bagging flowers, storing flowers overnight in water, and standing nectar crop (unmanipulated control). Moreover, we compared the effectiveness of two commonly used nectar extraction techniques, i.e., centrifugation and microcapillaries, across a range of flower morphologies. We compared nectar volume, sugar concentration, and total sugar content obtained by different methods for 23 flower species from 16 plant families. 3) We show that pollinator exclusion by bagging is an effective measure to obtain maximum nectar volume regardless of plant growth type. The nectar sugar concentration of herbaceous and woody species showed pre-treatment specific variation. Extraction with a centrifuge consistently yielded more nectar volume without altering the sugar concentration, while microcapillary extraction was not effective for most flower morphologies, especially lip (e.g. Salvia pratensis) and disc-shaped flowers (e.g. Rosa canina). 4.) Our results provide a foundation for the standardisation of floral nectar extraction protocols, improving comparability across studies, and facilitating broader ecological and evolutionary research that depends on consistent and reliable nectar sampling.

title: Disclose trade-offs in US emissions rule change | Science
content: In September, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rolled back Biden-era greenhouse gas emissions standards for fossil fuel–fired electric generating units without quantifying the likely adverse health effects (1). A year earlier, the EPA had estimated that such a change would lead to hundreds of additional deaths annually (1, 2). The agency’s decision to exclude the evidence of harm from its deregulation of greenhouse gas emissions reverses a long-standing federal practice to provide policy-makers and the public with quantitative estimates of benefits and costs of major regulatory decisions. To ensure public accountability, US agencies should continue this long-standing tradition of promoting transparency.

title: Save scientific terminology from executive orders | Science
content: The US National Library of Medicine (NLM) maintains the controlled vocabulary used to index the global biomedical literature, and its medical subject heading of “Artificial Intelligence” has been in use since 1986 (1). However, on 29 September 2026, US President Trump ordered federal executive agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with the term “super intelligence” in official documents, communications, websites, reports, and policy papers (2). Compliance with the September order is already underway: The National Institute of Standards and Technology has relabeled its evaluation research on language models and agents as super intelligence research (3). As medical researchers who depend on consistent and searchable literature, we urge US federal agencies to exempt scientific publications and controlled vocabularies from the order.

title: The Positive and Negative Selective Pressures Driving Polylysogeny
content:
Polylysogeny can benefit host bacteria by conferring resistance against heterologous phages. It also benefits prophages via shared induction pathways that enable simultaneous activation or hybrid phage formation. Multiple prophages engage in cooperative and antagonistic interactions, which can either boost host mortality through preemptive lytic induction or shape the stable polylysogenic state.

ABSTRACT
Prophages are widespread genetic elements dormant in bacterial genomes and fundamental to bacterial physiology, evolution, and ecosystem processes. Recent evidence reveals that lysogeny can generate benefits for both prophages and bacterial hosts, against other phages infection, host adaptation, and ecological process. Many bacteria harbour multiple prophages, yet most prior studies have emphasised single‐prophage effects and have not fully captured the evolutionary and mechanistic complexity of polylysogeny. Here, we aim to elucidate the major evolutionary forces and mechanistic determinants underlying polylysogeny. Because the behaviour of individual prophages underlies the emergence of polylysogeny, we first focus on the lysogenic decision and the stable coexistence of multiple prophages within a single bacterial host. Moreover, interactions among multiple prophages, ranging from cooperation (e.g., shared induction pathway and mutual stabilisation) to antagonism (e.g., competition and interference), collectively define polylysogenic states and their stability. Understanding these dynamics provides a framework for interpreting prophage‐driven bacterial evolution and for leveraging prophage biology in microbiome and microbial ecosystem research.

title: Keystone Microbial Taxa Regulate Nitrification and Denitrification Processes in Riverine Wetlands Across Eastern and Central China
content:
In riverine wetlands, rhizosphere soils are hotspots of nitrogen removal. The composition of keystone microbial taxa explains nitrification and denitrification better than keystone‐taxon richness or whole‐community attributes, with keystone taxa acting through direct functional effects and network‐mediated regulation.

ABSTRACT
Excess nitrogen (N) inputs threaten riverine wetlands worldwide, where microbially mediated nitrification and denitrification are key pathways for N transformation and removal. Although microbial communities are known to regulate riverine N cycling, the contribution of keystone microbial species remains unclear. Here, we combined high‐throughput sequencing of archaeal and bacterial amoA, nirK, and nirS genes with measurements of potential nitrification and denitrification rates in channel sediments, riparian rhizosphere soils, and riparian bulk soils across 30 riverine wetlands in eastern and central China. Habitat type and latitudinal zone significantly shaped nitrification and denitrification rates, with rhizosphere soils serving as hotspots of N removal. Local environmental factors, particularly total N and iron availability, strongly influenced these processes. Keystone species composition explained spatial variation in nitrification and denitrification more effectively than keystone species richness or whole‐community attributes. Moreover, keystone species regulated N removal through both direct functional effects and indirect, network‐mediated pathways. These findings highlight the critical role of keystone microbial species in sustaining N removal functions across riverine wetlands and provide new insights into microbiome‐informed management of nutrient‐enriched river ecosystems.

title: Acidification in coastal waters of Adélie Land, Antarctica (1985–2025)
content:
Acidification in coastal waters of Adélie Land, Antarctica (1985–2025)
Nicolas Metzl, Bronte Tilbrook, John Akl, Craig Neill, Alexandra Aymard, Claire Lo Monaco, Gilles Reverdin, Jean-Baptiste Sallée, Aude Barton, Frédéric Chevallier, and Marion Gehlen
Biogeosciences, 23, 8457–8475, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8457-2026, 2026
Ocean acidification is explored in the Adélie Land coastal region in East Antarctica. The region is a permanent CO2 sink leading to a positive increase of total CO2 concentrations and to a progressive decrease of pH and aragonite (Ωar). The lowest surface Ωar of 1.2 was observed in winter 2024, a critical limit for some marine species such as pteropod. A projection in the future suggests that aragonite saturation state will occur as soon as 2055 in the Adélie Land region.

title: Ground-truthing the application of compound-specific stable isotopes of amino acids to planktic foraminifera tests from Santa Barbara Basin
content:
Ground-truthing the application of compound-specific stable isotopes of amino acids to planktic foraminifera tests from Santa Barbara Basin
Shannon C. Doherty, Emily Havard, Stephanie Christensen, Genevieve M. Pugsley, Matthew D. McCarthy, and Catherine V. Davis
Biogeosciences, 23, 8437–8456, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8437-2026, 2026
Planktic foraminifera are plankton that form shells out of calcium carbonate. The chemistry of these shells can be used to reconstruct past ocean conditions from fossil specimens. The diet and behavior of the foraminifera can change how the shell chemistry is interpreted, and so we applied a chemical tool to the shells of planktic foraminifera to learn more about their ecology. We describe what we learned about the three species we studied and how others can apply this tool in the future.

title: Long‐Term Effects of Clear‐Cutting on Fungal Communities in Boreal Forest Soils
content:
ABSTRACT
Clear‐cut forestry has transformed boreal forests in Fennoscandia into a mosaic of homogeneous forest stands in different successional stages, while the proportion of old‐growth forests that have not been clear‐cut declines every year. We investigated long‐term consequences of clear‐cut forestry on fungal communities in boreal forest soils, focusing on how fungal communities in different soil depths respond to forestry. We established a paired‐plot study design that included 12 Norway spruce stands, clear‐cut 50–90 years ago and now ready for another round of clear‐cutting, each paired with a nearby near‐natural, non‐clear‐cut spruce forest. Fungal communities in seven different soil horizons, including two organic and five mineral horizons, were analysed using DNA metabarcoding of the ITS2 region as a fungal marker. While richness did not differ between the two forest types, community composition did. The fungal communities were strongly structured by soil depth, and a difference in community composition was found between the two forest types in most soil horizons. Numerous fungal groups showed strong long‐term responses to clear‐cut forestry. Archaeorhizomycetes, Elaphomycetaceae and Leotiales were more abundant in near‐natural forest soils and showed clear preferences for different soil horizons. Among ectomycorrhizal fungi, Cortinarius spp. were strongly associated with near‐natural forests. Our results demonstrate that clear‐cut forestry has long‐term effects on boreal soil fungal communities decades after clear‐cutting took place, even in deeper mineral horizons. Responses differed among genera and within ecological guilds, emphasising the importance of investigating the responses within guilds and not solely overall fungal community patterns.

title: Contrasting Patterns of Seascape Genetics in Acropora cf. tenuis and Their Symbiotic Algae
content:
ABSTRACT
Theory suggests that pairs of mutualist species will often co‐disperse and share the same dispersal patterns, though the extent to which this happens remains unclear. Photosynthetic corals constitute an example of this dynamic, as they rely on algal symbionts to meet their energetic needs, yet many acquire their symbionts environmentally after their larval dispersal phase. Consequently, corals and their symbionts may exhibit similar or contrasting patterns of genetic variation across the seascape, with implications for their evolutionary and ecological processes. Here, we densely sample corals of the key reef‐building taxon Acropora cf. tenuis and their algal symbionts across a reefscape in the central Philippines to examine genetic variation across space. Four distinct coral taxa show genetic evidence of long‐distance dispersal, including weak or absent isolation by distance signals and parent‐offspring pairs at widely spaced sites. These coral taxa all host a single group of algal symbionts from the genus Cladocopium, which shows landscape genetic structure independent from its coral hosts. In fact, Cladocopium genetics vary with both latitude and depth, potentially indicating genome‐wide local adaptation at a finer spatial scale than that seen in their hosts. Genetic variation at markedly different spatial scales between host and symbiont may be beneficial for hosts if these differences enable them to acquire symbionts adapted to their settlement environments.

title: A multistate Langevin diffusion for inferring behavior‐specific habitat selection and utilization distributions: Comment
A Framework for Understanding How and Why Animals Die
content:
Conceptual web linking potential drivers (whys) of mortality to proximate causes of death (hows). Environmental and ecological drivers influence mortality indirectly through interacting, intermediate whys such as movement, body condition, disease and life history state, culminating in diverse proximate causes of death. The shape, strength and ordering of these causal pathways remain incompletely understood, but conceptualizing these pathways could spark hypotheses and guide future research into how multiple drivers combine to produce mortality outcomes in wild animals.

ABSTRACT
Mortality is a fundamental demographic process that shapes populations and ecological communities. Yet, the pathways and processes underlying mortality are nearly as important as whether or not animals die. Misattributing mortality drivers in interventions, such as emphasizing predator control when declines are driven by food limitation or habitat loss, can lead to ineffective management actions due to incorrect inference. A richer understanding of mortality drivers across taxa is needed to advance ecological theory and improve conservation. We argue that there is a need to distinguish upstream drivers (whys) from downstream mortality events (hows) and to examine their interactions within causal pathways. We propose a conceptual framework for mapping these linkages across space and time. This framework clarifies underlying mechanisms and facilitates testable hypotheses about what drives mortality, including when particular drivers dominate, how multiple drivers interact and when causal relationships may be obscured. Together, the framework and associated approaches help structure hypotheses, identify poorly understood links and guide future data collection on the mechanisms shaping mortality in wild animals. These insights could improve our ability to detect vulnerability early enough to intervene effectively, particularly as anthropogenic change reshapes the causal chains leading to death.

title: AlphaInterp: Revealing how AlphaFold 3 processes structure, confidence, and evolutionary information
content:
by Jonathan Feldman, Jeffrey Skolnick

How does evolutionary information become structural knowledge? AlphaFold 3 predicts protein structures and biomolecular assemblies with remarkable accuracy, yet how it transforms comparative sequence information into three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. Here, we use mechanistic interpretability to follow this transformation through AlphaFold 3 and identify a computational principle underlying its structural inference. By extracting single- and pair-representations across the model’s forward pass and combining representational-geometry analysis, linear probing, activation patching, and perturbation of the multiple-sequence alignment (MSA) and its phylogenetic diversity, we show that AlphaFold 3 does not simply infer structure from raw sequence nor from MSA depth. Instead, a small number of sufficiently divergent homologues provides enough comparative information to largely recover the structure predicted using the full MSA. The pairformer transforms this evolutionary signal into a compact latent space in which residue-pair distances, contacts, fold similarity, and structural confidence become progressively decodable. Removing the MSA disrupts these latent geometries. Replacing it with evolutionarily similar homologues provides substantially less information, while evolutionarily unrelated sequences fail to rescue prediction despite preserving the formal alignment input. In contrast, phylogenetically diverse MSA subsampling largely restores both prediction accuracy and representational coherence. These results suggest that AlphaFold 3 has learned to infer structure by constraining its geometric priors and structural hypotheses by the sequence variation of the MSA. This framework helps explain both the model’s remarkable predictive power and its characteristic failure modes, with direct implications for protein design, conformational diversity, out-of-distribution generalization, and the interpretation of model confidence.

title: Gray bats heighten their response to social cues when navigating group flight in environments with obstacles
content:
by Eighdi Aung, Nicole Abaid

Bats are fast fliers with great maneuverability. Many species sense and communicate through echolocation, relying on acoustic signals in the environment. Bats also form large colonies, which necessitates that they fly in groups. When group size increases or obstacles are in their flight paths, the acoustic space can become cluttered, posing a non-trivial challenge for navigation. How do they interact with their environment and conspecifics, and how do they balance social and environmental cues? Recent research has uncovered individual adaptations to calling and flight patterns when flying in the groups or avoiding obstacles. Studies also suggest coordination when foraging, as well as strategies used by the group to mitigate acoustic clutter. However, there has yet to be a study on how bats weigh different navigational tasks when flying in spatially complex environments. Here, we collected stereoscopic video data from a wild colony of gray bats, Myotis grisescens, navigating their usual foraging flight paths in the presence of novel obstacles. We find that bats tend to stay close to a wall, but space out when flying in groups. We develop a data-informed agent-based model which reveals that their social repulsive behavior is strengthened when challenged to navigate novel obstacles.

title: GEI-17-mediated SUMOylation of GDP dissociation inhibitor GDI-1 regulates apoptotic cell clearance
content:
by Lei Yuan, Peiyao Li, Aiying Ma, Chao Li, Fuqiao Liu, Yunmin Xie, Qian Zheng, Hui Wang, Hui Xiao

Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans. The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. In the absence of GDI-1 SUMOylation, GDI-1 binds to GDP-RAB-1, sequestering it in the cytoplasm, resulting in impaired phagosomal degradation. Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

title: Altitude-induced hypoxia suppresses Varroa mite reproduction in Tibetan honey bees
content:
by Ruike Wei, Shangning Yang, Xinlan Chen, Yicheng Lu, Yao Liu, Fuliang Hu, Stephen J. Martin, Luo Zha, Huoqing Zheng

Our reliance on honey bees (Apis mellifera) for pollination services and honey production continues to increase due to the global decline in other pollinators and rising demand for honey. The ectoparasitic mite (Varroa destructor) remains the biggest pest of honey bees forcing beekeepers into continual miticide use. Beekeepers on the Tibetan Plateau, however, report rarely seeing mites in their colonies, unlike all other areas of China. We conducted a series of translocation experiments to investigate this phenomenon. Here, we show that hypoxic conditions above 3,500 m on the Tibetan Plateau reduce mite fecundity and arrest offspring development, and so prevent the long-term persistence of the mite population. This reduced mite fertility and arrested offspring development were also found in honey bee colonies maintained at low altitude but under hypoxic conditions like those found at 3,500 m. This discovery of a physiological limit to V. destructor reproduction highlights a previously unrecognized sensitivity of this mite to reduced oxygen availability, the mechanistic basis of which warrants further investigation. This discovery could unlock new chemical-free innovative mite-control methods that will benefit both the beekeeping industry and help ensure food security.

title: Local feedback governs cell fate transition to drive self-organized phenotypic equilibrium in hierarchical tumors
content:
by Emma Legait, Charlotte Rulquin, Lauranne Bouteille, Raphaël Clément, Cédric Maurange

How cell-state transitions are regulated along a tumor lineage to determine its overall cellular composition remains unclear. Using a simple hierarchical tumor model in Drosophila, we show that differentiation of cancer stem cells (CSCs) into transit amplifying progenitors (TAPs) depends on the fraction of TAPs among their immediate neighbors. This relationship is captured by a local feedback transition rule that quantitatively predicts CSC transition probability. Implementing this rule in 3D growth simulations spontaneously recapitulates CSC clustering and the emergence of a stable CSC fraction within tumors. Mechanistically, the local feedback is mediated by EGFR signaling from newly produced TAPs, propagating differentiation across CSC clusters. Consistently, we show that clustering protects the CSC pool from depletion driven by surrounding TAPs, indicating that spatial architecture and lineage dynamics are tightly coupled. Together, these findings show that a local feedback governing fate transitions drives emergent spatial organization that stabilizes the stem cell fraction in hierarchical tumors.

title: Decreased astrocytic CCL5 by Mir324 ameliorates ischemic stroke injury via the CCR5/ERK/CREB pathway
content: Following ischemic stroke, Ccl5 mRNA expression increased, while Mir324 expression decreased in the peri-infarct cortex of middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) mice. However, the roles of CCL5 and Mir324 in stroke remained largely unclear. Here, we show that inhibiting CCL5 using antibodies or Mir324 not only reduced infarct area and preserved neurological function in MCAO mice but also attenuated astrocyte reactivity and microglial activation, protected dendritic structures, and maintained spine density. In an astrocyte-neuron co-culture system after oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD), inhibiting astrocytic CCL5 by antibody or Mir324 decreased neuronal apoptosis and preserved dendritic structure. Importantly, the suppression of CCL5 enhanced ERK/CREB pathway signaling both in vivo and in vitro. Consistent with these findings, the application of Maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist, reduced infarct size, decreased neuronal apoptosis, and upregulated the ERK/CREB pathway in neurons treated with OGD. In conclusion, targeting the CCL5 pathway via Mir324 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for alleviating ischemic stroke damage through modulation of the neuronal CCR5/ERK/CREB pathway.

title: Analysis of the Google WeatherNext Tropical Cyclone Intensity Forecasts
content:
Abstract
We evaluate the Google WeatherNext Cyclone (WN‐C) ensemble and ensemble mean TC intensity performance for all storms between June 2022 and May 2026 and compare Google's model against select operational models, such as the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS), Statistical Hurricane Intensity Prediction Scheme Rapid Intensification Index (SHIPS‐RII), and Rapid Intensification Prediction Aid (RIPA). Results indicate WN‐C has comparable, if not better, performance metrics. WN‐C's ensemble mean has a lower mean absolute error than the HAFS model at all forecast hours. The model is comparable to the SHIPS‐RII and better than RIPA in terms of reliability of probabilistic rapid intensification (RI) forecasts over the first 24‐hr forecast period. However, the WN‐C ensemble is generally underdispersive and shows a negative bias in intensity change forecasts, including an underprediction of RI, that increases in magnitude with forecast lead time.

title: Noise Magnitude Alone Does Not Explain Model Failure: Critical Hydrological States Control Breakdown
content:
Abstract
The stability of machine‐learning models is generally evaluated by their ability to tolerate input noise. This study suggests that where the noise enters the physical trajectory is equally important. We predict subsurface soil moisture across depths of 10–40 cm from 5 cm observations at 21 globally distributed international soil moisture network stations by using lag‐aware Fourier Neural Operator. We apply perturbations separately to critical and non‐critical hydrological states to isolate state‐dependent model fragility. Critical states maintain the data‐efficient role, allowing reduced training subsets to recover the 70% baseline skill. However, the same states are also fragility points: perturbations applied to critical states produce stronger degradation, lower transition thresholds, and higher collapse probabilities than equal‐amplitude perturbations applied to non‐critical states. We find that the model breakdown is not governed by noise magnitude alone, but by the interaction between input uncertainty and physically informative states in the learned hydrological mapping.

title: Iron Spin Crossover in Ferromagnesite (Mg, Fe)CO3 and Its Contribution to Lower‐Mantle Seismic Heterogeneity
content:
Abstract
Carbonates host oxidized carbon in subducted slab and play a key role in controlling the distribution and seismic signatures of deep‐mantle carbon. Ferromagnesite, (Mg, Fe)CO3, is the stable carbonate in the lower mantle, yet its thermoelastic properties across the iron spin crossover (SCO) remain poorly constrained, limiting predictions of its seismic visibility. Using first‐principles calculations, we determine the pressure‐temperature evolution of iron SCO and its effect on elasticity and seismic velocities. The SCO, centered near ∼52 GPa at 300 K, shifts to higher pressures and broadens with increasing temperature and Fe content. This transition produces bulk softening and shear stiffening, reducing VP while moderately increasing VS. CO2 released during decarbonation of subducted oceanic crust can migrate upward and reprecipitate as ferromagnesite above the decarbonation front, forming localized carbonate enrichment. Our results indicate that ∼3–10 vol.% of (Mg0.875, Fe0.125)CO3 can generate shear‐wave impedance contrasts of −3% to +5%, comparable to mid‐lower‐mantle scatterers.

title: Electron and Ion Resonance Contributions to the Quasi‐Parallel Electron Firehose Instability in the Near‐Earth Plasma Sheet
content:
Abstract
We investigate the quasi‐parallel electron firehose instability (EFI) in the near‐Earth plasma sheet using a linear dispersion solver that incorporates a multi‐ion composition (H+, He+, O+). This instability exhibits higher frequencies and shorter wavelengths than electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) waves. Cyclotron resonance analysis shows that hot electrons, traditionally considered nonresonant, become weakly resonant with increasing wave obliquity. Notably, cold protons—despite being strongly resonant and expected to damp the waves—actually promote EFI growth as their density increases, because their absorption rate rises only moderately while hot electrons release energy much more efficiently. The underlying cause is that cold protons modify the dispersion relation in a way that enables hot electrons to transfer their free energy more efficiently. Cold protons therefore serve as “dispersion regulators” rather than as the primary energy sink. These results provide new insights into wave‐particle energy exchange governing EFI instability in multi‐ion magnetospheric plasmas.

title: Data‐Driven Insights Into the Deterministic and Stochastic Dynamics of Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation Transitions
content:
Abstract
During the last ice age, temperatures in Greenland frequently increased and decreased by up to 10° ${}^{\circ}$C. Detailed climate‐model studies suggest that these abrupt temperature changes were caused by collapses and recoveries of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). The causes of these AMOC transitions are debated. Here we describe the development of a neural‐network‐based surrogate model of the AMOC. It is trained on 32,000 years of climate model integrations to build a set of stochastic differential equations that emulate the climate model's AMOC behavior. In particular it reproduces the spectra and the asymmetry in the times it takes for the AMOC to recover and collapse, which makes it more realistic than previously published sets of coupled differential equations to study past AMOC transitions. Monte Carlo simulations suggest more deterministic and predictable collapses but stochastically forced recoveries.

title: Highly Anisotropic Forbush Decrease on 6–7 September 2025: Looking Into a Flux Rope?
content:
Abstract
A peculiar, moderately strong Forbush decrease, that is, suppression of the galactic cosmic ray (GCR) flux, was recorded by the global neutron monitor (NM) network on 6 – 7 September 2025. The event was exceptional, exhibiting a very asymmetric response in the bulk of the polar neutron monitors and an unusual time shift across different stations, both in amplitude and recovery. Here we present a comprehensive collection of available records, for example, observations of the Sun, heliosphere, and particle detectors, specifically neutron monitors, and provide an analysis for this event considering the station's acceptance. Using selected verified data sets related to this event and state‐of‐the‐art analyses of the available NM records, we deduced the anisotropy characteristics and spectral variation of the GCRs during the Forbush decrease and provided a plausible explanation.

title: New Early Cretaceous Paleomagnetic Results From the Central‐Western Lhasa Terrane Support the Diachronous Closure of the Bangong–Nujiang Ocean and the Existence of Two Subduction Systems Within the Neo‐Tethys
content:
Abstract
The spatiotemporal evolution of the Lhasa–Qiangtang collision remains debated. We report new paleomagnetic results from Early Cretaceous (∼123–113 Ma) strata in the central–western Lhasa terrane. Reliable characteristic remanence directions yield a paleopole at 83.3°N, 260.7°E (K = 63.0, A95 = 1.2°), corresponding to a paleolatitude of 24.9° ± 1.2°N. Combined with published data, our findings indicate ∼630 ± 180 km of northward translation of the Lhasa terrane during the mid‐Early Cretaceous. These results provide quantitative constraints on continued convergence during the late Early Cretaceous and, together with regional geological evidence, support continued closure of the Bangong–Nujiang Ocean during this interval. Such a tectonic setting places important constraints on the pre‐collisional subduction architecture of the Neo‐Tethys. Our results do not require large‐scale back‐arc extension to explain the observed paleolatitudinal evolution. Instead, an independent intra‐oceanic subduction system is consistent with the available paleomagnetic, petrological, and regional tectonic constraints.

title: The World's Longest Lake Ice Break‐Up Chronology: Capturing Precise Late‐Winter and Spring Temperatures in Central Scandinavia Since 1693
content:
Abstract
Using an assembly of historical documentary sources, from the areas surrounding the lake Storsjön, central Scandinavia, this study establishes the world's longest lake ice break‐up chronology, spanning 1693–2025. The study finds a strong late‐winter and spring temperature signal in ice break‐up dates. The correlation between the ice break‐up chronology and cumulative degree days above 0°C from 1 January–16 May reaches r = −0.88 (1860–1980) and the correlation with mean March–May temperatures is r = −0.82 (1860–2021). The Storsjön chronology and other cryophenological proxies show substantial differences from central and northern Scandinavian tree‐ring growing‐season temperature proxies in both multi‐decadal variability and long‐term trends, including a sustained spring warming beginning in the late‐17th century that is not evident in the tree‐ring records. Warming in recent decades is particularly pronounced, with almost all of the earliest ice break‐ups in the record occurring since 1990.

title: Ionospheric Ion‐Neutral Collision Frequency Revisited: Dependence on Ion Drift Velocity
content:
Abstract
Ion‐neutral momentum‐transfer collision frequencies are fundamental parameters governing ionosphere‐thermosphere coupling. Conventional formulas for these frequencies were derived from oversimplified interaction potentials and assumed a low‐velocity limit. Using updated interaction potentials for major ionospheric ion‐neutral pairs, we revisit ion‐neutral collision frequencies through first‐principles calculations, focusing on their dependence on ion drift velocity. For non‐resonant collisions, our collision frequency coefficients agree with conventional values at low velocities, fall below them at moderate drifts, and exceed them under strong ion flows. For resonant collisions, the O+‐O collision frequency coefficients generally increase with ion drift velocity; the associated Burnside factor (∼1.3) for weak‐to‐moderate drifts is found to align with that reported in recent observations. Despite the non‐Maxwellian O+ distribution under enhanced flows, an isotropic Maxwellian assumption might produce an acceptable estimate of the O+‐O collision frequency over a broad range of drift velocities. The new ion‐neutral collision frequency coefficients are made publicly available.

title: Land Temperature Sensitivity to the Extreme Oceanic Conditions of 2023 in CESM2
content:
Abstract
Global mean surface temperature reached unprecedented levels in 2023, alongside record‐high sea surface temperatures and sea ice retreat. However, how land temperature responds to such anomalous oceanic conditions remains unresolved. Using a land‐atmosphere coupled model with prescribed observed sea surface temperature and sea ice conditions in 2023 relative to a 1982–2001 climatology baseline, we quantify this land temperature sensitivity. The 2023 oceanic conditions produce a land warming of 0.9 ± 0.1°C (±1 standard deviation across the 50‐member ensemble) compared to the baseline. The ensemble‐mean response features enhanced divergence of vertically integrated moist static energy (DMSE) over the central‐eastern Pacific and is accompanied by a negative Pacific‐North American (PNA)‐like pattern and a weakened East Asian Subtropical Jet (EASJ). The 2023 oceanic state, which includes both background ocean warming and the 2023 anomaly, is a strong boundary forcing for simulated land warming, and is accompanied by large‐scale circulation anomalies.

title: The M4 Earthquakes Induced by the Quest Carbon Capture and Storage Project
content:
Abstract
Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) projects have not yet induced significant earthquakes, and many experts assume that seismicity poses a small risk. Recent earthquakes in Canada challenge this assumption. Since August 2015, the Quest CCS project has been injecting ∼1 Mt/year of CO2 into basal sediments that overlie crystalline basement. Contemporaneously, induced earthquakes have reactivated reverse‐slip on basement faults. We find a strong temporal relationship (>99% confidence) between earthquakes and injection. These events have now reached M4, were widely felt in Edmonton, Canada, and are the largest known CCS induced earthquakes worldwide. Reservoir modeling suggests small overpressures (∼2 to 40 kPa) at the time of the distant (∼35 km) earthquake, and require additional data for validation. Pressure management efforts could take several years before reductions are realized at these distances. Our results highlight that CCS projects require careful monitoring and risk assessment strategies, above‐and‐beyond the currently applied levels.

title: A Sustained High Growth Regime After Collapse of the Arctic Sea Ice Volume Feedback
content:
Abstract
We investigate changing Arctic sea ice growth behavior by synthesizing 29 years (1994–2023) of remote sensing products into a sea ice volume budget. By resolving dynamic and thermodynamic terms, we reveal a regime change in growth. Arctic sea ice has undergone a 1,077 (± $\pm $259) km3 increase in mean winter growth following the 2007/08 winter. Before 2007, the volume of survived summer ice explained 62.5% of seasonal winter growth (p<0.001) $(p<  0.001)$, a strong negative feedback consistent with prior understanding. This feedback collapsed after 2007. Basin growth has since decoupled from snow depth and sea surface temperature, retaining a link only to air temperature since 2014, which suggests a regime in which high internal variability and regional thickness distributions govern basin‐wide growth rather than any single forcing. This observational record resolves growth regimes that shorter records cannot separate, and serves as a benchmark for CMIP7 assessment.
