title: First global assessment of the Eddy-Diffusivity Mass-Flux (EDMF) parameterization for oceanic convection in NEMO: implications for global temperature and surface heat fluxes
content:
First global assessment of the Eddy-Diffusivity Mass-Flux (EDMF) parameterization for oceanic convection in NEMO: implications for global temperature and surface heat fluxes
Violaine Piton, Hervé Giordani, Romain Bourdallé-Badie, and Charles Pelletier
Ocean Sci., 22, 3771–3793, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3771-2026, 2026
Vertical ocean mixing regulates climate by transferring heat from the surface to depth. Because most models use simplified schemes, they often misrepresent convection and bias temperatures and air–sea heat exchange. We test a new mixing scheme in a global ocean model. It better captures daily tropical surface mixing and deep winter convection at high latitudes, reduces upper-ocean temperature biases, and alters surface heat balance, improving climate model realism.

title: Body-wide microbial ecosystem reorganization across the cognitive impairment spectrum in Parkinsons disease
content: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a major determinant of disability in Parkinsons disease (PD), yet how microbial alterations across multiple body sites accompany cognitive dysfunction remains poorly understood. We characterized microbial communities from five body sites (stool, saliva, tongue, nasal cavity, and axilla) in 150 participants spanning healthy controls, PD with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and PD dementia (PDD), generating 616 samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis v2 (MOFA2) identified a multisite microbial signature with prominent oral and gut contributions that varied across clinical groups (Factor 8; {beta} = -0.58, p < 0.0001). MintTea analysis identified stable multisite microbial assemblies associated with cognitive status, including a module distinguishing PD-MCI from PDD (in-sample AUROC = 0.810). Core microbiome analysis revealed a net reduction of 45 genus-site core memberships across four anatomical sites in cognitively impaired participants, including reduced prevalence of the butyrate-associated genus Roseburia. Multivariable models incorporating microbial signatures and demographic covariates explained an average of 35.4% of cognitive-outcome variance, with microbial features contributing an additional 8.0 percentage points beyond age, sex, and education. Procrustes analysis revealed a pronounced, non-linear pattern of weakening cross-site microbial community correspondence at the dementia stage. The Global Body-wide Organization Index remained relatively stable between HC (0.335) and PD-MCI (0.341) but declined to 0.257 in PDD, representing a 23% reduction relative to HC. Together, these findings identify disease-associated multisite microbial signatures and altered core-community composition across the PD cognitive impairment spectrum, supporting further investigation of multisite microbiome profiling for cognitive stratification.

title: Temporal blood sampling improves parameter recovery in a model of enterohepatic bile acid circulation using surrogate-accelerated Bayesian inference
content: Bile acids (BAs) are essential signaling molecules whose enterohepatic circulation (EHC) is disrupted across hepatobiliary disorders. Despite their potential as biomarkers, clinical utility is limited by high inter-individual variability, the inability of accessible peripheral blood to reflect true hepatic exposure, and the difficulty of directly measuring key physiological parameters governing the EHC. While mechanistic models can infer inaccessible hepatic profiles and patient-specific parameters from peripheral blood, personalizing them is computationally prohibitive due to multiscale dynamics causing numerical stiffness and the thousands of evaluations required for Bayesian inference. To overcome this, we developed an accelerated Bayesian inference pipeline combining timescale model reduction with neural network surrogates. Eigenvector participation factor analysis of a human EHC model revealed that rapid portal vein and hepatic sinusoidal transport drive stiffness. Applying the quasi-steady state approximation to these fast variables reduced integration times by over 97% with an integrated relative error <1.0%. A neural network surrogate further accelerated population ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo inference from days to hours, accurately recovering parameter distributions in 100 virtual individuals 95-98% coverage. Crucially, this tractability allowed us to dissect EHC physiological mechanisms and their disease perturbation. Single fasting measurements yielded practical non-identifiability due to strong posterior correlations among hepatic synthesis, intestinal motility, and absorption. A systematic comparison of sampling protocols showed peripheral sampling at multiple time points progressively disentangles these processes, while portal vein sampling offers no added benefit. Three peripheral time points emerged as an optimal protocol, recovering >90% of the identifiability of five time points. Furthermore, the framework captured EHC compensatory dynamics, revealing a persistent positive correlation between intestinal transit and absorption. By making stiff EHC models tractable, our framework guides clinical study design and enables minimally invasive, mechanistic characterization of BA dysregulation, advancing our mechanistic understanding and personalized diagnosis of hepatobiliary diseases.

title: The Neuroimmune Signature Underlying HPV Infection and Cervical Cancer Progression
content: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) is the principal cause of cervical cancer, yet the multicellular signalling programmes that accompany disease progression remain incompletely defined. Here, we integrated Single cell RNA sequencing, independent microarray and bulk RNA-sequencing meta analyses, and TCGA CESC tumor data to characterize the neuroimmune transcriptional architecture of HPV associated cervical disease. Single cell profiling revealed progressive remodeling of epithelial, stromal, endothelial and immune compartments across HPV infection, high grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and cervical cancer. Although immune dysregulation predominated, lesion and tumor states showed coordinated enrichment of nervous system associated programs, including synapse organization, trans-synaptic signaling, axon development, neurogenesis and neurotransmitter-related signaling. These programs formed interconnected networks with cytokine production, leukocyte activation, chemotaxis, cell adhesion, apoptosis, and immune effector regulation. Cross-platform integration identified a recurrent 12-gene neuroimmune signature associated with tumor grade related transcriptional variation, including CXCL12, P2RY6, P2RX5 and TACR1. Ligand receptor inference further highlighted glutamatergic, adrenergic, noradrenergic, GABAergic and purinergic signaling circuits. Notably, these signals were distributed across immune, epithelial, stromal and endothelial populations rather than confined to a canonical neural cell compartment. P2RX5 showed the strongest association with advanced tumor grade, whereas P2RY6, P2RY11 and GABRP displayed cell type and stage dependent regulation. Together, our findings define cervical carcinogenesis as a distributed neuroimmune state in which HPV associated immune evasion converges with ectopic neurotransmission-related programs, revealing candidate biomarkers and potentially actionable signaling axes in the cervical tumor microenvironment.

title: Visual Search and ASD: Basic vs. Superordinate Category Search
content: We study visual search and categorization among individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and a neuro-typical comparison group (NT). Individuals with ASD often exhibit distinct sensory processing patterns and may face challenges in efficiently detecting and categorizing visual stimuli. They may also process categories differently compared to NT groups, reflecting variations in typical sensory processing mechanisms. Based on our previous findings, this study employs visual search categorization tasks, testing reaction time and set-size slopes for different target categories. Participants included 26 individuals with ASD and 11 NT individuals, with similar mean ages and mean IQ Block Design subtest scores. They performed basic-level and superordinate-level visual search, as well as a categorization task. In the visual search task, participants identified targets within arrays of varying set sizes (4, 16, 36, 64). Face detection remained rapid across groups, and Basic-level search was similar in ASD and NT groups (mean set-size slopes: 48.7 and 45 ms/item, respectively). In contrast, superordinate search was much slower in ASD (99 ms/item) compared to NT (70.8 ms/item), reflecting increased cognitive demands. Object typicality influenced performance, with less typical items being slower to both categorize and detect. These findings suggest that basic-level processing is relatively preserved in ASD, whereas superordinate categorization imposes greater demands. The results highlight the role of typicality and support differences in perceptual and cognitive processing in ASD. Our findings contribute to better understanding visual cognition in autism and may inform strategies for improving conceptual generalization and visual learning.

title: A modular workflow for biomedical entity normalization across heterogeneous biological ontologies
content: Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying rare diseases requires integrating information about phenotypes, cell types, anatomical structures, and molecular functions and processes. Although some of this knowledge is available in structured resources, additional relationships remain dispersed across biomedical literature. Extracting and integrating this information requires normalizing heterogeneous biological entities against specialized ontologies. This motivated the development of a common biomedical named entity normalization (NEN) workflow and the evaluation of its performance across different entity types and ontologies. We developed a modular NEN workflow combining exact matching, lexical and semantic candidate retrieval, and reranking, without requiring ontology-specific training. Candidate retrieval integrates BM25, fuzzy matching, character n-gram similarity, and SapBERT. We evaluated the workflow across the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), Cell Ontology (CL), Uberon, and Gene Ontology (GO) using multiple benchmarks, separately assessing candidate retrieval, reranking accuracy, and overall normalization accuracy. We also investigated factors associated with retrieval difficulty and compared the workflow with CellExLink, a specialized cell-type normalization system. Retrieval performance varied across ontologies and benchmarks, with lexical and semantic methods providing complementary candidate coverage in some settings. Increasing candidate-set size improved retrieval recall but did not necessarily improve overall normalization accuracy, as larger candidate sets could reduce reranking performance. Retrieval difficulty was associated with mention characteristics and ontology categories. Our evaluation identifies the performance characteristics and limitations of a common normalization workflow across heterogeneous biological ontologies, highlighting the importance of assessing candidate retrieval and selection separately. The workflow provides a methodological foundation for extracting and integrating biological information from rare disease literature, with potential applicability to other biomedical information-extraction tasks requiring normalization against these ontologies.

title: CellVADIS: Inferring cross-tissue immune cell trafficking dynamics from single-cell snapshots
content: The ability of immune cells to traffic between and enter different tissues is an important hallmark for effective immune responses. However, despite advances in high-throughput single-cell profiling, identifying circulating cell populations that drive tissue-specific immunity remains elusive. Here we present CellVADIS, an optimal transport based computational framework to infer cross-tissue immune cell dynamics. By connecting single-cell measurements across tissue sites, CellVADIS enables the prediction of cell migration fates, characterization of tissue-specific trafficking signatures on circulating cells, as well as identification of tissue entry points. We benchmarked our method against synthetic data and applied CellVADIS to two cross-tissue single-cell datasets which revealed characteristic marker expression patterns that define tissue-specific trafficking signatures and homing niches of tissue-entering CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. CellVADIS provides a flexible, open-source tool for identifying cross-tissue single-cell dynamics from various high-throughput single-cell measurements, which would support the design of vaccination and immunotherapeutic regimens to generate tissue-specific immunity.

title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.
content: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

title: Depth-partitioned oxidation of atmospheric hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methane in a glacier forefield soil
content: Glacier forefields are model systems for pioneer ecosystem assembly under extreme oligotrophy. Their microbial communities carry widespread genomic potential to oxidize atmospheric trace gases, yet whether this potential is transcribed in situ, and by which lineages, remains largely untested. Here we combined depth-resolved profiling of hydrogen (H2), carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH4) at ten locations in the Wildstrubel glacier forefield, Swiss Alps, with mesocosm experiments, long-read metagenomics, and genome-resolved metatranscriptomics. Soils were consistent net sinks for atmospheric H2 and CH4, with fluxes ~2-fold and ~6-fold higher, respectively, in older than in younger terrain. H2 uptake was concentrated in the upper 20 cm, whereas CH4 uptake extended deeper. In the field, CO uptake was masked by apparent subsurface production, but in mesocosms lacking this source both CO and H2 were drawn below atmospheric concentrations. Although 57% of metagenome-assembled genomes encoded trace-gas oxidation enzymes, topsoil transcription was dominated by Group 1h [NiFe]-hydrogenases from a few Actinomycetota populations, in which the CO dehydrogenase coxL was transcribed 20- to 35-fold less. The second most transcribed marker was smoX, most closely related to C2-C6 alkane monooxygenases, suggesting the use of short-chain alkanes of possible subsurface origin. Mobile genetic elements were widely transcribed, matching host transcription, but a 104-kb plasmid-borne coxMSL operon was largely silent. Acetylene perturbation induced no detectable switching between trace-gas pathways. Together, these data suggest that trace-gas metabolism is partitioned across soil depth: atmospheric H2 scavenging dominates topsoil transcription, whereas methanotrophy and CO production occur deeper. Net surface fluxes, particularly for CO, therefore, underestimate gross trace-gas turnover.

title: Flow Virometry-Based Profiling of Viral Population Diversity
content: Viruses exhibit great phenotypic heterogeneity. Flow virometry enables high-throughput analysis of phenotypic diversity in viral populations, while flow-based sorting allows subpopulations to be isolated for separate characterization. Despite their advantages, flow virometry and sorting have not yet been widely adopted in virology partly because of limited protocols and underexplored applications. Here, we provide a practical guide for analyzing and quantifying virus particles from diverse families using flow virometry enhanced by fluorescence labeling. We further explore applications beyond basic and static characterization of virus populations. We demonstrate that flow virometry can report on interactions between virions and binding partners, as well as between virions. It provides a particle denominator that, combined with genome copy measurements, enables estimation of viral population ploidy. We also show how dynamic processes, such as viral membrane fusion, can be measured in real time. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of sorting virions based on their intrinsic properties, such as morphology, for downstream study. This practical guide provides a roadmap for wider implementation of flow virometry in virology, while the applications illustrated here demonstrate potential to address a variety of questions about virion properties, interactions, and dynamics at the single-particle level.

title: Spatial coordination of peptidoglycan synthesis by MreB directs morphogenesis in Xanthomonas citri
content: The cytoskeletal proteins MreB and FtsZ coordinate cell wall synthesis during elongation and division in rod shaped bacteria. How these two systems interact in the citrus canker pathogen Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri (X. citri) remains unclear. Previously, we showed that disruption of FtsZ ring placement, by deletion of minC, uncouples cell wall synthesis from division, leading to branching and filamentation. Now, using a MreB-GFP sandwich fusion, we show that MreB localizes at the inner membrane, independently of MinC. Peptidoglycan (PG) synthesis (visualized with the fluorescent D-amino acid analogue HADA) happens mostly at the division septum. Perturbation of MreB with A22 disrupts rod shape maintenance and leads to a dose-dependent growth inhibition. A22 induces a reversible relocalization of MreB into the cell cap region, which is accompanied by a shift of PG synthesis from midcell to the poles. This indicates that MreB is required for proper spatial regulation of PG insertion. This loss of spatial control is exacerbated in {Delta}minC cells, which display increased A22 sensitivity, indicating a synthetic dependence on MreB when FtsZ ring placement is affected. Furthermore, MreB inhibition disrupts ParABS-mediated chromosome segregation, leading to anucleate cells. Our findings establish MreB as a key coordinator of cell wall synthesis, cell shape, and chromosome segregation in X. citri

title: Comparative exometabolome and extracellular-vesicle metabolome of Bifidobacterium
content: Bifidobacterium species are early colonisers of the human gut and are widely used as probiotics, yet their extracellular chemistry remains largely unexplored, and the small-molecule cargo of their extracellular vesicles (EVs) has not been characterised. We carried out an exploratory, descriptive characterisation of the exometabolome and EV metabolome of Bifidobacterium longum 35624 and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis at 24 and 48 h of anaerobic growth, using untargeted LC MS/MS coupled with feature-based molecular networking and semi-targeted analysis of conjugated lipids. The two strains reshaped the shared culture medium through distinct, strain-specific nutrient conversions. B. longum 35624 deamidated nicotinamide to nicotinic acid and produced the tryptophan catabolite indole 3 lactic acid, whereas B. animalis subsp. lactis catabolised purine nucleosides and accumulated hypoxanthine; the two strains also differed in carbohydrate utilisation. EVs, purified by ultracentrifugation and size exclusion chromatography and characterised by nanoparticle tracking analysis, immunoassay and electron microscopy, carried a sparse small-molecule cargo. A membrane glycolipid represented the clearest vesicle-associated signal of bacterial origin, whereas bile acid and N acyl lipid conjugates were also detected but could not be attributed to bacterial production, as they were present in the culture medium. Together, these data provide a first reference description of the Bifidobacterium exometabolome and EV metabolome and identify strain specific extracellular metabolic activities as priorities for targeted validation.

title: Single-cell transcriptomics of human astrovirus VA1-infected intestinal organoids reveals cell-type-specific responses and a requirement for cholesterol biosynthesis during infection
content: Human astroviruses are prevalent but understudied enteric viruses that cause gastroenteritis and neurological disease, particularly in children and immunocompromised individuals. No vaccines or antivirals are available, partly because their biology and pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize transcriptional responses to VA1, a non-classical human astrovirus associated with the majority of extraintestinal disease cases, in fetal ileum-derived human intestinal organoids. VA1 altered epithelial cell-type proportions and progressively spread through the organoids. Differential gene expression analysis of enterocytes and progenitor cells, the cells most prevalent in the organoid model, revealed shared antiviral responses, including interferon signaling, as well as cell-type-specific responses. Enterocytes exhibited a broader early transcriptional response and specifically upregulated cholesterol metabolism and biosynthesis pathways at 1 dpi. By 3 dpi, progenitor cell-specific genes suggested inflammatory and epithelial-defense responses. In two different intestinal epithelial cell lines, T84 and Caco-2 cells, limiting extracellular lipid availability did not alter replication but increased VA1 binding in Caco-2 cells. Pharmacologic inhibition of cholesterol biosynthesis and 25-hydroxycholesterol treatment reduced VA1 replication, while disrupting intracellular cholesterol transport had no detectable effect. Together, these findings expand our knowledge on HAstV biology by defining shared and cell-type-specific epithelial responses to VA1 infection and identifying cholesterol biosynthesis as an important host pathway for successful VA1 replication.

title: Exploitative competition among different dormancy strategists shapes community diversity, recovery from perturbations and response to dispersal
content: Dormancy is a reversible physiological state of reduced metabolic activity that occurs in plants and animals, but is particularly common among microorganisms. Microorganisms can switch into dormancy spontaneously or in response to environmental cues. While previous work has investigated the ecological and evolutionary consequences of the switching mechanism, it is unknown how different dormancy-switching mechanisms within a microbial community interact to shape composition and community-level response to environmental changes. Here, we used mathematical modelling to investigate how different microbial strategies for entering and existing from dormancy shape community dynamics under stable conditions, following perturbation, and after dispersal. We modelled strategists that had no dormant state (non-switching), those that employed spontaneous switching, those that switched given a cue (triggered switching), and those that used a combination of spontaneous and triggered switching (mixed switching). We also examined how competition and the costs of switching influence activity dynamics within the community. Our simulations revealed the importance of exploitative competition among dormancy strategists in shaping the community response to perturbation and dispersal. In a mixed community containing different dormancy strategists, spontaneous switchers maintained a dormant pool, but suffered an implicit competitive disadvantage. Meanwhile, triggered switchers were more competitive under favourable conditions but could be pushed into dormancy by exploitative competition from other strategists. Interestingly, dispersal events could intensify competition, induce dormancy in resident populations and alter the relative activity of different strategists, while also restoring community members lost during perturbation. To evaluate these predictions, we then analysed an existing dataset of soil mesocosms that experienced heat perturbation and subsequent dispersal. The data showed a stable dormant pool, consistent with the presence of stochastic switchers, and the observed dormancy dynamics following dispersal supported competition-driven inactivation among triggered switching strategists. However, we found no evidence that dormancy provides general protection against the heat perturbation. Instead, the results suggest that survival may depend on the inherent tolerance of community members, while subsequent recovery reflects the interplay between dormancy, immigration, and competition. Our work shows how dormancy not only impacts community-level resilience to perturbations but also alters, and is altered by, exploitative competition among community members.

title: EFFECT OF A LACTOBACILLUS POSTBIOTIC ON DIGESTIVE HEALTH IN DOGS RAISED IN CONDITIONS AT RISK OF GIARDIA DUODENALIS INFECTION
content: Giardia duodenalis infection is associated with diarrhea and dysbiosis in dogs, while metronidazole treatment can further disrupt the microbiota. We evaluated adjunctive LB fermentate HF (LBHF), a Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic, in a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study of 30 naturally infected dogs (Terriers). Animals received metronidazole (50 mg/kg/day) with LBHF (50 mg/kg/day) or microcrystalline cellulose placebo (70 mg/kg/day) for 21 days. Clinical outcomes, fecal biomarkers, canine dysbiosis index, and cyst shedding were monitored over 45 days. Fecal shotgun metagenomics was performed at baseline and day 45. After baseline covariate adjustment, LBHF was associated with significantly lower Giardia burdens during treatment, particularly at days 10 and 20, improved fecal consistency, and reduced odor. No significant effects were found for fecal calprotectin, secretory IgA, blood biomarkers of digestive function, or canine dysbiosis index. Overall microbiome turnover was similar between groups, but multivariate analyses identified distinct treatment-associated community trajectories. LBHF was associated with increased Bacteroidota representation and functional capacity for plant polysaccharide degradation, alongside depletion of gene sets involved in flagellar assembly, quorum sensing, biofilm formation, and epithelial-cell signaling. Baseline microbiome composition also predicted Giardia burden, highlighting an association between parasite load and bacterial community structure. Adjunctive LBHF supplementation was associated with faster resolution of canine giardiasis, improved fecal quality, and coordinated microbiome remodeling. Further mechanistic studies are needed to establish whether the observed microbiome functional changes contribute to parasite clearance and recovery of intestinal health.

title: Persistence of Non-industrial Gut Microbiota Discriminates Health and Disease States in Industrial Populations
content: Industrialization has sharply reduced gut microbial diversity, possibly affecting human health. To isolate the effects of industrialization, we assembled 18,075 human metagenomes spanning hunter-gatherer, agro-pastoral, and industrial lifestyles. We confirmed individual-level diversity reductions in industrial populations, but also found that nearly all known human-associated microbes exhibit population-level persistence. Previously hypothesized 'vanishing' microbes are reduced from high prevalence in non-industrial populations to above-median prevalence in industrial populations. Species-level signatures in industrial case-control cohorts suggest that harboring 'vanishing' taxa can be associated with health or pathology, depending on the condition. Controlling for background prevalence, 'vanishing' microbes were more likely associated with cases than controls in obesity, both 'vanishing' microbes and those now 'blossoming' in industrialized populations were associated with glucose intolerance, while 'blossoming' taxa were associated with inflammatory bowel disease. We conclude that most microbes have not gone extinct under industrialization, and that the health effects of lifestyle-associated taxa are context-dependent.

title: Persistence of commensal Escherichia coli strains and plasmid transfer in a healthy adult
content: Little is known about the ecological dynamics of Escherichia coli strains in the healthy human intestinal tract. Here, the composition of commensal E. coli in a healthy adult was tracked over 700 days. 100 E. coli isolates recovered directly from each of 21 faecal samples collected at monthly intervals were characterised. In total 15 strains were recovered; five were resistant to one or more antibiotics. Five "persistent" strains were found in multiple samples spanning 1- to 5-month periods. The relative abundance of persistent strains ranged from 1-100% of E. coli per sample, but they were dominant (>80%) in 14/21 samples and the only strain in 12. Complete genomes were determined for all strains, including isolates of persistent strains from their first and last appearances. Persistent strains belonged to phylogroups B2 (ST1236 and ST420), A (ST10 and ST93), or D (ST362). Single-sample strains were phylogroup A, B1, B2, D or F. Confirming extended survival in the gut, only minor changes were detected in the chromosomes of persistent strains over their residence periods. However, one lost a plasmid and two gained plasmids, providing evidence for horizontal gene transfer in the gut. A Z-type multidrug resistance plasmid moved from one persistent strain to the next and exchanged a small backbone region with a plasmid in the recipient. An M-type arsenic resistance plasmid was acquired by two different strains and transferred to laboratory E. coli with two co-resident plasmids. All persistent strains, but only 2/10 single-sample strains, carried one or more plasmid-borne bacteriocin determinants.

title: History of coadaptation to the cag pathogenicity island in Helicobacter pylori
content: Most Helicobacter pylori strains use genes encoded on the cag pathogenicity island (cagPAI) to inject the CagA oncoprotein into human cells, where it alters cell signalling and morphology to promote bacterial colonization. However, cag- H. pylori strains are found worldwide. Here, we use a global sample of >9,000 Helicobacter genomes to investigate how strains adapt to cag status. We identified variants genome-wide associated with cagPAI presence, including many in vacA and hopQ, as well as in genes not previously linked to cag. We use these variants to construct a cag polygenic coadaptation score, allowing us to systematically explore the dynamics and evolutionary history of the island. Score distribution is bimodal in many populations, showing there is a stable adaptive strategy associated with cag- status. However, these cag- coadapted variants have historically been unavailable to strains in East Asia, providing a potential explanation for the low frequency of cag- strains in this region. We also infer that the cagPAI arrived in H. pylori before the human populations which colonized Australia and Papua New Guinea split from other groups 50,000-70,000 years ago. Adaptation to the island in other populations was achieved in part by using existing variants from the Hardy ecospecies. Our study illustrates how gene coadaptation shapes pathogen evolution after import of a major virulence factor and highlights genetic configurations that may predict increased or decreased disease risk, informing eradication strategies.

title: BRO is a proteinaceous binding receptor for human coronavirus OC43
content: Embecoviruses such as human coronavirus (HCoV) OC43 have long been viewed as sialic acid-dependent viruses that attach to cells through interactions with cell surface sialoglycans. Here, we identify a specific proteinaceous receptor that harbors the sialoglycan determinant and also contributes protein contacts for viral spike (S) recognition. Using an unbiased surfaceome CRISPR activation screen for OC43 spike binding, we discovered that the previously uncharacterized human gene C1ORF54 encodes this receptor, which we name Binding Receptor for OC43 (BRO). BRO engages the OC43 S N-terminal domain through O-linked 9-O-acetylated sialoside determinants and neighboring protein contacts. BRO expression in human cells promotes OC43 infection, whereas BRO knockout or blockade with the BRO ectodomain or anti-BRO antibody inhibit infection, including in differentiated primary human airway cultures. BRO orthologs from diverse mammals support OC43 infection when expressed in human cells, suggesting potential contributions to OC43 zoonotic circulation and cross-species transmission. Our findings reshape our understanding of OC43 entry, and pave the way to develop countermeasures targeting this receptor interaction.

title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal a cyst-neuron-microglia network underlying brain damage during Toxoplasma gondii infection
content: Toxoplasma gondii infects approximately one-third of the world's population, and persistent brain infection links to neuropsychiatric disorders. How cysts interact with host brain cells and tissue to sustain infection and cause neuronal damage remains unclear. We combined single-nucleus RNA sequencing with Stereo-seq spatial transcriptomics to map mouse brains across acute and chronic T. gondii infection. We found neurons in the cyst neighbourhood recruit interferon-responsive microglia via the APP-CD74 axis; these microglia breached the cyst wall with invasive pseudopodia, the released parasites formed secondary cysts; and microglial depletion with PLX5622 during chronic infection significantly reduced brain cyst burden, supporting that continual cyst turnover facilitates persistent infection. In mice with chronic infection, suppressed NMDA receptor signalling, enhanced complement-mediated synaptic pruning, impaired adult neurogenesis, and induced lipid reprogramming was found in the cyst neighbourhood. This cyst-neuron-microglia network thus underpins both infection persistence and neuronal injury, offering new mechanistic insights into pathogen-host interactions.

title: Gram-positive bacteria have different susceptibilities to the host-derived antimicrobial lysophosphatidylcholine and adapt to lysophosphatidylcholine-induced stress via distinct mechanisms
content: The human lipid metabolites, lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) and plasmenyl-LPC (pLPC), modulate both the metabolic health status and innate immunity of an individual. Previous studies reported direct antibacterial activity of LPC, while pLPC has not been evaluated. Meanwhile, some bacteria harvest LPC for producing phosphatidylcholine (PC); others produce plasmalogens under anaerobic conditions. These discoveries suggest that both LPC and pLPC can mediate host-microbe interactions. In this study, we demonstrated diverse susceptibility profiles of human pathobionts to LPC(18:0) and pLPC(18:0) at physiologically-relevant concentrations. Though the Gram-negative bacteria Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were not susceptible to LPC or pLPC, all tested Gram-positive bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus agalactiae, Enterococcus faecalis, and E. faecium were susceptible to pLPC, suggesting robust antimicrobial activity of this lipid in vivo. While LPC can effectively kill S. aureus and S. agalactiae, it does not completely inhibit the growth of enterococci. Moreover, pretreatment of LPC-containing medium with E. faecalis rescues S. agalactiae from LPC killing, suggesting that E. faecalis deactivates LPC extracellularly and can protect co-resident LPC-sensitive pathobionts. Finally, we observed the emergence of spontaneous LPC-resistant S. aureus. These strains have point mutations in sensor kinase gene walK and the lipid metabolism genes fabF and farR, which lead to increased expression of the efflux pump gene farE. Collectively, these results support the antibacterial effects of LPC and pLPC and indicate distinct bacterial adaptation mechanisms, providing novel insights on lipid-mediated host-bacterial interactions.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes
content: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.

title: Behavioural response diversity of individual seabirds can correlate positively with colony stability
content: Ensuring ecosystems are stable has become a priority given humanity's dependence on the services those ecosystems provide. There has consequently been significant research effort demonstrating that ecosystem stability is driven by 'response diversity', whereby different species respond uniquely to the environmental conditions and 'insure' the ecosystem against collapse. However, response diversity theory has only been applied at the ecosystem/community level, when the response diversity of individual animals' behaviour or traits is also theoretically linked to population-level stability. Therefore, we may be overlooking a viable indicator of extinction risk. Using long-term behavioral and energetic expenditure data from two seabird species breeding in the North Atlantic (Atlantic puffin Fratercula arctica and black-legged kittiwake Rissa tridactyla), we demonstrate that the response diversity in foraging effort of individual birds correlates with the stability of their colony's population size, while energetic expenditure does not. Further, the diversity of bird responses increases when environmental conditions (here represented by sea surface temperature) are outside of the colony's norm. Our work shows that response diversity provides a new perspective on the role of individual behavioral differences in creating stable populations, offering insights to better manage vulnerable groups.

title: Long-read metagenomics reveals unexplored viral diversity andgenomic novelty in the mesopelagic Andaman Sea
content: The mesopelagic zone (200 to 1000 m) of the ocean represents Earth's largest yet most underexplored biome, particularly with respect to viral diversity and function. The deep-sea virome of the Indian Ocean remains largely unexplored despite the ecological significance of marine viruses in regulating microbial mortality, biogeochemical cycling and carbon flux via the viral shunt. In this study, we explored the diversity of DNA viruses across mesopelagic depths in the Andaman Sea. Seawater samples collected from multiple depths were enriched for viral particles, followed by viral DNA extraction and long-read metagenomic sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies. We used three complementary approaches for the identification of assembled contigs of viruses. Based on the consensus from these three approaches followed by quality assessment, we retained 1,604 viral contigs of high-confidence and high-quality. Among the taxonomically assigned viruses, members of the class Caudoviricetes dominated across all samples. The assignment decreased substantially at lower taxonomic ranks, highlighting the limited representation of environmental viruses in existing reference databases. Gene-sharing network analysis further revealed genomic novelty and showing limited gene-sharing relationships with reference genomes. Host prediction analyses assigned putative hosts to 10.7% of viral contigs, of which 98.3% were associated with bacteria and 1.7% with archaea. Among predicted bacterial hosts, Pseudomonadota predominated. Structure-informed functional annotation of complete viral contigs identified predominantly structural and tail-associated proteins, while a substantial proportion of viral proteins remained functionally uncharacterized. Collectively, these findings reveal previously under-explored viral diversity in the mesopelagic Andaman Sea study and provide the first comprehensive insight into the deep-ocean virome of this region.

title: Adaptation of Mimulus cardinalis to drought through changes in stomatal conductance
content: Many areas around the globe are experiencing warmer temperatures, more extreme drought, and wildfires because of climate change. Therefore, plant populations may experience strong natural selection on traits associated with adaptation to rapid change. One trait likely under selection is stomatal conductance, which determines the rate at which water vapor and carbon dioxide diffuse through the stomata and is sensitive to environmental factors such as drought, CO2, and vapor pressure deficit. The purpose of this study is to understand how plants respond both ecologically and evolutionarily to an extreme multiyear drought. Using six populations of a perennial herb (Mimulus cardinalis), we measured the evolution of operational stomatal conductance in pre-drought ancestral and post-drought descendant cohorts planted in three common gardens across the species' range. This design allowed us to test (1) whether stomatal conductance evolved in response to drought and (2) whether populations with greater genetic variance evolved more. Patterns consistent with drought escape were more common than patterns consistent with avoidance (6 versus 4 of 18 population-by-garden combinations), but evidence for evolutionary change in stomatal conductance was limited overall, and the extent of change was not correlated with genetic variance. These findings offer a framework for future research on stomatal traits and insight into the rate at which plants respond to environmental change.

title: Synchronized Seasonal Shifts in the Climate, Diet, and Gut Microbiome of a Rainforest Lemur (Eulemur rufifrons)
content: Gut microbiome (GM) flexibility extends the adaptive potential of host species in the face of rapid ecological change. Madagascar's endemic primates offer a powerful natural system to study GM plasticity as the island experiences substantial environmental change throughout the year. This is especially true in the eastern rainforests, which experience marked variation in temperature, rainfall, and fruit availability between the wet and dry seasons. To elucidate interactions between climate, diet, and the GM, we conducted a 10-month study of the ecologically flexible red-fronted brown lemur (Eulemur rufifrons) in Ranomafana National Park. We detected significant shifts in gut microbial communities correlated with monthly rainfall, temperature, and dietary diversity. Trade-offs between abundances of carbohydrate- and fiber-metabolizing bacteria reflected shifts between frugivory and folivory, suggesting that the GM buffers energetic and/or nutritional imbalances when resources are scarce. Finally, we observed synchronized shifts in climate and the GM despite deviation from normal seasonal patterns, demonstrating the GM's rapid response to environmental cues. Our results suggest that the GM contributes to phenotypic plasticity across seasons, enabling endangered primates to better cope with environmental stressors like climate change.

title: Continuity, not accuracy: how canopy approximations shape competition and selection in size-structured vegetation models
content: Light competition drives ecological and evolutionary processes in forests. Real canopies are too complex to simulate in full, so stand models approximate them. We assessed three canopy approximations, the Perfect Plasticity Approximation (PPA), Flat Top and Deep Crown, in two stages. First, we compared their instantaneous light interception with a high-resolution reference model (MAESPA), focusing on competition among individuals and on vulnerability to self-shading. Second, we embedded them in a dynamic vegetation model and traced effects on stand development, demographic equilibrium and invasion fitness, the basis of evolutionary prediction. Deep Crown, which allows leaf area to overlap between individuals, reproduced MAESPA's continuous response of light capture to height. The PPA, and the Flat Top in stands of uniform height, instead produced a stepwise response around the point where a focal tree becomes taller than its neighbours. In the dynamic model, the PPA's discontinuities were tolerable for stand development but shifted demographic equilibrium by an order of magnitude. Every runnable representation produced a continuously stable strategy (CSS), but under the PPA it was reached through a stepped, erratic selection gradient and was not robustly located. All approximations overestimated light capture under self-shading, increasingly so at realistic leaf area. Our results show that continuity of the shade each plant casts as a function of height, rather than average accuracy or assimilation detail, determines whether an approximation can support evolutionary inference. Approximations adequate for stand-level light interception can mislead for competition and selection among individuals.

title: Unravelling the role of plant alpha-, beta-, and gamma- chemodiversity in shaping canopy insects of plants within the same species
content: Plant intraspecific chemodiversity drives plant-herbivore and -pollinator relationships in plots, but whether it also impacts other members of the canopy arthropod community remains unclear. Furthermore, little is known of how different spatial components of plot intraspecific chemodiversity; chemical composition of individual plants within plots (i.e. -chemodiversity); differences in chemical composition among plants within plots (i.e. {beta}-chemodiversity); and cumulative chemical composition of all individuals in plots (i.e. {gamma}-chemodiversity), impact aboveground community assemblage. Using a chemodiversity field experiment containing 84 plots each planted with different combinations of Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare L., Asteraceae) chemotypes (i.e. a manipulated gradient of plot-level chemotype richness), we investigated the effect of plot-level chemodiversity and its components on the diversity and composition of canopy-associated arthropod communities within plots. We found significant impacts of the presence of certain chemotypes on the effective number of common arthropod taxa (Hill q = 1) and the effective number of dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots. Importantly, the observed pattern was independent of the actual terpenoid (-)chemodiversity of these chemotypes. We also found that plot-level chemotype richness ({beta}-chemodiversity) reduced the effective number of dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots, driven by impacts on dominance of a nematoceran species associated with Tansy. Cumulative plot terpenoid richness ({gamma}-chemodiversity) did not significantly impact arthropod communities. Instead, we observed that increased terpenoid abundance negatively influenced the effective number of common (Hill q = 1) and dominant arthropod taxa (Hill q = 2) within plots. Our results suggest that within plants of the same species, the chemotypic identity of plants and presence within plots and plot-level chemotype richness ({beta}-chemodiversity) may impact arthropod communities by selecting for specific arthropod taxa making arthropod communities less even. Our results emphasize the nuanced impacts of chemodiversity at different levels and highlight taxon-specific arthropod responses.

title: Unravelling the association between non-essential elements and redox homeostasis in wild roe deer
content: Redox homeostasis, i.e. the balance between oxidative damage and antioxidant defences, is crucial for overall physiological function. Disrupting this balance may lead to oxidative stress. Non-essential elements (e.g. lead, cadmium) exhibit toxicity even at low concentrations and can increase the production of pro-oxidant molecules and impair antioxidant mechanisms. While the adverse effects of acute exposure are well documented, little is known about the impact of chronic, low-level exposure in the wild. Here, we investigated the relationship between non-essential element exposure and redox status in two roe deer populations (Capreolus capreolus), while accounting for the potential modulation by essential elements (e.g. selenium, zinc) and local weather conditions. We measured the concentrations of nine non-essential and thirteen essential elements in hair, and assessed the oxidative status through seven biomarkers in blood samples (n = 649 samples collected between 2016 and 2019). Our findings revealed an elevation of oxidative damage (malondialdehyde and protein carbonyl levels, and reactive oxygen metabolites), and a depletion of an enzymatic antioxidant (SOD activity) but an increase in total antioxidant capacity, with increasing non-essential element content, especially cadmium and mercury. Essential elements showed limited and biomarker-specific associations with redox status, and modulated some of the reported associations between non-essential elements and oxidative stress biomarkers. Finally, individuals that had recently experienced higher temperatures or rainfall exhibited stronger responses. Overall, our study raises concerns regarding the broader consequences of chronic exposure to non-essential elements for wildlife health.

title: Relationships between the isotopic signatures of dissolved inorganic carbon and environmental variability in Northern Ireland coastal waters
content: The isotopic signatures of dissolved inorganic carbon ({delta}13C-DIC) can provide a sensitive tracer of biological and biogeochemical processes in aquatic environments. However, isotopic measurements remain uncommon within routine coastal monitoring programmes. This pilot study investigated spatial variability in {delta}13C-DIC in surface waters across twelve Northern Ireland coastal monitoring stations sampled during July 2020. We tested the relationships between {delta}13C-DIC, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentration, nutrients, chlorophyll-a, temperature and salinity. {delta}13C-DIC exhibited substantial spatial variability, ranging from 1.25 to 2.53{per thousand}. Significant positive relationships were observed between {delta}13C-DIC and temperature (R2 = 0.55, p = 0.009), chlorophyll-a concentration (R2 = 0.38, p = 0.045) and DIC concentration (R2 = 0.52, p = 0.012), while significant negative relationships occurred with dissolved inorganic nitrogen (R2 = 0.53, p = 0.011) and phosphate (R2 = 0.44, p = 0.026). No relationships were detected between {delta}13C-DIC and salinity, suggesting that conservative mixing processes exerted little influence on isotopic variability across the study area. Bulk DIC concentration exhibited comparatively weak associations with environmental variables. The relationships we observed indicate that biological carbon fixation and nutrient use were important controls on spatial variation in {delta}13C-DIC in the coastal waters of Northern Ireland. These findings demonstrate the potential value of {delta}13C-DIC measurements as sensitive indicators of coastal carbon-cycle dynamics and support their inclusion within future coastal monitoring and assessment programmes.

title: Natural pest control in African agriculture: can migratory birds offset the decline of native insectivores?
content: Agricultural expansion and intensification are reducing populations of resident insectivorous birds worldwide, with potentially negative consequences for natural pest control, particularly in the tropics. Many migratory insectivores spend the non-breeding season in the tropics, often favouring disturbed habitats, potentially fulfilling ecological roles once played by resident species. However, few studies have examined the relative impacts of agricultural land-use change on resident and migratory bird species, particularly in the Afrotropics. Using field survey data from five study areas in Zambia, we examine how resident and migratory birds respond to land-use change and assess the contribution of long-distance migrants to invertivore functional diversity in human-modified landscapes. We show that, while resident invertivore richness and abundance decline, migrants are more species-rich and abundant in agricultural habitats than in forests. Trait-based analyses further reveal that migrants contribute unique functional diversity, particularly in smallholder and commercial farms, where their morphological traits overlap and extend beyond the current diversity of residents, occupying an estimated 44% of the total community morphospace in commercial farms. On one hand, our findings highlight the crucial importance of Afrotropical farmland for the conservation of migratory birds. On the other hand, the seasonal influx of migrants may have an important functional consequence, boosting the diversity and pest-predation potential of tropical bird communities. The conservation of migratory bird populations, throughout their breeding and wintering ranges, offers one route to supporting more sustainable agriculture in rapidly changing Afrotropical landscapes.

title: Considering African savanna elephant conservation as a nature-based climate solution
content: The conservation of African savanna ecosystems is recognized as making important contributions toward capturing and storing atmospheric carbon in vegetation and in soils to help mitigate climate change. Also, savannas are important for elephant conservation, which is an increasing priority throughout Africa. However, there is concern that elephants can damage and transform vegetation thereby compromising savanna ecosystems capacities to capture and store carbon. Yet, elephants can have positive effects by releasing body wastes that contribute to nutrient cycling to enhance vegetation productivity (and hence carbon capture). The release of carbon in dung and trampling of soils can enhance long-term carbon storage in soils. Thus, an ecologically holistic assessment of net elephant effects on carbon capture and storage requires accounting for the negative and positive effects together. We report on a holistic assessment of elephant effects using a carbon cycle model that compares savanna ecosystem carbon capture and storage between scenarios with and without elephants. The modeling estimates that elephants at a density of approximately 0.5 individuals per square kilometer could increase average net ecosystem carbon capture by 1.4 times (range of uncertainty of 0.4 to 5.5 times). Elephants are estimated to increase average long-term aboveground carbon stocks by 6.5 times (uncertainty of 2 to 10 times). Average long-term soil carbon storage is estimated to increase by 1.7 times (uncertainty of 0.6 to 5.3 times). The estimated annual carbon capture is large enough to be considered a negative emission in national emissions accounting from land use change, suggesting that savanna elephant conservation should be considered as a nature-based climate solution.

title: Seasonal Ecological Transitions During Wheat Cultivation Reshape Soil Phage‐Host Networks and Carbon Metabolism
content:
Rice–wheat rotation reshaped microbial assembly, enhanced network resistance and modified ecological niche distributions and phage infection patterns. It also increased carbon metabolic potential, with intermediate‐niche bacteria replacing specialists as the dominant contributors to carbon‐related functions.

ABSTRACT
Rice–wheat rotation is a widespread agricultural practice, yet how seasonal crop transitions reshape microbial assembly, phage–host interactions and community functions remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated metagenomic and metaviromic analyses with ecological modelling, network analysis, and functional profiling to compare rice monocropping with winter fallow (RM) and rice–wheat rotation (RWR) across a complete cropping cycle. Crop transitions strongly restructured bacterial and phage communities, with phage assemblages exhibiting greater temporal turnover and stage specificity than bacterial communities. Wheat cultivation increased the contribution of stochastic processes, with bacterial NST increasing from 0.50 to 0.68 and phage NST from 0.12 to 0.25, accompanied by substantial community turnover (maximum RC = 0.800 and 0.894, respectively). Compared with RM, RWR enhanced microbial network stability under simulated disturbances, promoted specialist recruitment, expanded phage–host interaction diversity, and increased carbon metabolic potential with 56 enriched carbon metabolism‐related genes. Collectively, these findings suggest that winter wheat cultivation drives ecological reorganization of soil microbiomes, strengthening network resistance and functional capacity in rice agroecosystems.
