title: Climate warming-induced agricultural nitrous oxide emissions can offset mitigation benefits of fertiliser reduction
content:
Climate warming-induced agricultural nitrous oxide emissions can offset mitigation benefits of fertiliser reduction
Jize Jiang, Lenny H. E. Winkel, Andrea Stenke, Magdalena Necpalova, Moritz Laub, Iris Feigenwinter, Nina Buchmann, and Johan Six
Biogeosciences, 23, 8537–8557, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8537-2026, 2026
We studied how fertiliser management and a warming climate affect nitrous oxide emissions from agricultural soils in Switzerland over the past fourty years. Using computer simulations and nationwide data, we found that lower fertiliser use reduced emissions, but rising temperatures cancelled part of these mitigations. The results show a trade-off between mitigation actions and environmental-driven feedback, highlighting future efforts must also account for the effects of a changing climate.

title: Vegetation Pest Disturbance Detected by Spectral Investigation of Sentinel 1 Time Series: The Case of Toumeyella parvicornis
content:
Abstract
In this study, we assessed the capability of Sentinel‐1 SAR time series to identify disturbances in vegetation linked to the initial stages of pest infestations caused by Toumeyella parvicornis. We utilized Sentinel‐1 VV and VH time series data from 2015 to 2023, available through Google Earth Engine. The analyses focused on two Pinus pinea (stone pine) test sites in central Italy: Castel Porziano (Lazio), which was affected by Toumeyella parvicornis, and Follonica (Tuscany), which remained unaffected throughout the study period. The spectral behavior of the SAR backscatter was analyzed using the correlogram‐based periodogram and the wavelet power spectrum. The correlogram‐based periodograms revealed distinct spectral signatures between the two sites: both exhibited a strong annual cycle related to vegetation seasonality, but Castel Porziano showed an additional low‐frequency component (>2–3 years) indicative of structural changes and degradation. Wavelet analysis highlighted the temporal evolution of these dynamics, showing that in Castel Porziano the annual periodicity weakened or disappeared after mid‐2018, whereas Follonica maintained a stable annual cycle over the entire observation period. Overall, the results demonstrate that Sentinel‐1 data are effective in capturing signs of forest degradation, emphasizing the potential of SAR observations for the retrospective identification of the onset of Toumeyella parvicornis infestations.

title: Impacts of Landscape Sourcing and Dissolved Organic Matter Signatures From the Illinois Waterway to the Mississippi River
content:
Abstract
Watershed land use and hydrology regulate the sourcing of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) into rivers, but uncertainty remains about how these drivers impact organic matter composition and processing throughout river networks. This study investigated the seasonal composition of dissolved organic matter (DOM) throughout the Illinois Waterway, a navigable portion of connected rivers, canals, and channels, spanning 541 km from Lake Michigan to the Mississippi River. We examined the DOM composition via optical and fluorescence spectroscopy combined with ultra‐high resolution mass spectrometry (FT‐ICR MS) to identify organic matter sources and understand their downstream fate. DOM contributions arise from diverse source areas along a landcover gradient that extends from the heavily developed Chicago, Illinois metropolitan area to agricultural watersheds downstream. Aliphatic and sulfur‐containing molecular formulae consistent with wastewater, industrial effluent, and stormwater were enriched in the waters surrounding Chicago and consumed in the middle reaches, while tributaries delivered aromatic, oxygenated, and nitrogen‐containing formulae to the mainstem from watersheds draining row crops. We demonstrate that DOM exported from agricultural watersheds differs between the spring and summer growing seasons, with highly condensed formulae and microbially processed DOM enriched in the summer reflecting the impacts of landscape cultivation. Finally, aliphatic and sulfur‐containing formulae, presumably originating from summer algal blooms, were exported from the Illinois River downstream as a potential biolabile DOM source. This study highlights how seasonal changes in watershed sourcing impact carbon cycling and water quality in the Mississippi basin as well as how specific land use changes influence carbon export across large, developed river networks.

title: Increasing Model Resolution Reveals Nonlinear Ocean–Shelf Exchange Across Submarine Canyon Rich Bathymetry on the Northwest European Shelf
content:
Abstract
Ocean‐shelf exchange is crucial to global biogeochemical cycles. They bring essential nutrients onto the shelf and export carbon of atmospheric origin into the deep ocean via shelf‐edge circulations that have strong depth varying structures, for example, downwelling and upwelling. Numerical models are essential for upscaling observations to estimate shelf‐scale exchange budgets. Small‐scale bathymetric features such as submarine canyons are ubiquitous features of the continental margin and a model's representation of these features impacts the simulated shelf‐edge circulation. We use momentum budgets and a model configured at 1.5 and 7.5 km resolutions to investigate ocean‐shelf exchange on the Northwest European shelf (NWES). We demonstrate that a substantial exchange circulation associated with nonlinear momentum advection emerges at 1.5 km resolution along the submarine canyon‐rich Celtic–Armorican shelf‐edge, but is largely absent at 7.5 km resolution. The circulation is heavily modulated across the spring‐neap tidal cycle. The time‐mean nonlinear circulation increases the simulated 2015 ocean‐shelf exchange circulation across the Armorican‐Celtic shelf‐edge by 9.5× when increasing resolution from 7.5 to 1.5 km in 2015. Total annual‐mean NWES exchange increased from 0.8 to 2 Sv. The nonlinear circulation is highly seasonal with amplified transports in summer and autumn. The large increase in transport at finer resolution is associated with both the emergence of substantial nonlinear contributions to the time‐mean momentum balance and an increase in the resolved length of the shelf‐edge. Our results suggest that coupled biogeochemical models, which are typically coarser resolution, could significantly underestimate regional biogeochemical ocean‐shelf exchange.

title: Damping Effects of Viscous Dissipation on Growth of Symmetric Instability
content:
Abstract
Symmetric instability (SI) is a frontal instability arising from the interaction of rotation with lateral and vertical shear of a frontal jet and is a generalization of shear, centrifugal, and gravitational instabilities. While onset of SI has been studied in numerous observations and models, intuition about its growth comes primarily from constant‐viscosity linear instability analysis and large eddy simulation (LES). Energetic forward cascade arising from SI in the real ocean, where numerous fine‐to‐microscale processes interact with growing SI velocity cells, is less understood. While many instances of symmetrically unstable flow have been observed, observations of enhanced turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) dissipation (ϵ) $({\epsilon})$ at these sites are less common, suggesting a more nuanced forward energy cascade from SI to dissipation. We use numerical instability analysis of an idealized geostrophic jet to show that viscous‐diffusive effects of preexisting turbulence from other turbulent processes (e.g., competing instabilities, internal wave processes, or boundary layer processes) can suppress the growth of SI in the real ocean. For example, a moderate level of ambient turbulence, represented by uniform diffusivity and viscosity of κ=ν=10−4 $\kappa =\nu =1{0}^{-4}$ m2 ${\mathrm{m}}^{2}$/s, restricts the wavelength range of SI’s fastest‐growing mode from O $\mathcal{O}$(10–100)m to O $\mathcal{O}$(100)m and elongates its e‐folding timescale by O $\mathcal{O}$(1–10) hrs, suggesting the net viscous‐diffusive effects of preexisting turbulence can damp the growth of SI. Viscous damping is one possible explanation for the rarity of SI structures in the real ocean, and our results motivate the inclusion of this dependence when parameterizing SI in regional models.

title: Correction to: The plastisphere: not a unique biofilm but a unifying concept for the interdisciplinary plastic biofilm research community
Carbon monoxide utilization by Thermanaeromonas species and description of Thermobium azorense gen. nov., sp. nov.
content:
Abstract
Syngas fermentation by carbon monoxide (CO)-utilizing acetogens offers a sustainable route for converting gasified waste materials into value-added chemicals. In this study, we isolated a novel thermophilic CO-utilizing bacterium, strain AZ2, from marine hydrothermal sediment collected on the island of São Miguel, Azores, Portugal. Strain AZ2 is an obligately anaerobic, spore-forming bacterium. Average nucleotide identity (ANI) and digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) analyses indicate that strain AZ2 represents a novel species within a previously uncharacterized lineage represented by the GTDB placeholder genus UBA 12545 in Neomoorellaceae. It is also the first cultured representative of this genus. Strain AZ2 was able to consume CO, producing acetate. We further demonstrated that its closest isolated relatives—Thermanaeromonas toyohensis and Thermanaeromonas sp. strain 9S—are capable of utilizing CO, producing either acetate or hydrogen gas (H2). Additionally, we unveiled the genomic potential for CO utilization within other members of the GTDB placeholder class DSM-521 (previously Moorellia) to which our isolate belongs, expanding the list of possible thermophilic CO-utilizing acetogens. We propose that strain AZ2T represents the type strain of a novel genus and species, named Thermobium azorense gen. nov., sp. nov. (= DSM 121889T = JCM 39698T).

title: Host species identity drives temporally stable octocoral microbiomes in Florida
content:
Abstract
Octocorals are foundational components of Caribbean reef ecosystems, yet their bacterial microbiomes remain poorly characterized compared to scleractinian corals. We present an extensive 16S rRNA gene survey of western Atlantic octocoral microbiomes, characterizing 180 samples from four co-occurring South Florida species over three years: the encrusting species Briareum asbestinum and Erythropodium caribaeorum, and the branching species Eunicea flexuosa and Muricea muricata. Host species identity was the strongest predictor of microbiome composition, explaining 14.4% of bacterial community variation, while temporal and spatial factors contributed <2% each. Core microbiome analysis at three prevalence thresholds (80%, 90%, and 100%) revealed host-specific bacterial associations. All four species harbored largely host-specific Endozoicomonas ASVs as dominant core members, with encrusting species maintaining larger and more taxonomically diverse cores than branching species. Phylogenetic reconstruction placed the dominant Endozoicomonas ASVs among described Endozoicomonas species, three lineages related to E. euniceicola, which was described from Florida octocorals, while the dominant Mycoplasma ASVs were highly divergent from described type strains, suggesting undescribed octocoral-associated lineages. Differential abundance analysis identified only a few significant temporally or spatially variable ASVs, reinforcing overall community stability. These findings demonstrate strong host control over microbial associations and provide a phylogenetic framework for understanding octocoral–bacteria symbioses in the western Atlantic.

title: The RNA virome of intertidal kelp in New Zealand reveals novel viral lineages associated with unhealthy kelp
content:
Abstract
Pathogens can have major impacts on ecosystem function, especially when they infect foundational taxa such as habitat-forming kelp. Understanding which potentially pathogenic microbes are in an ecosystem is increasingly important as environmental change intensifies ecosystem imbalances, yet few studies have examined which viruses are associated with key habitat-forming macroalgae. Here, we screened multiple populations of intertidal / shallow-subtidal macroalgae in New Zealand for viruses. Samples were collected from three southern bull kelp species: Durvillaea antarctica, Durvillaea poha, and Durvillaea willana. Total RNA was extracted and sequenced from both obviously ‘unhealthy’ kelp tissue and apparently ‘healthy’ tissue. We identified putative novel viral lineages belonging to the families Mitoviridae, Narnaviridae, Partitiviridae, Totiviridae, and the recently proposed Ormycovirus group. Viral abundance and diversity were notably higher at Lawyers Head (the site closest to a city) compared to other sites, especially in unhealthy kelp samples. The elevated viral presence at Lawyers Head may indicate that human impacts, such as pollution, are influencing viral prevalence. This study reveals that coastal macroalgae in New Zealand host diverse viral lineages, some likely pathogenic, and hints at the potential influence of anthropogenic pollution on marine virome composition.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Targeted Metabolomic Analyses Reveal Hepatopancreatic Responses to Prolonged Heat and Cold Exposure in the Invasive Apple Snail Pomacea canaliculata
content:
ABSTRACT
Temperature is a key environmental factor affecting the survival, persistence, and invasion success of Pomacea canaliculata, yet its molecular responses to prolonged thermal stress remain poorly understood. In this study, we integrated transcriptomic and targeted metabolomic analyses to investigate hepatopancreatic responses of P. canaliculata to prolonged heat (35°C) and cold (15°C) exposure for 14 and 28 days in females and 28 days in males, using 25°C as the control. Both treatments altered central carbon and energy metabolism, with dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and xylulose‐5‐phosphate (Xu5P) identified as shared metabolites associated with temperature‐responsive pathways. However, the temporal response patterns differed markedly between the two treatments. High‐temperature stress induced the strongest early response in females, with 1700 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 63 significantly changed metabolites (SCMs) after 14 days, predominantly showing decreased expression or abundance. By day 28, the number of DEGs declined to 1092, while metabolic changes persisted and HSP70 was upregulated, suggesting partial molecular readjustment rather than complete recovery. In contrast, low‐temperature stress produced a more progressive metabolic response, with the number of SCMs increasing from 32 on day 14 to 50 on day 28, accompanied by a shift from fatty acid metabolism toward sphingolipid and amino acid metabolism. Sex‐specific differences were also evident after 28 days, with females exhibiting more extensive transcriptional responses under heat stress, whereas males showed a greater predominance of decreased metabolite abundances under cold stress. Overall, prolonged thermal exposure elicited a shared disturbance of central carbon metabolism together with temperature‐, time‐, and sex‐specific response patterns. These findings provide insight into the molecular and metabolic basis of thermal acclimation and tolerance in invasive P. canaliculata.

title: Effects on Genetic Architecture From Mountain Pine Beetle Mortality in Lodgepole Pine
content:
ABSTRACT
The most recent mountain pine beetle (MPB) [Dendroctonus ponderosae Hopkins (Coleoptera: Curculionidae: Scolytinae)] epidemic caused substantial lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta Dougl. ex Loud. var. latifolia) mortality in western North America over the past three decades. Yet even in stands experiencing considerable MPB‐caused mortality, some surviving lodgepole pine remain on the landscape. Taking advantage of lodgepole pine cone serotiny, we collected cones from MPB‐killed and MPB‐survivor maternal trees to establish a common garden of their progeny to investigate the genetic architecture that is associated with host survival. We genotyped 418 progeny at 14,267 loci and used population, quantitative and landscape genomics to investigate (i) the extent to which severe MPB outbreaks influence genetic diversity of lodgepole pine, (ii) whether progeny of lodgepole pine survivors from a hyperepidemic have different genetic signatures than progeny of MPB‐killed lodgepole pine, (iii) the heritability of pine survival of these MPB outbreaks, and (iv) patterns of spatial variation in genomically‐predicted pine survival of MPB outbreaks. We observed significant reductions in lodgepole pine standing genetic diversity at most sampled sites. Through genomic selection and genome‐wide association analyses we identified loci that differentiated progeny of MPB‐survivor and MPB‐killed trees. Spatial mapping of polygenic survivorship scores shows broad enrichment for predicted survival in the MPB endemic range, with regions of elevated predicted survival also in the expanded range. This study provides evidence that MPB exerts selection pressure on lodgepole pine genotype, and that natural regeneration of lodgepole pine from survivors may increase the genetic variation associated with reduced MPB host quality.

title: The biodiversity of human dwellings: A dataset of 24,000 observations of indoor life in the United States and Canada
content:
Abstract
While modern ecologists spend much of our lives indoors, we have long overlooked the ecological processes taking place there: inside our homes, offices, and classrooms. Yet, the indoors can be a biodiverse landscape in which a variety of interesting ecological phenomena take place. To better understand the indoor ecosystem, we created a citizen science project called Never Home Alone that encourages users of the biodiversity monitoring project iNaturalist to document wildlife found in their homes and other indoor spaces. These observations consist of photos, spatiotemporal data, and notes provided by the observer. In April 2024, we began reviewing project observations from the United States and Canada, removing records that did not meet our inclusion criteria that organisms must be (1) wild, and (2) observed indoors. A team of taxonomic experts then identified every observation to the finest possible taxonomic resolution. The final reviewed dataset contains 23,782 observations of indoor life observed by approximately 3000 observers between May 1996 and April 2024. The data span all US states and Canadian provinces (though not the Canadian territories). Most observations were from homes, but participants also submitted observations from offices, schools, airports, and other human dwellings. Approximately 95% of observations were arthropods, predominantly insects (60%; mostly Coleoptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera, Hymenoptera, and Hemiptera) and spiders (30%). Chordates (4%)—primarily reptiles and mammals—made up most of the remainder, though the database also contains indoor fungi, plants, annelids, mollusks, crustaceans, ciliates, and many other groups. The most common species (>200 observations each) were, in descending order, the Asian lady beetle (Harmonia axyridis), brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys), house centipede (Scutigera coleoptrata), varied carpet beetle (Anthrenus verbasci), long‐bodied cellar spider (Pholcus phalangioides), triangulate combfoot spider (Steatoda triangulosa), bathroom moth fly (Clogmia albipunctata), and Eastern parson spider (Herpyllus ecclesiasticus). In total, the dataset includes nearly 2100 unique species, though this is likely an undercount given that 44% of observations could not be identified to species level. Approximately 52% of the species in the dataset were only observed indoors once. This dataset represents the first continental‐scale survey of indoor species. While a few previous studies have surveyed indoor biodiversity, this prior work was either at a much smaller spatial scale or used eDNA techniques that have certain taxonomic biases and comparatively lower taxonomic resolution. Given that data collection for this project was not effort‐controlled, this dataset likely contains biases of its own (e.g., overrepresentation of large‐bodied taxa). Additionally, some organisms observed indoors are not necessarily synanthropic, instead, being documented after becoming trapped inside human structures. Nevertheless, this dataset provides a useful complement to the few existing indoor biodiversity surveys and the data are particularly relevant to understanding the synanthropic species most commonly encountered by people. As indoor space expands globally, this dataset offers new opportunities to explore the life traits, evolution, natural history, and distribution of organisms that may be exploiting new niches created by the built environment. Such studies may lead to findings relevant to evolutionary ecology, community ecology, urban ecology, global change, and human health. The data are available for reuse under CC BY 4.0 licensing. Please cite the data release on Zenodo and this data paper when reusing the dataset.

title: Ionic condition-dependent allostery shapes ribosomal dynamics
content:
by Danis Yangaliev, Gürol M. Süel, S. Banu Ozkan

Ionic composition is a key determinant of ribosomal RNA structure and function. Metal cations such as potassium (K+) and magnesium (Mg2+) stabilize rRNA architecture. While certain positions in the ribosome are strictly occupied by either potassium or magnesium for distinct structural or functional reasons, their broader role in modulating ribosomal dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we use microsecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of the bacterial 70S ribosome to examine how ionic composition affects structural flexibility and long-range communication. We compare a native ribosome with experimentally resolved ions to two variants: a magnesium-enriched model, in which K+ ions are replaced with Mg2+, and a hydrated magnesium model. While these substitutions do not aim to reproduce physiological ionic conditions, they provide a controlled framework to isolate the physical effects of ion identity on ribosomal dynamics. Increasing magnesium content reduces ionic and backbone mobility and enhances rigidity within the ribosomal core. Dynamic Flexibility Index analysis shows that these changes extend beyond local coordination sites, producing flexibility shifts at distances exceeding 30 Å. Dynamic Coupling Index analysis further reveals that ionic perturbations reshape long-range communication pathways. Functionally important regions, including the L1 and L7/12 stalks, exhibit distinct, ion-dependent responses, while the L10–L11 region shows enhanced long-range coupling under varying ionic conditions. These results demonstrate that ionic composition modulates both local stability and global ribosomal dynamics, with implications for translational efficiency and fidelity.

title: A hybrid mixture approach for clustering and characterizing biomedical data
content:
by Kazeem A. Kareem, Fan Dai

Model-based clustering (MBC) is widely used for identifying latent groups and characterizing heterogeneous structures in biomedical data. However, modern biomedical studies often generate datasets with large sample sizes and many variables, for which standard MBC approaches can be difficult to fit reliably and efficiently. Mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) addresses part of this challenge by representing high-dimensional covariance structures through a few underlying factors, thereby reducing the covariance dimensionality. However, current estimation methods for MFA are often computationally impractical for massive data due to the slow convergence of nested EM-type algorithms. Moreover, many existing implementations require a common number of latent factors across clusters, limiting their ability to capture group-specific structures. We propose a hybrid matrix-free computational scheme for accurate and efficient estimation of Gaussian mixture of factor analyzers, which avoids explicit construction or storage of large covariance matrices. We further develop a generalized version that allows different clusters to have varying numbers of factors, providing additional flexibility for group-specific characterization. Simulation studies show that the proposed approach achieves substantially faster convergence than the existing method, especially in high-dimensional settings, while preserving high clustering and estimation accuracy. Applications to the Wisconsin breast cancer dataset, a lymphoma gene-expression dataset, and a human brain single-cell RNA sequencing dataset demonstrate accurate identification of benign/malignant breast tumors, lymphoma subtypes, and neuronal and astrocytic cell populations. The fitted factor-loading structures reveal biologically meaningful differences in nuclear morphology for breast tumors, with malignant samples showing stronger irregularity-related variation, group-specific gene-expression heterogeneity among the three lymphoma subtypes, and distinct patterns of transcriptional variation between neurons and astrocytes, with neuronal variation reflecting a broader set of coordinated transcriptional directions and astrocytic variation concentrated in a more compact latent structure.

title: Inferring population-level physiologically based model parameters for sleep in infancy and young childhood
content:
by Lachlan Webb, Andrew J. K. Phillips, James A. Roberts

The sleep patterns of infants and young children differ from adult sleep patterns, with longer duration and multiple bouts per 24 hours. There is also considerable heterogeneity in infant sleep, both between individuals and within individuals across development. While mathematical models have been used to understand the mechanisms that regulate adult sleep, the development of sleep from infancy through early childhood has remained largely unexplored. Here we used an established mathematical model for adult sleep regulation to investigate how the underlying mechanisms of sleep mature from ages 1 month to 5 years, and identify a basis for inter-individual differences at each age. Using a Bayesian approach to estimate joint distributions of model parameters at different ages, we found that: (i) decreases in the rate of accumulation of sleep homeostatic pressure captured the reduction in sleep duration across development; while (ii) increases in the time scale of the sleep homeostatic drive captured the consolidation of sleep into fewer sleep bouts per day across development. In terms of inter-individual differences, we found larger spread in the parameters within the earlier stages of infancy (<1 year). The center and boundaries of the joint distributions evolved with age through the parameter space, converging towards previously described adult parameter values. A bifurcation analysis of the homeostatic time scale parameter revealed that progressive consolidation of sleep occurs through abrupt loss of bouts one at a time, punctuated by narrow intervals of non-entrained (>24-h) cycles. These results establish plausible, population-level trajectories in physiological parameters underpinning maturation of sleep regulation through infancy and early childhood.

title: Rollout models of human planning with exact action probabilities
content:
by Jeroen Olieslagers, Wei Ji Ma

One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or “rollout,” of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.

title: Simulation-guided design of exotendons to reduce the energetic cost of running
content:
by Jon Stingel, Nicholas Bianco, Carmichael Ong, Steve Collins, Scott Delp, Jennifer Hicks

A passive device that attaches to the feet, called an exotendon, can reduce the energetic cost of running at moderate speeds, but its efficacy and optimal design parameters at higher speeds are unknown. Identifying optimal parameters at new speeds experimentally would require many experimental trials with different exotendon designs, which is challenging for participants at higher running speeds. We developed a muscle-driven simulation framework to predict the effect of various exotendon designs on the energetic cost of running at an experimentally untested speed (4 m/s). We used these predictions to select four designs, which we evaluated experimentally as users ran at this speed. The framework correctly predicted that an exotendon that reduced energetic cost at 2.7 m/s would also reduce energetic cost at 4 m/s (10% predicted vs. 5.7% measured) and that a short, stiff exotendon and a long, compliant exotendon would not significantly reduce energetic cost. However, exotendon parameters predicted by the simulation to maximize energetic savings did not significantly reduce energetic cost when evaluated experimentally. There was variability between participants in both the magnitude of maximum energy savings and the exotendon condition associated with those savings. In a 5-km time trial performed with and without the exotendon condition that elicited the largest energy savings for each participant during the experiment, we observed a lower average heart rate (-3.9 ± 3.8 beats/min; P = 0.03; mean ± standard deviation) and increased cadence (15.9 ± 9.6 steps/min; P = 0.002) when participants ran with the exotendon but did not observe a statistically significant difference in finishing time (-13.5 ± 24.6 sec; P = 0.3). These results demonstrate exotendons can reduce energetic cost across multiple running speeds and that predictive simulations provide a framework for guiding experiments to evaluate assistive device designs.

title: Pupil dynamics reflect uncertainty-driven adjustments of probability learning
content:
by Aaron Greenhouse-Tucknott, Cedric Foucault, Anne Buot, Florent Meyniel

Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain’s ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.

title: When and how is preregistration in experimental biology worth the effort?
content:
by Olavo B. Amaral, Clarissa F. D. Carneiro, Bruna Valério-Gomes, Kleber Neves, Mariana B. Abreu

Preregistration can improve the credibility of published research, but its uptake in the life sciences remains low. What is hampering its adoption in experimental biology, and can the format be adapted to better suit the needs of researchers? Preregistration can improve the credibility of published research, but its uptake in the life sciences remains low. This Perspective asks what is hampering its adoption in experimental biology, and can the format be adapted to better suit the needs of researchers?

title: Tipping the frontier of climate and nature investment
content:
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00862-3

The world is not short of capital, yet investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation, biodiversity conservation, and ecosystem restoration remains well below required levels. A key constraint lies in how investors assess complex investment environments. Rethinking their assessment frameworks could thus help tip finance towards climate and nature goals.

title: Achieving transformative recovery following natural disasters
content:
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00863-2

Natural disasters create pressure to rebuild quickly, but rushing to reinstate the status quo can restore or amplify the very exposures and inequities that contributed to losses. Recovery systems must aim to reduce future risk, centre equity, and integrate physical, social, economic, and environmental resilience across decades rather than funding cycles.

title: Cognitive control networks in human and macaque
content: A much-replicated finding in human brain imaging is a distributed ‘multiple-demand’ or MD system, increasing in activity for many kinds of cognitive demand, and centrally involved in cognitive control. MD regions are proposed to encode a distributed mental model of critical task events, bound together in the roles and relationships needed to direct action selection. Though previous data hint at a corresponding network in the macaque, there has been no direct comparison to human data. Here we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure whole-brain activation in a multi-step saccadic maze task, compared to a control requiring similar moves but without goal-based decisions. Human data were a close match to the canonical MD network, extended to include adjacent regions, and in particular much of the canonical dorsal attention network. Data from two monkeys suggested correspondences in dorsomedial frontal, insula/orbitofrontal, and posterior temporal cortex. In lateral frontal cortex, there was just a single, largely dorsal activation patch, in contrast to multiple distinct human patches. In one animal, as in humans, there was accompanying activation of dorsal and medial parietal cortex. In macaques, as in humans, together with previous data, our findings suggest an extended and strongly interconnected brain network recruited by increased cognitive challenge.

title: Blood-derived dietary protein promotes sleep in the mosquito Aedes aegypti
content: Sleep is a ubiquitous, yet highly variable, behavior across species. The duration and timing of sleep are influenced by ecological demands and dietary context. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti, a blood-feeding insect with specialized nutritional requirements, the relationship between feeding and sleep remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how blood-derived dietary protein influences sleep regulation. Using postural analysis, videography, and arousal-threshold assays, we established that immobility bouts of ≥10 min reliably define sleep in A. aegypti. Mosquitoes lacking the circadian clock gene cycle still maintained daily sleep rhythms but exhibited reduced sleep duration and heightened overall activity. Infrared activity monitoring revealed that blood-fed females showed a marked increase in sleep beginning immediately after feeding and persisting for several days, accompanied by reduced locomotor activity. Notably, this sleep elevation lasted well beyond the cessation of previously reported host-seeking phases, raising the possibility of distinct phases of opportunistic vs. targeted host pursuit. To determine the dietary basis of this effect, we tested mosquitoes fed a bovine serum albumin (BSA)-based diet. BSA feeding alone was sufficient to mimic the sleep-promoting and activity-reducing effects of blood, suggesting dietary protein is a major nutritional regulator. Moreover, RNAi-mediated knockdown of the leucokinin receptor (Lkr), which has previously been associated with fluid homeostasis and feeding behavior, resulted in enhanced sleep and reduced activity, implicating mosquito LK signaling in the modulation of postprandial sleep. Together, these findings demonstrate that blood-derived proteins drive sustained increases in sleep and reductions in locomotor activity in A. aegypti. This work positions A. aegypti as a model for dissecting nutrient-specific regulation of sleep and highlights potential adaptive functions of protein-induced quiescence, such as energy conservation and predator avoidance. More broadly, it provides insight into how specialized diets shape the neural and behavioral architecture of sleep.

title: Correction: MotorNet, a Python toolbox for controlling differentiable biomechanical effectors with artificial neural networks
Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
content: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal–neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

Extreme precipitation events are increasing in many regions. Here the authors discuss how the increasing concurrence of atmospheric phenomena could contribute to these trends under anthropogenic warming.

title: Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier–lake interactions
content:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02808-5

The contribution of glacial lakes to glacier mass loss is unclear. This work maps global glacial lakes in 2000 and 2020 to quantify changes in number, volume and area, showing that they explain 11 ± 7% of lake-terminating glacier loss, with climate forcing and glacier geometry the dominant factors.

title: Mediterranean low-salinity and anoxic sapropel events triggered by Atlantic atmospheric moisture
content:

Elevated Atlantic-sourced atmospheric moisture was a key driver of low-salinity events in the Mediterranean linked to Pleistocene sapropel formation, according to precipitation reconstructions from the region.

title: A differential-trend-subtype strategy for integrated serum proteomics and N-glycoproteomics reveals ovarian cancer-associated remodelling
content: Protein glycosylation is increasingly implicated in cancer, but its macro- and microheterogeneity complicate cohort-scale resolution of disease-associated remodeling. Here we performed matched peptide-level proteomic (PEP) and intact N-glycopeptide (NGP) profiling of serum from 100 participants, comprising 23 healthy controls, 27 individuals with benign ovarian disease and 50 patients with ovarian cancer. We identified 12,634 intact NGPs with plausible linkages spanning 6,127 protein-site glycosites and 4,438 glycoproteins. We developed a Differential-Trend-Subtype (DTS) target-prioritization framework integrating ovarian cancer versus non-malignant differences, cross-sectional healthy-benign-cancer trends and within-cancer subtype effects. Independent PEP and NGP clustering supported two aligned molecular states, assigning 47 of 50 cancer samples concordantly. Among 171 subtype-associated NGPs, cluster 1-high (C1-high) features were more frequently fucosylated, whereas cluster 2-high (C2-high) features were more frequently sialylated. DTS strategy prioritized a more informative pool of candidate features. Under leakage-controlled nested resampling, the best exploratory diagnostic panel-comprising PON1, HP and C9 peptide features together with an IGHM N209 N-glycopeptide-achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.843+-0.026, whereas the best subtype panel-comprising C2 N621 and IGHG1 N180 N-glycopeptides together with SERPINA3-achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.997+-0.005. These findings demonstrate the utility of DTS for prioritizing candidate markers and reveal coordinated protein and site-specific N-glycan remodelling with potential relevance to ovarian cancer diagnosis and molecular stratification.

title: CsrA-dependent RNA accessibility landscapes prioritize new mRNA and sRNA targets and link CsrA to polyphosphate homeostasis
content: The global RNA-binding protein CsrA (Carbon Storage Regulatory Protein A) regulates diverse physiological processes in Gammaproteobacteria, but the full set of RNAs through which it actuates and how they intersect with small RNA (sRNA) regulation and stress physiology remain incompletely defined. We asked how CsrA shapes RNA accessibility across 431 untranslated mRNA regions and 87 sRNAs in Escherichia coli. Using a previously published RNA accessibility profiling method (INTERFACE), we compared wild type and CsrA mutant (csrA::kan) strains. Permissive screening for accessibility peaks at GGA/AGA motifs nominated 87 5'UTRs, 32 3'UTRs and 28 sRNAs as candidate responsive RNAs but did not pass a permutation null (p=0.43), however it can be used to guide selection of candidates for validation. Eleven 5'UTRs had no prior experimental evidence, and all 3'UTRs and most sRNAs were nominated manually because of limited probe numbers in these targets. In reporter assays, six of nine RNAs tested showed CsrA-dependent expression (mdtE, ribB, patA, metC, ppk and proS) including three candidate activated-targets, although only two of five reporters from the primary candidate list responded. CsrA bound the sRNAs SsrA and RalA in vitro, and reporter assays suggested CsrA-dependent modulation of previously identified ArrS-ribB and GcvB-crp interactions. Mutating sequence elements in the ppk 5' UTR altered CsrA-dependent expression, and loss of CsrA-activity was associated with reduced polyphosphate and fewer Hfq-containing HP-bodies during nitrogen starvation. Together, these findings expand the CsrA regulon and its overlap with sRNA networks, and support accessibility profiling to prioritize RNA-binding protein targets for follow-up characterization.

title: Detection of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium and discrimination of vanA and vanB genotypes by VITEK MS Prime MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry and machine learning
content: Rapid identification of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and discrimination of resistance mechanisms (VanA and VanB) are critical for appropriate antimicrobial therapy and infection control, particularly during outbreaks. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), combined with machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool for this purpose. We evaluated whether MALDI-TOF mass spectra acquired on VITEK MS PRIME, combined with machine learning, could provide this information. Spectra from 388 from clinical and rectal surveillance samples (135 vancomycin-susceptible (VSEfm), 138 vanA and 115 vanB VREfm) were processed with Clover MSDAS, and four algorithms (partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), linear and polynomial support vector machines (SVM-L and SVM-P) and random forest (RF)) were trained to discriminate VSEfm from VREfm and VanA from VanB isolates. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation and using independent set of characterized E. faecium isolates from routine practice. Pairwise and triplet ensembles of these algorithms were also assessed. In the test set, PLS-DA was the best individual classifier for VSEfm versus VREfm (balanced accuracy, 78.9%), and the ensemble of PLS-DA and linear SVM reached 80.7%. Validation within routine isolates confirmed the models robustness, achieving 100% correct classification. Discrimination of VanA from VanB was more accurate: 93.2% with RF and up to 97.1% with ensembles. Identical sequence types were found among susceptible, VanA and VanB isolates, indicating that classification was not driven by clonal lineage. MALDI-TOF MS combined with machine learning is a promising, low-cost tool for VREfm screening and vanA/vanB differentiation.

title: Comprehensive identification of bacterial and archaeal habitat associations using IndicPiper
content: Taxa that are prevalent and abundant in a particular habitat more so than other habitats can be considered indicators of that habitat. In addition to providing basic natural history information, indicator taxa can be used to verify metadata assignments in large public databases, identify potential contamination, and assess contributions of different source populations to a sink population. Despite these potential applications, a comprehensive database of microbial indicator taxa for major habitats of interest does not yet exist. Here we present IndicPiper, a database and methodology that uses the Sandpiper database combined with indicator taxa analysis to identify the habitat associations of bacterial and archaeal genera. IndicPiper includes a clearly defined methodology and set of functions such that any user with a list of habitats of interest could run the functions and generate their own database. IndicPiper uses the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) for taxonomy, and the provided database or custom databases can be used to analyze any prokaryotic sample-by-taxa abundance table, including those from shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA marker gene sequencing. After presenting the methodology and results, we then present three applications of IndicPiper on actual modern and ancient DNA sequencing datasets. We used IndicPiper to assess the contribution of different source habitats to Lake Tjornin sediments in Iceland over the past 2000 years, to paired indoor and outdoor dust samples from homes across the U.S, and to freshwater samples across the Willamette River watershed in Oregon, USA.

title: Beyond the tripartite genome: a widespread, mobile and gene-rich accessory plasmidome expands the genomic landscape of the model symbiont Sinorhizobium meliloti
content: Sinorhizobium meliloti is one of the best-studied nitrogen-fixing symbionts, yet research has focused almost entirely on its chromosome and two megaplasmids, pSymA and pSymB. Many strains carry additional accessory plasmids, but these large, pSymA-like elements are rarely recovered from short-read assemblies, leaving a hidden part of the genome unexplored. By sequencing 346 strains with long reads, we recovered 386 accessory plasmids from 76% of strains, with 318 absent from public databases, showing that accessory plasmids are the rule and not the exception. These plasmids were large (34-749 kb), including the largest accessory plasmid reported in S. meliloti, and most were mobilizable or conjugative (relaxases in 85% and mating-pair formation systems in 75% of plasmid clusters), equipping them to move between strains. RepA typing defined 13 replicon groups unique to Sinorhizobium, which could serve as a framework for tracking these plasmids in natural populations. We also found evidence of plasmid expansion by fusion, and one ~315 kb plasmid was a cointegrate of two smaller plasmids from our collection. About two-thirds of plasmid gene families were absent from the main replicons, including defense systems, the anti-restriction protein ArdC, and biosynthetic gene clusters, 53% of which had never been observed before. Overturning the view that S. meliloti lacks restriction-modification systems, we found them in 153 genomes, including on 32 accessory plasmids. Most inferred gene transfers stayed within the family Rhizobiaceae. Accessory plasmids thus form a large, mobile and largely unexplored gene pool that may shape how this model symbiont competes and adapts.

title: Gene identity, not recoding strategy, determines the fitness cost of synonymous recoding in bacteriophage {Phi}X174
content: Synthetic biology allows for the synthesis of genomes from scratch. Although technically achievable, our abilities in designing genomes that result in live organisms are in their infancy. One important consideration is synonymous codon usage bias, which is present in most organisms and shaped by selection for efficient translation. Many studies have edited the synonymous codon usage patterns of viruses with the goal of viral attenuation, but these studies almost always build a single construct per design, so we know little about how repeatable the effects of recoding are. We designed and built 111 synonymously recoded {Phi}X174 genomes, applying four recoding strategies at up to five levels of attenuation to each of three genes, with three independently designed replicates of most combinations. Which gene we recoded mattered considerably more than how we recoded it. Recoding genes for the major capsid protein F, the major spike protein G and the DNA pilot protein H in full, with the least-used synonym codons from E. coli cost 12.0, 10.8 and 5.9 doublings per hour, respectively. Recoding strategy per se had no detectable effect once the number of codons changed was accounted for. Predicted mRNA folding stability also had no measurable effect on fitness when tested in gene F, whose wildtype transcript is highly stable and could easily be destabilized with synonymous codon rearrangements. While the number of codons changed was correlated with the degree of attenuation, divergence between independently designed replicates increased as more codons were edited. Replicates of designs with small fitness effects varied little, while replicates of strongly attenuating designs diverged by several doublings per hour. The fitness outcome of large-scale genome recoding is therefore substantially unpredictable from the design variables alone: even among independently designed genomes receiving the same treatment, fitness can diverge substantially.

title: Pharmacological CARD9 Inhibition Reduces Pneumocystis murina Burden In Vivo and Ex Vivo
content: Caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 9 (CARD9) is an important adaptor protein of the innate immune responses to various fungal pathogens, including Pneumocystis species. CARD9 signaling is paramount in Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) host defense, and excessive inflammatory responses driven by this molecule can promote deleterious lung injury. We previously demonstrated that BRD5529, a first generation small-molecule CARD9 inhibitor, attenuates pulmonary inflammatory cytokine production during PCP. Here, we investigated the previously unreported effects of BRD5529 on Pneumocystis murina burden in vivo and in an ex vivo PCP-infected precision-cut lung slice (PCLS) model. In vitro, BRD5529 treatment (1 mg/kg) reduced lung organism burden in mice with established PCP, with an effect similar in magnitude to standard-of-care trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) therapy. In infected PCLS cultured with BRD5529 for 72 h, P. murina viability was also reduced, with the greatest reduction observed at lower BRD5529 concentrations. BRD5529 treatment did not reduce PCLS metabolic activity and viability after 72 h, as assessed by resazurin reduction. Together, these findings suggest that pharmacological CARD9 inhibition may impact organism burden/viability in addition to reducing lung inflammation during PCP.

title: Linking Early Bacterial Responses to Growth Inhibition via Glucose-Turbidity Dynamics for Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing
content: Earlier susceptibility information can guide timely antibiotic selection, while metabolic measurements can broaden the characterization of bacterial drug responses. We developed glucose-turbidity antimicrobial susceptibility testing (GT-AST) to pair residual-glucose assay signals with turbidity and relate early responses to growth inhibition. Among 43 cultured isolates, some antibiotic-exposed cultures showed glucose-associated changes despite attenuated turbidity responses. These observations provide physiological clues for studying metabolic activity when growth is limited, including future investigations of viable but non-culturable states or persister cells. Conventional broth microdilution relies on overnight growth readings; GT-AST used trajectories collected during approximately 2 h of antibiotic exposure to predict subsequent growth and estimate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Across 100 repeats of isolate-grouped cross-validation, essential agreement between predicted MICs and independently measured reference MICs averaged 87.1%. Eight bronchoalveolar lavage fluid specimens were tested directly without prior bacterial isolation. Levofloxacin susceptibility classifications based on observed growth agreed with hospital results in all four culture-positive specimens. Exact and essential agreement between predicted and hospital MICs each averaged 99.0%. Together, these findings support developing GT-AST to provide earlier susceptibility information for effective, appropriately targeted treatment of patients. Keywords: antimicrobial susceptibility testing; glucose metabolism; turbidity; machine learning; minimum inhibitory concentration

title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Host Gene Expression Patterns Associated with Naegleria fowleri Infection in the Murine Brain
content: Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM), caused by the free-living amoebae Naegleria fowleri, is a devastating disease with a mortality rate exceeding 97%. Despite its severity, the spatial and temporal characteristics of the host immune response to infection within the brain remain poorly understood. Here, we used spatially resolved transcriptomic profiling to characterize region-specific gene expression patterns in brain tissue collected at multiple time points following intranasal inoculation of N. fowleri in mice. Our analysis revealed pronounced pro-inflammatory transcriptional signatures that varied across brain regions and over the course of infection. Cell type-associated gene expression profiles suggested the involvement of several immune cell populations, including macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer T cells, alongside transcriptional changes associated with neural cell populations. Notably, inflammatory transcriptional signatures also were detected in brain regions without detectable amoebae, indicating that host responses extend beyond regions of apparent parasite localization. Collectively, these findings provide a spatial and temporal characterization of the host transcriptional response during experimental PAM, highlighting inflammatory gene expression signatures and putative immune and neural cell populations associated with disease progression. This study provides a foundation for future investigations into the cellular and molecular processes underlying neuroinflammation during N. fowleri infection.

title: An Infected Cryopreserved Precision-Cut Lung Slice Model for Drug Susceptibility Testing in Pneumocystis murina Pneumonia
content: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.

title: MetaEntropy: quantifying protein variability in complex viral mixtures via entropy
content: High-density sequence data has become commonplace in the study of complex viral mixtures from wastewater. Established algorithms are available for lineage deconvolution and labelling of clinically-elusive mutations. However, less attention has been paid to the quantification of translated amino acid diversity. We present MetaEntropy, a modular R package for assessing protein sequence variability and identifying sites under potential selection via Shannon entropy. MetaEntropy integrates utility functions for visualizing genome-wide and protein-specific variability, extracting nucleotide and amino acid mutation profiles, and identifying entropy hotspots. Despite being designed for wastewater surveillance, the package can also profile protein diversity from cross-sectional intra-patient data. However, it does not analyze population structure or quasispecies, for which several tools are available. By focusing on positional entropy, MetaEntropy bypasses the sequence constraints, computational overhead, and consensus-based variant loss typical of traditional haplotype reconstruction and multiple sequence alignment strategies. To balance sensitivity against neutral variation, the package evaluates entropy using a standard 20-class canonical amino acid scheme and a 7-class model based on traditional physicochemical properties. Calculated entropy values are normalized to a 0-1 scale, enabling direct comparisons of protein diversity across loci and sample strata. As proofs of concept, we employ MetaEntropy to detect well-known SARS-CoV-2 functional changes from wastewater data, and to explore tissue-specific heterogeneity in systemic infections. MetaEntropy is available from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) at https://CRAN.R-project.org/.

title: Charge-engineered nanohybrid coatings for microbial fouling resistance
content: Microbial attachment is the gateway to biofouling and microbially influenced corrosion. Yet biocides and passive barrier coatings do not actively regulate the charged metal-microbe interface at which adhesion begins. Here we report a charge-engineered coating, a graphene thin-film nanohybrid (gTFN) on nickel (Ni) forming an asymmetric metal-graphene-metal junction, that suppresses cell attachment through interfacial charge redistribution rather than soluble toxicity. Against the model sulfate-reducing bacterium Oleidesulfovibrio alaskensis G20, gTFN combines an impermeable graphene scaffold, an immobilized low-leaching Ag cap and a serrated topology, reducing microbial surface coverage by 98%, increasing charge-transfer resistance 47-fold and lowering corrosion current 167-fold relative to Ni. Surface-potential mapping and density functional theory reveal interfacial dipoles that pattern the surface potential, while imaging shows graphene wrinkles channeling residual attachment. Transcriptomic profiling reveals downregulation of biofilm-associated and energy-metabolism genes. These results establish interfacial charge redistribution as an active antifouling and anticorrosion mechanism for controlling microbial biointerfaces.

title: HIV-1 Mutational Bias Shapes the Supply of Drug Resistance Mutations
content: The development of durable HIV-1 therapeutics requires understanding not only which mutations confer resistance, but also how readily those mutations arise. Prior work has characterized the effects of individual mutations on viral fitness and drug or immune escape; however, the contribution of mutational bias to HIV-1 evolutionary pathways remains largely unquantified. Here, we report and provide an interactive HIV-1 Mutation Rate Atlas (MRA), built on a dataset of empirical measurements of single-cycle HIV-1 mutation accumulation in the absence of selection pressure, using error-corrected long-read sequencing. The MRA estimates the mutation rate at every genomic position to each possible nucleotide, enabling evaluation of amino acid mutability across the genome. Using the MRA, we show that mutation rate biases predict HIV-1 drug resistance variant frequencies across patients. These results demonstrate that mutational biases shape HIV-1 evolutionary outcomes, providing a framework for predicting HIV-1 evolution and drug resistance.

title: Pyrenophora teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures to facilitate effector-driven promotion of in planta colonization on barley
content: Pyrenophora teres f. teres is a necrotrophic fungal pathogen that causes net form net blotch (NFNB) of barley. Infection of susceptible barley leaves initially causes dot-like lesions that progress to transverse and longitudinal striations, that form the net-like pattern of necrosis for which the disease was named. While the complex genetic architecture of the P. teres f. teres-barley interaction involves both dominant resistance and susceptibility and quantitative resistance, the in planta infection structures, compatible infection timeline, and the influence of effectors remain poorly defined. This study used fluorescent staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to define infection structures and characterize the compatible infection timeline of P. teres f. teres. Using CLSM in conjunction with image-segmentation machine learning, we generated a clear comparative infection timeline showing how P. teres f. teres isolates harboring zero, one, or two virulence effector alleles infect the barley cultivar Rika. We believe that the effector genes VR1 and VR2 contributed to virulence in a synergistic manner. The effector genes combined presence accelerated the timing and spread of programmed cell death, resulting in significantly greater hyphal volume and visibly more severe macroscopic lesion development. This suggests that P. teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures alongside effectors to maximize fungal colonization and hyphal positioning to optimize nutrient uptake, perpetuating its polycyclic life cycle.

title: Multiple Glycans and IFITM Proteins Mediate Human Coronavirus OC43 entry
content: Human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43 is the most prevalent seasonal coronavirus, causing colds, and occasional severe disease. HCoV-OC43 attachment is reportedly mediated by 9-O acetylated sialic acid (9-O-Ac-Sia); no proteinaceous receptor has been identified. Using genome-wide CRISPR-cas9 screens, we identify several host factors that mediate HCoV-OC43 entry. First, we identify NXPE3, an esterase, as required for HCoV-OC43 attachment and infection, both in vitro and in vivo, and demonstrate a previously unknown role for NXPE3 in 9-O-Ac-Sia synthesis. However, we further show that single residue substitutions in HCoV-OC43 spike, in the S1A domain at the 9-O-Ac-Sia binding site, or two substitutions in the S1B domain, confer 9-O-Ac-Sia independence and a switch to heparan sulfate-dependent entry. Additionally, we find that IFITM1/2/3 proteins act post-attachment to drive HCoV-OC43 virion-cell fusion and entry, irrespective of which attachment mechanism is used. Thus, flexible use of glycan attachment factors enables HCoV-OC43 to access fusion-driving IFITM proteins during entry.

title: Deletion of two candidate depolymerases with overlapping genetic effects increases PHA yield in Rhodopseudomonas palustris TIE-1
content: Polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) is a microbial carbon-storage polymer with potential as a renewable bioplastic, but intracellular remobilization can limit polymer retention. The metabolically versatile bacterium Rhodopseudomonas palustris TIE-1 accumulates PHA during photoheterotrophic growth, yet the enzymes that control PHA turnover in this organism remain incompletely studied. We identified PhaZ2 (Rpal_0568) as a second candidate PHA depolymerase that is evolutionarily and architecturally distinct from the previously annotated PhaZ1 (Rpal_0578). Deleting either PhaZ1 or PhaZ2 alone did not substantially increase PHA content under tested growth conditions, whereas the double mutant accumulated 2.3-fold and 1.7-fold more PHA than wild type under non-nitrogen-fixing and nitrogen-fixing photoheterotrophic conditions, respectively, supporting overlapping roles in PHA turnover. All deletion strains showed longer doubling times but reached final culture densities similar to wild type. The double mutant showed its strongest retention phenotype under severe but growth-permissive nutrient limitation, including 3.7-fold more PHA than wild type at 33% phosphorus availability. A two-stage cultivation strategy that separated biomass formation from nutrient-limited storage raised volumetric PHA titer to 0.180 mg per mL culture in the double mutant, 1.5-fold more than wild type and approximately 3.4-fold higher than single-stage 33% phosphorus limitation and 4.0-fold higher than single-stage 8% nitrogen limitation (cross-experiment comparison), despite lower PHA content per unit biomass. Finally, an LC-MS-calibrated FTIR spectroscopy model predicted PHA content with an R2 of 0.928 (n = 15) and reproduced the major biological trends. These results identify genetically redundant candidate depolymerases as targets for improving PHA retention in TIE-1 and establish a cultivation and screening framework for strain engineering. Importance Persistent pollution from petroleum-based plastics has intensified the need for biodegradable plastics produced from renewable resources. Polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) is a microbially synthesized bioplastic, but microbial cells can also consume the stored polymer, reducing its net yield. The metabolically versatile, photosynthetic purple non-sulfur bacterium (PNSB) Rhodopseudomonas palustris TIE-1 is a promising production organism because it can photosynthesize, assimilate atmospheric nitrogen, and utilize diverse carbon sources. We show that two candidate PHA depolymerases, PhaZ1 and PhaZ2, likely have overlapping roles in PHA turnover. Removing both candidates increased polymer retention, particularly when nitrogen or phosphorus was limited, and a two-stage cultivation strategy further increased PHA titer to 0.180 mg per mL of culture. We also developed a rapid infrared spectroscopy method to track polymer content across strains and growth conditions. These findings offer complementary genetic, cultivation, and screening strategies for improving microbial bioplastic production and may help advance sustainable alternatives to petroleum-derived plastics.

title: Targeting host eIF4A with zotatifin inhibits Bundibugyo virus and other filoviruses
content: Filoviruses, including Ebola and Marburg viruses, depend on host eIF4A helicase activity for replication. Zotatifin is a first in class, clinical stage eIF4A inhibitor that acts as a molecular glue, stabilizing the interaction between eIF4A and selected polypurine rich RNA sequences, thereby inhibiting RNA unwinding and ribosomal scanning. Here, we identify pronounced polypurine enrichment in the 5'untranslated regions (5'UTRs) of the seven major filoviral protein-coding genes NP, VP35, VP40, GP, VP30, VP24, and L across four virus species, including Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). Consistent with these findings, zotatifin inhibits the replication of Ebola, Marburg, Sudan, Tai Forest, and Bundibugyo viruses at low nanomolar concentrations. Zotatifin has been administered to humans in oncology and COVID19 clinical studies. Clinical pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic (PKPD) modeling indicates that exposures resulting in inhibition of BDBV replication are achievable in humans at tolerated doses following subcutaneous administration. Together, these findings support the repurposing of zotatifin as a host directed antiviral candidate against BDBV and other filoviruses, with potential applications in preparedness for future outbreaks.

title: The virome of New Zealand fur seals reveals novel viral diversity and evidence of continued Canine distemper virus circulation
content: Canine distemper virus (CDV) has recently been detected in New Zealand fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri), including retrospective samples from 2020 and outbreaks associated with substantial mortality in late 2024 and 2025. However, the geographic distribution of CDV and the broader viral diversity harboured by New Zealand fur seals remain poorly understood. Characterising the fur seal virome can provide insights into viral diversity, dispersal and the occurrence of viral co-infections, while assessing the distribution of CDV across colonies. We used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the viromes of 178 live and recently deceased fur seals sampled from four large fur seal colonies (Kaik[o]ura, Dunedin, West Coast and Wairarapa). We investigated viral diversity, community composition and geographic structure using phylogenetic analyses to examine viral evolutionary relationships and CDV distribution. We identified 23 viral species, including 20 putatively novel species. Several were related to viruses previously identified in terrestrial mammals. One viral species was detected across geographically separated colonies, while several other closely related viruses were identified across colonies, with viral sharing most frequent between Kaik[o]ura and Wairarapa. Viral diversity was similar between live and recently deceased fur seals, while community composition showed geographic structuring. CDV was detected only in Kaik[o]ura, where the lineage associated with the 2024 outbreak remained in circulation. No CDV was detected in the other sampled colonies. This study reveals substantial previously undocumented viral diversity in New Zealand fur seals, improving our understanding of viral distribution and CDV circulation in marine mammal populations.

title: Phenotypic plasticity reshapes the evolution of species coexistence
content: Modern coexistence theory (MCT) has been the mainstay of recent research on coexistence of competing species. Competition not only drives evolutionary changes in traits that affect coexistence, but also induces rapid plastic changes. However, a generalised framework that integrates plasticity and evolution into MCT is lacking. We formulate such a framework for a system of two competing species and analyse how breadth of available resources modulates the effect of competition-induced plasticity on the evolution of coexistence components (niche and fitness difference). We find that, in broad environments, divergent plasticity accelerates evolution towards positive invasion growth rates for both species, facilitating coexistence, whereas convergent plasticity hinders this process. Surprisingly, in narrower environments, divergent plasticity can hinder coexistence, leading to exclusion, whereas convergent plasticity can facilitate coexistence. Our results show that plasticity reshapes the eco-evolutionary trajectories to coexistence, highlighting the importance of integrating short-term plastic responses with long-term evolutionary dynamics.

title: From individual movement to ecosystem response: how landscape structure shapes herbivore impacts
content: Understanding how local interactions generate large-scale ecological dynamics is a central challenge in ecology. In heterogeneous environments, consumer movement links resource distribution with exploitation, producing responses that may not be predicted from consumer abundance or resource availability alone. Here, we develop a spatially explicit stochastic individual-based model of two herbivore populations with contrasting movement and foraging strategies that share renewable resources. The model incorporates heterogeneous resources, consumer movement and feeding, resource regeneration, predation, and refuge availability. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we examine how herbivore pressure and landscape structure shape population dynamics and resource depletion. Movement strongly determines the spatial pattern of depletion, while resource vulnerability depends on the overlap between resource distribution and consumer activity. Counterintuitively, increasing the extent of a productive region increases initial resource biomass but can also increase relative resource loss. Additional resources sustain consumer activity where herbivores concentrate, showing that greater resource availability does not necessarily buffer ecosystems against herbivory. Resource biomass can also decline substantially before major reductions in vegetation occupancy become apparent. These results demonstrate how individual behaviour and landscape structure jointly shape ecosystem responses. The model provides a framework for investigating how spatially coupled consumer-resource interactions generate ecological dynamics.

title: HiFi long-read metagenomics reshapes genome-resolved interpretations of activated sludge microbiome
content: Genome-resolved metagenomics is widely used to characterize activated sludge microbiomes and infer the microbial processes underpinning system performance. However, the reliability of metabolic inferences drawn from fragmented short-read (SR) genomes remains insufficiently examined. Using (near-)complete genomes reconstructed from HiFi long-read (LR) sequencing as references, we traced genome recovery through SR assembly and post-assembly processing. Assembly fragmentation and subsequent sequence loss during post-assembly processing compromised the recovery of high-quality genomes despite adequate sequencing depth and breadth of coverage. This incomplete recovery biased inferences regarding denitrification modularity, underestimating complete denitrifier populations and distorting the inferred balance between N2O producers and reducers. Poor recovery of nitrifier and Ca. Accumulibacter genomes, exacerbated by population microdiversity and structurally complex genomic regions, precluded reliable inferences regarding nitrification and phosphorus accumulation. Our findings caution against uncritical interpretation of SR-based microbiome-function linkages and highlight the value of incorporating HiFi LR sequencing into genome-resolved metagenomic analyses.
