title: Conversion of Cyanotoxins to Harmless Peptides: Mechanistic Modelling of the MlrABCD‐Mediated Microcystin Detoxification Pathway
content:
The Sphingopyxis MlrABCD pathway enables spatially coordinated microcystin detoxification. Membrane‐associated MlrA initiates degradation by linearizing microcystins, followed by MlrB‐mediated peptide cleavage, MlrD‐facilitated transport, and cytoplasmic MlrC degradation into smaller products. Molecular modelling and dynamics simulations reveal microcystin congener‐dependent interactions with MlrA/MlrB. Binding is strongly influenced by the variable R2 residue, with positively charged arginine‐containing congeners, particularly MC‐RR and MC‐LR, showing stronger predicted binding than hydrophobic congeners, highlighting structural determinants of substrate recognition and biodegradation efficiency.

ABSTRACT
Microcystins are among the most prevalent cyanobacterial toxins threatening freshwater ecosystems and human health, yet the molecular basis of their bacterial detoxification remains incompletely understood. Here, we present an integrated structural model of the MlrABCD pathway from Sphingopyxis sp. C‐1, providing mechanistic insight into the sequential transformation of microcystins across distinct bacterial cellular compartments. Comparative genomics, structural modelling, ligand‐binding predictions, and molecular dynamics simulations reveal a spatially coordinated detoxification process in which membrane‐associated MlrA initiates toxin linearization, periplasmic MlrB hydrolyses linear intermediates, MlrD transports degradation products across the cytoplasmic membrane, and cytoplasmic MlrC completes peptide degradation. Analysis of environmentally relevant microcystin congeners showed that substrate recognition is governed by the interplay between toxin chemistry and enzyme architecture. MlrA preferentially recognises MC‐LR, whereas MlrB displays enhanced affinity for linearized MC‐RR, indicating that ring opening reshapes substrate selectivity during pathway progression. Substrate binding also stabilises MlrD, supporting a ligand‐induced alternating‐access transport mechanism. Collectively, these findings indicate that the Sphingopyxis sp. C‐1 biodegradation machinery has evolved under environmental selective pressures into a compartmentalised and highly coordinated detoxification system optimised for the predominant environmental congeners, MC‐LR and MC‐RR, providing a molecular framework for the rational development of enhanced cyanotoxin bioremediation strategies.

title: Shrubification Has Limited Effects on Prokaryotic Communities in Northern Permafrost Regions
content:
There are major differences in microbial diversity and community assembly between the sub‐Arctic and the Arctic. In the sub‐Arctic, encroaching erect shrubs have an effect on microbial communities, which is mediated through their effect on soil pH. Soil type and characteristics are also important.

ABSTRACT
The northern landscape is greening due to climate change. Yet, little is known about the effect of increasingly more abundant erect shrubs on Arctic soil microbial communities, which play a crucial role in climate feedback. Soil samples were collected from soil pits with and without erect shrubs at a sub‐Arctic (Umiujaq, Quebec) and Arctic (Bylot Island, Nunavut) site in Canada. These samples were analysed for carbon density, nitrogen density, bulk density and pH, while the soil microbiome was studied using 16S rRNA metabarcoding. Both alpha and beta diversity were lower at the Arctic site compared to the sub‐Arctic site, while heterogeneous selection pressures had a greater influence on Arctic microbial community assembly processes. Additionally, soil depth and properties played a critical role in shaping the microbial communities, suggesting that both broad‐scale geographic factors and small‐scale environmental heterogeneity drive the microbiome composition and structure. Shrubs had a weak effect on microbial diversity, through their effect on soil pH. Moreover, the shrub effect varied with soil depth in the sub‐Arctic, likely due to the podzolic soils there. However, additional research is needed to understand the functions of this diverse microbial community and its role in climate feedback as the Arctic changes.

title: Effect of Shallow Water Depth on Sea Surface Temperature Cooling Induced by Landfalling Tropical Cyclones
content:
Abstract
Tropical cyclone (TC)‐induced sea surface temperature (SST) cooling in coastal waters is often distinct from that in the open ocean because of shallow bathymetry. However, a systematic quantitative assessment of the influence of shallow water depth on SST cooling across landfalling TCs remains lacking. To address this issue, we investigate 49 landfalling TCs in the South China Sea (SCS) using numerical simulations with realistic bathymetry (control run [CTRL]) and with the bathymetric constraint removed (NoBathy). The results show that shallow bathymetry generally reduces TC‐induced SST cooling across the 49 landfalling TCs. The magnitude of this cooling reduction is closely related to how the TC‐induced mixing depth compares with water depth. Once vertical mixing reaches the seafloor, shallow bathymetry limits its downward extent and restricts further entrainment of colder subsurface water, resulting in weaker cooling in CTRL than in NoBathy. Statistical analyses further show that this cooling reduction becomes pronounced in waters shallower than 50–60 m, consistent with the depth range over which vertical mixing becomes constrained by the seafloor. Thermal structure analyses indicate that shallow coastal waters in CTRL contain relatively little cold subsurface water available for entrainment, whereas the deeper water column in NoBathy allows vertical mixing to access colder water at greater depths. Consequently, mean SST cooling at landfall is approximately −0.40°C in CTRL and −1.45°C in NoBathy, corresponding to an average reduction of about 1.05°C. Overall, this study provides a quantitative basis for understanding how shallow water depth affects TC‐induced SST cooling.

title: Phytoplankton Dynamics in the Antarctic Seasonal Sea Ice Zone Under Large‐Scale Climate Forcing
content:
Abstract
The Antarctic Seasonal Sea Ice Zone (SIZ) supports strong but spatially variable phytoplankton biomass, yet its relationship with large‐scale climate variability remains poorly resolved. We analyzed the 1997–2024 satellite chlorophyll‐a (Chl‐a) data, used here as a proxy for surface phytoplankton biomass, across five Antarctic SIZ sectors: Indian, Pacific, Ross, Weddell, and Amundsen–Bellingshausen. We used an unsupervised Expectation–Maximization Gaussian Mixture Model (EM–GMM) to identify recurring Chl‐a anomaly regimes. At the pan‐SIZ scale, the intermediate regime was most frequent (∼64%), while low (∼22%) and high (∼14%) regimes occurred less often. Regime frequencies and anomaly distributions varied among El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Southern Annular Mode (SAM) phases, but most phase‐frequency differences were not statistically resolved. In the Indian and Pacific sectors, Chl‐a showed a modest but statistically significant positive correlation with SAM at all tested lags (0–3 months), with a maximum correlation of r = 0.31. No ENSO lagged correlation was significant in any sector. Entire SIZ sector physical associations were generally weak; significant partial correlations were limited to negative relationships with 15‐m stratification in the Weddell Sea and Amundsen–Bellingshausen Seas. Shelf–offshore analyses revealed stronger subregional differences in both the magnitude and sign of these relationships. These results show that Antarctic SIZ phytoplankton variability and its climate associations depend strongly on spatial scale, and that broad sector or pan‐SIZ averages can mask contrasting regional responses.

title: Geoclimatic and Host‐Driven Speciation in Colletotrichum
content:
ABSTRACT
Understanding speciation in plant pathogens is essential for predicting the emergence of novel virulent strains and deciphering biodiversity dynamics. This study explored the evolutionary history and diversification patterns of Colletotrichum, a globally significant plant‐pathogenic fungal genus. Divergence dating analysis places the origin of Colletotrichum in the middle Eocene (~47.57 Mya) with an ancestral state of broad host range, followed by host specialization particularly towards monocots and legumes during the Eocene–Oligocene transition (~32–39 Mya), a period coinciding with global cooling and aridification. While early‐diverging lineages formed during this period (i.e., C. gigasporum and C. orbiculare species complexes) exhibit limited extant diversity, the genus in general underwent accelerated diversification from the late Miocene onward. This acceleration is particularly prominent within the C. gloeosporioides species complex, which may be related to Pliocene vegetation shifts and late Neogene‐Quaternary environmental changes. Genomic analyses revealed that genome size evolution in Colletotrichum is significantly correlated with phylogenetic constraints and repetitive sequence ratio. We also observed extensive gene tree‐species tree incongruence, suggesting roles for incomplete lineage sorting or introgression. Overall, our findings reveal a macroevolutionary pattern in which ancient climatic shifts, host adaptation dynamics, and genomic plasticity have jointly shaped Colletotrichum diversification, while possible anthropogenic effects on the youngest lineages remain further investigation.

title: Flow-topography interactions modulate zooplankton abundance and vertical carbon flux along the Vitória-Trindade Seamount Chain (Southwestern Atlantic)
content:
Publication date: Available online 20 November 2026

Source: Deep Sea Research Part I: Oceanographic Research Papers

Author(s): Gleice Santos, Danilo A. Silva, Silvana B. Penninck, Ilson C.A. da Silveira, Lionel Guidi, Amanda Elineau, Paulo H.R. Calil, Rubens M. Lopes

title: Attribution of Summer Total Precipitation Changes in China and Decomposition Into Dynamic and Thermodynamic Effects
content:
Abstract
Understanding the impact of external forcings on regional precipitation changes is scientifically relevant and provides useful hints for elaborating climate‐change adaptation policies. However, detection and attribution of long‐term changes in summer total precipitation over China remain challenging due to pronounced spatial heterogeneity and models' generally poor performance. Here, we propose a novel attribution framework with decomposition of precipitation changes into dynamic and thermodynamic effects. Precipitation changes are decomposed into three terms of multiplication: the frequency for a synoptic circulation pattern (CP) (dynamic effects), the frequency of precipitation under that pattern, and the mean intensity of precipitation when it occurs (the latter two, thermodynamic effects). Results show that summer total precipitation changes over eastern China are overwhelmingly driven by changes in CP frequency, which are very likely attributable to anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing. Also, models' superior performance in reproducing changes in CP frequency lends confidence to our attribution findings.

title: Migration of Clustered Seismicity Controlled by Fluids, Aseismic Deformation, and Lithology in the Northern Apennines
content:
Abstract
The Alto Tiberina Fault (ATF) extensional system in the Northern Apennines is an ideal natural laboratory for observing seismic clustering, swarm behaviors, cluster migration, and their interplay with highly pressurized fluids (CO2) in the crust. Using a 13‐year high‐resolution earthquake catalog and density‐based clustering, we identify over 70 migrating clusters within the ATF hanging wall. Spatiotemporal analysis reveals multi‐scale migration patterns, from localized bursts to regional transients, that we characterized by both diffusive and linear fronts. Scaling relationships between migration speeds, durations, and magnitudes indicate a strong underlying influence of fluid diffusion and aseismic creep, modulated by local structural and lithological heterogeneity. Furthermore, we observe a clear positive correlation between maximum magnitude and apparent diffusivity. Notably, the 2013–2014 Gubbio swarm was preceded by a regional transient initiated in late 2012, suggesting a self‐similar process involving a large portion of the ATF hanging wall.

title: Mechanisms Controlling Northern Hemisphere Summer Extreme Temperature Trends
content:
Abstract
Using observational and reanalysis data sets, we diagnose summer surface warming trends over Northern Hemisphere mid‐ to high‐latitude land, focusing on hotspots over Eastern Europe–Western Asia, Mongolia–Northern China, and Western North America. In these hotspots, extreme‐temperature intensification largely follows seasonal‐mean warming, with little evidence that the hottest summer days are warming faster than the contemporaneous seasonal mean. We therefore examine the processes associated with seasonal‐mean warming. Regional warming is shaped by the combined influence of seasonal‐mean large‐scale circulation associated with the circumglobal Rossby wave train, land–atmosphere interactions that regulate evaporative cooling, and longwave radiative responses. The relative importance of these processes differs across the hotspots. These diagnostic results show that extreme‐temperature intensification is closely tied to seasonal‐mean warming, highlighting the need to understand the regional processes that shape future extreme heat risk.

title: Quantifying Nitrogen Oxide Point Sources With the EMIT Satellite Imaging Spectrometer
content:
Abstract
Nitrogen oxides (NOx = NO + NO2) are major drivers of air pollution and ecosystem damage. We present high‐resolution (60‐m) NO2 column retrievals from the EMIT imaging spectrometer and use them to quantify NO2 concentrations and NOx emissions for 55 plumes from 17 U.S. and Saudi Arabian power plants on 149 cloud‐free passes. EMIT NO2 plumes are consistent in shape with coarser (km‐scale) TROPOMI observations on coincident passes over Riyadh Power Plant 9, but have 24%–46% greater mass. This may reflect improved ability to resolve strong near‐source NO2 gradients. NOx source rates inferred from EMIT using a cross‐sectional flux method match continuous emission monitoring system data for U.S. power plants with <10% relative mean bias and 52% precision. Plume detection probability exceeds 90% for NOx emissions ≥0.1 kg s−1 per m s−1 wind. Our results show that high‐resolution hyperspectral satellite observations can accurately quantify instantaneous NOx emissions from industrial point sources.

title: Spatial Variability of 1993–2025 Ocean Temperature Trends Shaped by Poleward Shifts of the Subtropical Gyres
content:
Abstract
Spatial patterns of subsurface ocean temperature trends from 1993 to 2025 are analyzed globally using eddy‐resolving observation‐based maps. Beyond a globally‐integrated, surface‐intensified warming over that time period, temperature trends exhibit substantial spatial variability. Except for the Agulhas Return Current in the South Indian Ocean, warming rates are largest, up to a few times the global average and relatively deep‐reaching, in the subtropical western boundary current extensions. There is also generally some subsurface cooling where isotherms slope upward toward the equator in the equatorward limbs of most of the subtropical gyres. Both temperature signatures are consistent with a poleward shift of the subtropical gyres. Wind stress curl zero lines and subtropical extrema generally shift poleward over the same period, suggesting these ocean trends are linked with wind changes. Variations in the patterns of temperature trends and wind stress curl trends among the five subtropical gyres are generally consistent with that hypothesis.

title: Revisiting the Signal‐to‐Noise Paradox in Climate Predictions: An Extended Mathematical Framework
content:
Abstract
The signal‐to‐noise paradox—where climate model predictions correlate more highly with observations than with their own ensemble members—remains a challenge for interpreting predictability. We present an extended theoretical framework explaining the role of different types of model errors in the paradox. Analytical results show, despite the non‐identifiability of the latent parameters, that the paradox arises only when the shared signal is underestimated relative to observations and this underestimation is sufficiently large, rather than from differences in signal‐to‐noise ratios. The paradox therefore likely reflects intrinsic model errors that become apparent through correlation scores, without contradicting predictability theory. The paradox can also be obscured by missed and spurious signals. We further propose an improved estimate of a lower bound on real‐world predictability that exceeds conventional estimates under paradox conditions.

title: Cyclic Buoyant Currents With Residual Trapping Set Recovery Limits for Underground Hydrogen Storage
content:
Abstract
Seasonal hydrogen storage in aquifers generates cyclic buoyant currents, with hydrogen recovery limited mainly by residual trapping in the absence of another cushion gas. We derive a depth‐averaged model for such operations in an axisymmetric conical permeable stratum, identify the controlling dimensionless groups, and distinguish near‐ and far‐field regimes. Constant‐flux withdrawal produces near‐well depletion, or coning, which hydrodynamically strands some of the mobile mass. In the far‐field gravity‐stabilized limit, this stranded mass becomes negligible, radial advection weakens, and the interface becomes horizontal. We obtain closed‐form expressions for interface position, mass evolution, and recovery. The recovery laws depend on hysteretic mass partitioning and are geometry‐independent. We show that residual mass approaches a periodic state, and incremental recovery approaches unity geometrically. Ensemble simulations validate these limits across much of the sampled parameter space and match a field‐relevant example. The solutions provide lower bounds on unrecovered hydrogen and realistic targets for storage design.

title: A Kp‐Dependent Model of Earth's Auroral X‐Ray Emission Boundary From Polar/PIXIE
content:
Abstract
Polar/Polar Ionospheric X‐ray Imaging Experiment (PIXIE) low‐energy X‐ray observations (2–12 keV) provide a global view of energetic auroral electron precipitation through atmospheric bremsstrahlung. We construct Kp‐binned Northern Hemisphere median maps and derive empirical descriptions of the PIXIE X‐ray auroral oval. The model family includes a fixed‐intensity baseline at 300 photons cm−2 s−1 sr−1, a Gaussian above‐background profile method that extracts equatorward and poleward emission boundaries, and a regularized closed Fourier curve that summarizes the boundary morphology. The maps show systematic brightening and expansion with increasing Kp, with crescent‐like emission and a persistent minimum near 15:00 magnetic local time. The results show that the equatorward boundary shifts to lower magnetic latitude as geomagnetic activity increases, and the modeled oval width generally broadens at high Kp. The poleward boundary is quantified but is more local‐time dependent and method‐sensitive. These boundary descriptions provide a reproducible reference for future X‐ray auroral studies and multi‐instrument precipitation comparisons in space weather contexts.

title: Shallow Coseismic Slip on Low‐Healing Pelagic Clay in the 2011 Tohoku‐Oki Earthquake Rupture Area
content:
Abstract
The 2011 Tohoku‐oki earthquake generated large slip near the trench. It remains unclear whether this slip was driven by the release of locally accumulated interseismic shear stress. We conducted slide‐hold‐slide and high‐velocity friction experiments on a smectite‐rich megathrust fault zone sample recovered during International Ocean Discovery Program Expedition 405, under an in situ effective normal stress of 6 MPa. The results show that the megathrust clay exhibits overall low frictional healing, but does not show a systematic log‐linear increase with increasing hold times. The sample also shows low peak and dynamic friction coefficients of 0.15–0.20, with negligible breakdown work. These findings indicate that the megathrust pelagic clay has a small capacity for accumulating interseismic shear stress, yet can readily accommodate shallow coseismic slip due to its minimal resistance. Limited healing, low frictional strength, and very low breakdown work on shallow megathrusts composed of pelagic clay favor large shallow coseismic slip.

title: Absorbing Aerosols Amplify Vertical Heterogeneity in Cold‐Topped Precipitation
content:
Abstract
The vertical structure of precipitation (VSP) links cloud processes to surface rainfall, yet aerosol effects on VSP remain poorly constrained. Combining high‐resolution observations and idealized simulations (May–September, 2015–2023) over eastern China, we show that aerosols reshape precipitation profiles in cold‐topped clouds with storm‐tops above the freezing level (FL). Aerosol‐associated precipitation‐rate changes above the FL are opposite to those near the surface, consistent with substantial evaporative loss below the FL. With increasing aerosol loading, storm‐top height, solid‐phase precipitation, precipitation rate and precipitation particle size above the FL increase and then decrease, peaking under moderate pollution. Near the peak, the greater abundance of melting ice particles cools the surrounding air, steepens the low‐level temperature gradient, and promotes evaporation of large raindrops. Near‐surface absorbing aerosols further warm the lower atmosphere and strengthen evaporative loss, amplifying the vertical decoupling between upper‐layer and near‐surface precipitation responses.

title: Urbanization Doubles Future Compound Heatwave Risk in the Yangtze River Delta Urban Agglomeration Based on a Machine Learning‐Statistical Hybrid Framework
content:
Abstract
Urbanization intensifies compound heatwaves (CoHot) involving concurrent hot days and nights, yet coarse‐resolution climate projections cannot resolve urban‐scale processes. Dynamical downscaling can bridge this gap but requires substantial computing for long‐term projections. Here we introduce a novel and efficient hybrid framework combining daily‐scale stacking ensemble machine learning with monthly‐scale quantile mapping to downscale CMIP6 projections to urban resolution. Applied to China's Yangtze River Delta (YRD), a highly developed urban area, this framework improves simulation of CoHot frequency, duration, and intensity, increasing spatial correlation from −0.26–0.50 to 0.29–0.77 and reducing RMSE by 18%. High‐resolution (5‐km) projections reveal cities as evolving CoHot hotspots, where urban expansion drives shifting spatial patterns. By 2050, city centers could experience about four CoHot events and over 20 CoHot days annually, with total duration twice that in surrounding rural areas. This scalable, efficient tool aids urban heat risk assessment with broad applicability to rapidly urbanizing regions worldwide.

title: Secondary Microseisms' Propagation Effects Highlighted by Joint DAS Observations and Full Waveform Modeling Offshore Sicily
content:
Abstract
The use of Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) on submarine cables provides new opportunities to investigate the microseism wavefield generated by ocean surface gravity waves at the seafloor, but its interpretation requires understanding how signals propagate through seafloor heterogeneities to reach the cable. Here, DAS data collected on a submarine cable offshore Catania, Sicily is investigated to analyze an episode of enhanced secondary microseism activity originating in the Mediterranean Sea. Comparison with the expected microseism source region derived from ocean‐wave model reveals differences with the apparent direction of propagating microseism wavefield observed on the DAS data. Seismo‐acoustic simulations reproduce this behavior, demonstrating that continental‐shelf morphology can refract and redirect the wavefield. These results demonstrate the strong influence of bathymetry and source‐receiver geometry on microseism propagation. They provide new insights into microseism interpretations from DAS observations in morphologically complex marine environments, important to consider for offshore passive imaging applications using DAS.

title: Nonlinear Dynamics of Ecosystem Resilience Under Drought Disturbances
content:
Abstract
Drought is increasingly challenging ecosystem stability under climate change, yet the mechanisms underlying ecosystem resilience remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated remote sensing observations with a Coupled Vegetation‐Water Dynamics (CVWD) model to quantify vegetation‐water responses to drought across five major ecological regions. The model successfully reproduced observed drought trajectories and revealed that resilience is jointly governed by environmental sensitivity, ecological regulation, and recovery capacity. Ecological regulation weakened with increasing drought severity, whereas recovery capacity increased with recovery duration. A strong trade‐off between environmental sensitivity and ecological regulation emerged across ecosystems, indicating that resilience cannot be explained by recovery alone. Long‐term stochastic simulations revealed substantial regional differences in persistence, with characteristic collapse times ranging from 3.29 years in the La Plata Basin to 4.64 years in the Amazon rainforest. These findings identify key controls on ecosystem resilience and provide a scalable framework for assessing drought vulnerability under climate change.

title: Altitude‐Triggered Lightning Produces X‐Ray Emission With Temporal Characteristics Comparable to Those of Natural First‐Stroke Stepped Leaders
content:
Abstract
This study presents the first detection of X‐rays from a first‐stroke downward stepped leader in altitude‐triggered lightning. During 2023–2025, only one of seven altitude‐triggered flashes exhibited a clear X‐ray burst during the first‐stroke leader. This burst lasted ∼327 μs and contained 98 pulses, with a mean energy of ∼550 keV and a mean pulse interval of 20.9 μs. High‐speed imaging confirmed the emission was synchronous with downward stepped‐leader development. The burst's temporal structure differs markedly from the short, dense X‐ray bursts of subsequent‐stroke leaders, but closely resembles those observed from natural first‐stroke stepped leaders. Our analyses indicate that detectable X‐rays depend on both strong leader activity and the propagation environment. These findings demonstrate that altitude‐triggered lightning can produce X‐ray emission with temporal characteristics comparable to those observed from natural first‐stroke stepped leaders under controlled conditions.

title: Secular Melting of Mantle Pyroxenite Records Mantle Dynamics Coupled With Supercontinent Cycles
content:
Abstract
Supercontinent cycles dictate Earth's long‐term tectonic and magmatic evolution, yet the variations in the lithologies of the mantle sources of global basalts remain poorly constrained. Tracking the balance between these two source lithologies, peridotite and pyroxenite, is notoriously difficult as extensive fractional crystallization obscures primary mantle signatures in global basalt records. Here, we present a machine learning framework trained using experimental and thermodynamically modeled primary melts to directly distinguish peridotite‐ and pyroxenite‐derived magmas. Applying this method to a global basalt data set spanning the past 3 Ga shows that the source lithologies of global basalts shift cyclically with supercontinent cycles, with pyroxenite contributions peaking during the assembly stages and peridotite contributions dominating during the breakup stages. These shifts coincide with variations in lithospheric thickness and δ18O of continental crust, pointing to a persistent association between the supercontinent cycle, lithospheric dynamics, and the sources of global magmatism throughout Earth's geological history.

title: The Influence of ENSO on the Winter NAO Is Mostly Unpredictable Noise
content:
Abstract
Seasonal forecast systems are able to skillfully predict the winter‐average North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) a season ahead, but the source of this skill remains unclear. Some studies have suggested El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) as a source of skill, drawing on prior literature on a proposed ENSO‐NAO teleconnection. We examine the role of ENSO as a source of skill by using seasonal hindcasts with prescribed sea surface temperatures (SSTs) that show high levels of NAO forecast skill. By removing all SST variability in a broad tropical Pacific ENSO domain in the forecast, we find only a minimal and non‐significant drop in NAO skill, with the forecast sometimes improving by having removed ENSO. This suggests that the apparent ENSO‐NAO teleconnection is largely unpredictable noise and not a robust source of NAO skill.

Nitrogen acquisition strategies in stream biofilms under varying nitrogen, iron, and phosphorus conditions
content:
Abstract
Nitrogen (N) is a commonly limiting nutrient in stream ecosystems due to high demand by organisms, and as a result, many studies have focused on how limited N availability influences microbial nutrient acquisition. However, N acquisition is likely influenced by the availability of other nutrients, such as phosphorus (P) or iron (Fe), either directly through the requirement of these elements in pathways that are important for N acquisition, such as Fe within N fixation, or indirectly through the division of resources toward acquisition of multiple nutrients. We examined the role of P and Fe in N acquisition with a mesocosm experiment drawing water and microbes from a stream known to be N‐limited. We performed full factorial additions of P, Fe, and N across 32 flow‐through mesocosms and measured the effects of the nutrient additions on N fixation, extracellular enzyme activity, and ammonium uptake and regeneration rates. We found that the algal carrying capacity was co‐limited by the availability of both N and Fe. Additionally, N enrichment had an inhibitory effect on all processes that we measured. P had no significant effect while Fe enrichment may have an indirect effect on N cycling as shown by a positive effect on ammonium regeneration but no significant effects on any other pathway measured. These results indicate that micronutrients such as Fe can significantly influence microbial communities and the cycling of other nutrients.

title: Myeloid DNA methyltransferase 3A loss impairs macrophage polarization and promotes inflammation, phagocytosis and hepatosplenomegaly
content: Background: Genetic variants in the de novo DNA methyltransferase DNMT3A increase inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) risk, yet the mechanisms linking defective DNMT3A to IBD remain unclear. As macrophages gatekeep immune homeostasis, we characterized how myeloid-specific DNMT3A loss affects monocytic differentiation and inflammatory properties. Methods: We generated myeloid-specific Dnmt3a-deficient mice (Dnmt3a-LysM) via LysM-cre. Deletion was confirmed in gut lamina propria CD11b+ cells and bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM). M1/M2-polarized BMDMs were characterized by methylation profiling, mRNA-sequencing, flow cytometry, arginase/NOS activity, phagocytosis (FITC-zymosan), and co-culture with wounded ModeK epithelial monolayers. Colitis was induced using dextran sodium sulfate (DSS). Results: Dnmt3a expression was induced by M2 and repressed by inflammatory stimuli in wild-type (Dnmt3afl/fl) BMDMs. Upon IL-4/IL-13 stimulation, Dnmt3a-LysM BMDMs exhibited heightened ERK1/2 and PI3K signaling, reduced M2 markers, increased pro-inflammatory Irg1/Tnf transcripts, and acquired M1-like features; amplified in BMDMs from aged (>34 weeks) mice (disrupted morphology, enhanced phagocytosis, reduced arginase and elevated iNOS activity). These cells impaired epithelial regeneration in co-culture. In vivo, young Dnmt3a-LysM mice showed splenic immune alterations and DSS-colitis hypersensitivity. Aged Dnmt3a-LysM mice displayed altered bone marrow architecture, hepatosplenomegaly, and myeloproliferation. Conclusions: Dnmt3a is required for physiological macrophage polarization. Its myeloid-specific loss drives pro-inflammatory skewing, potentially contributing to IBD pathogenesis.

title: Gene regulatory networks and the organization of cell differentiation in multicellular organisms
content: Across their development, clonal multicellular organisms generate new cell types from less differentiated cell types. Differentiation pathways arrange into a hierarchical, tree-like organization: regressions from specialized to undifferentiated cell types rarely occur and undifferentiated cell types often have the potential to produce, when subject to distinct stimuli, two or more differently specialized cell types. How cell type transitions acquire such a peculiar disposition requires an explanation that must reside in the properties of gene regulatory networks (GRNs); after all, GRNs orchestrate the changes in gene activity that define cell types. We studied vast numbers of small dynamic model networks to search for elementary GRNs that could yield the simplest hierarchical, developmental-like, differentiation patterns. We found that only a small minority of GRNs are compatible with hierarchical cell type transitions. Importantly, GRNs that yielded developmental-like differentiation patterns shared common traits: One is the presence of tangles of cycles of positive interactions. Genes in such a tangle produce an all-or-none one-way response to a signal. Another such trait is mutual inhibition between genes associated to different specialized cell types, enforcing their mutually exclusive activation. Moreover, these regulatory patterns are more abundant in published experimentally sustained developmental GRNs than as expected by chance. In addition, we show that it is easy to maintain hierarchical cellular differentiation throughout evolution, even when undergoing changes in gene regulatory interactions and developmental mechanisms. Our work supports the prevalence of design principles that organize hierarchically differentiation pathways in clonal multicellular organisms.

title: Homologs of the Major Vault Protein defend bacteria against ribotoxins
content: Bacteria use sophisticated mechanisms to defend themselves against antibiotics and bacteriophages, yet how they combat toxins deployed during interbacterial competition remains poorly understood. Bacteria use type VI secretion, bacteriocins, and contact dependent inhibition systems to deliver antibacterial toxins that inhibit growth by antagonizing essential processes. Here, we discover that Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses homologs of the eukaryotic major vault protein and a tRNA-like noncoding RNA to defend against RNA-damaging ribotoxins. Using an engineered pyocin delivery system, we showed that P. aeruginosa sensed ribotoxin damage and activated transcription of an RNA repair operon, which included band7, a homolog of the major vault protein. Genetic analyses demonstrated that band7-expressing bacteria were significantly more protected against growth inhibition by a ribotoxin that cleaved the anticodon loop of specific tRNA. Band7 was necessary but not sufficient, and defense also required a non-coding band7 RNA (bRNA). bRNA was cleaved by the ribotoxin, suggesting a mechanism for specificity and defense. Bioinformatic analyses revealed that band7 and candidate bRNA are widely distributed within RNA repair systems across diverse bacteria. Our data suggest that bacteria use structures related to the eukaryotic vault complex to respond to RNA damage thereby providing a hypothesis for the function of the enigmatic human vault.

title: Hyphal differentiation and cell wall remodeling in Trametes versicolor underlie a layered architecture in pure mycelium materials
content: Background: Pure mycelium materials grown at the air-liquid interface are promising leather alternatives, yet they are generally treated as homogeneous sheets of fungal biomass. Because basidiomycetes differentiate their hyphae into generative, skeletal and ligative cell types, the properties of such materials may instead arise from an internal tissue organisation. In this study, cell types produced by the trimitic white-rot fungus Trametes versicolor during Liquid State Surface Fermentation were characterized and the impact of their spatial organisation, mechanics and cell wall composition on the resulting material was analysed. Results: Optic and electron microscopy revealed the mats are not homogeneous but consist of two layers: a dense bottom layer of thin-walled generative hyphae in contact with the liquid medium, and a looser, air-exposed top layer made of thick-walled skeletal hyphae. Both layers had comparable hyphal diameters (2.43 {+/-} 0.42 and 2.33 {+/-} 0.50 {micro}m), but the skeletal hyphae in the mat were roughly half the diameter of their fruiting-body counterparts (5.10 {+/-} 1.05 {micro}m). Untreated mats stress-strain curves displayed sequential failure: brittle fracture of the generative bottom layer followed by ductile failure of the skeletal layer. The two faces also differed in wettability, the top being hydrophobic and highly adhesive and the bottom hydrophilic. Solid-state NMR showed extensive rigid cell wall remodelling between the two cell types: alpha-1,3-glucan accounted for about one third of the rigid polysaccharides in the generative layer but was undetectable in the skeletal layer, which contained approximately 74% beta-1,3-glucan and 26% chitin and was overall more rigid and more lipid-rich. Conclusions: These results show that Trametes versicolor differentiates into a very specific type of skeletal hyphae in liquid state surface fermentation, which involves remodelling of the molecular architecture of the cell wall rather than a simple thickening of it, and that the mechanical and surface behaviour of the material can be traced to that remodelling and to the cellular organisation.

title: Emergence of mobile fosA3-blaCTX-M-65 with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) on conjugative plasmids in avian pathogenic Escherichia coli from industrial poultry in Pakistan
content: The emergence of plasmid-mediated resistance to critically important antimicrobials poses a growing threat to global health. Here we report the first genomic evidence of plasmid-mediated fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 coexisting with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli from clinically healthy broiler chickens in Pakistan. Among 1,677 high-quality genomes collected through antimicrobial resistance surveillance in Punjab, Pakistan, three isolates recovered between 2022 and 2024 harboured all four resistance determinants. Hybrid genome assemblies showed that fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 were co-located on IncHI2A plasmids, whereas mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) were carried on separate IncI2 and IncFIA/IncFIC plasmids, all predicted to be conjugative; in one isolate the tet(X4) contig did not circularise. The isolates belonged to sequence type 93 and exhibited resistance to fosfomycin, colistin, tigecycline and cefotaxime. Comparative genomic analysis revealed highly conserved IncHI2A plasmid backbones, with an additional integron-associated resistance region in the 2024 isolates, suggesting acquisition of accessory resistance determinants. Resistance to three last-line antimicrobial classes and a canonical virulence profile now coexist on conjugative plasmids in poultry E. coli, a combination that favours co-selection and argues for plasmid-resolved surveillance in poultry production.

title: Electron Transport Chain-inhibiting fungicides increase resistance to widely used azole antifungals
content: Rising antifungal resistance in human and crop fungal pathogens poses significant challenges. Azole-based antifungals that inhibit ergosterol biosynthesis are a key first-line treatment for human fungal infections. Importantly, azole-based ergosterol-inhibiting fungicides are also widely used in agriculture alongside electron transport chain (ETC) Complex III inhibiting compounds. However, it is unknown whether the combined use of these distinct fungicides is entirely synergistic. We find that exposure of fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces pombe to ETC-Complex III inhibitors, prior to or simultaneously with azoles, attenuates azole efficacy by inducing mitochondrial dysfunction. Our analyses show that reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation as a result of ETC inhibition activates oxidative stress response pathways thereby decreasing azole potency. Related responses in pathogenic fungi indicate that the use of ETC inhibiting fungicides in agriculture may inadvertently promote azole resistance. We conclude that the use of specific fungicide combinations should be re-evaluated in order to preserve both their clinical and agricultural effectiveness.

title: Multi-Cohort Blood Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Reproducibility of a 50-Gene Interferon Signature and Benchmarking of a 4-Gene Classifier
content: Background: Most blood transcriptomic signatures for tuberculosis (TB) come from a single population or a single platform. Few have been built by meta-analysis and benchmarked against published signatures. Methods: We meta-analysed three UK blood transcriptomic datasets (two Illumina microarray, one RNA-seq; 247 samples: 87 active pulmonary TB (PTB), 160 healthy controls (HC)). GSE107991 reanalyses the Berry test set, and two discovery datasets overlap Sweeney's discovery data, so the datasets are not fully independent. Genes were retained if they replicated in all three studies (FDR < 0.05, same direction) and passed random-effects meta-analysis (|logFC| > 1.5, FDR < 0.01). Performance was estimated in GSE28623 (The Gambia, n = 83) and GSE56153 (Indonesia, n = 36); direction was checked in GSE34608 (Germany, n = 26) and GSE81746 (India, n = 6). A LASSO and random-forest classifier was compared with the Berry 393-gene and Sweeney 3-gene signatures. Immune composition was assessed with MCPcounter and CIBERSORTx. Results: We identified a 50-gene core signature dominated by interferon-stimulated genes. All 50 were upregulated and reached FDR < 0.05 in every dataset. ssGSEA gave an AUC of 0.830 (95% CI 0.743-0.917) in GSE28623 and 0.941 (0.868-1.000) in GSE56153. Direction agreement was 95.7% in Germany and 95.8% in India. PTB versus latent TB infection gave 0.848 (0.756-0.940). LASSO selected four genes (BATF2, ANKRD22, GBP5 and EPSTI1). The frozen classifier gave an external AUC of 0.864 (0.785-0.944). The Sweeney 3-gene score, re-tested in one of its validation cohorts, reached 0.912 and exceeded the 50-gene score (47/50 genes; Holm p = 0.0234). Berry 393-gene scoring gave 0.910 with directions reconstructed from GSE19439 (Holm p = 0.0071 versus the 50-gene score). The signed score is a reconstruction, not Berry's published score. MCPcounter showed myeloid expansion and lymphoid suppression; CIBERSORTx recovered the former but not the broader lymphoid suppression. Conclusions: The 50-gene signature was consistent across three overlapping UK discovery datasets. External evaluation was partial, comprising AUCs for 47 of the 50 genes in two cohorts and direction concordance in two smaller cohorts. This is a benchmarking study, not a claim of superiority: the Sweeney 3-gene and signed Berry scores were higher, and the 4-gene classifier did not differ significantly from Sweeney. The classifier warrants prospective validation. The Berry and Sweeney comparisons are not independent.

title: Environmental heterogeneity and microbial community architecture shape N2O fluxes in intertidal coastal sediments
content: Seagrass meadows are key ''blue carbon ecosystems'', yet their contribution to nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions remains poorly constrained. We investigated environmental and microbial descriptors of N2O fluxes in intertidal sediments of Arcachon Bay, home to Europe's largest Zostera noltii meadow. At six sites, we measured in situ N2O fluxes in adjacent bare and vegetated sediments and characterized sediment properties, N2O-cycling genes using qPCR and targeted metagenomics, and microbial co-occurrence networks. Fluxes ranged from -3.7 to 8.4 mol N2O m-2 d-1. Spatial location was the strongest descriptor of flux variation, with inner-bay sites showing higher emissions associated with environmental conditions, carbon accumulation, pH, and microbial community characteristics. Vegetation effects were comparatively small and site-dependent. Metagenomic descriptors of N2O-cycling genes were more informative than qPCR-based descriptors. Taxa associated with nirS (Thiohalophilus), nirK (Planktotalea) and nosZ1 (Roseobacter) were identified as potential contributors to N2O production or reduction, respectively. These findings indicate that spatially structured environmental conditions and microbial community characteristics better describe N2O flux variation than seagrass presence alone. Measurements across tidal and seasonal cycles are needed to establish the temporal consistency of these patterns.

title: Genomic Characterization of a Typical Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli Isolate from an Egyptian Fruit Bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus from Coastal Kenya
content: Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality cases among young children under the age of five, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Atypical EPEC has frequently been reported from animal hosts, however, information on the occurrence and genomic characteristics of typical EPEC in wildlife reservoirs remains limited. This study characterized an Escherichia coli isolated from an Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) sampled in coastal Kenya using whole-genome sequencing. Oral and rectal swabs were collected from 24 bats captured in Kikambala, Kilifi County, Kenya. Bacterial isolates were cultured, sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform, and analyzed using a bioinformatics workflow that included in silico taxonomic classification, serotyping and multilocus sequence typing, virulence gene profiling, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, plasmid identification, and core genome phylogenetic analysis. One isolate, KIKB-471-SWR-A (O128:H6; ST15625), was classified as typical EPEC. Genomic analysis confirmed the characteristic virulence architecture of typical EPEC. Despite numerous antimicrobial resistance-associated genes being detected, the isolate remained phenotypically susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The isolate clustered within an EPEC lineage, closely associated with a human-derived EPEC strain, and genetically distinct from both commensal and laboratory E. coli reference strains. Despite no evidence of zoonotic transmission, the findings demonstrated that wildlife can harbor E. coli lineages possessing virulence determinants associated with human pathogenic EPEC strains, underscoring the importance of genomic surveillance at wildlife?human interfaces within a One Health framework to improve the understanding of ecology, evolution, and public health significance of diarrheagenic E. coli.

title: Deletion of Furin Facilitates Efficient and Versatile Coronavirus Pseudotyped Particle Generation
content: Coronaviruses bring threats to both humans and animals. To initiate successful infections, coronaviruses must first navigate entry into a host cell. Coronavirus spike-bearing pseudotyped particle systems are indispensable tools for studying coronavirus entry and evaluating neutralizing antibodies and entry inhibitors. However, pseudotyped particle titers can be low when packaged particles bear coronavirus spikes that contain the furin cleavage site, and this has been a limitation for pseudotyped particle production and applications. Here, we demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of furin protease in HEK293T cells significantly enhances the production of functional pseudotyped particles bearing spikes containing the furin cleavage site, including those from SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and MHV-JHM. Moreover, deletion of endogenous furin in producer cells yields an effect equivalent to deletion of the furin cleavage site, but with broader application across different spike proteins, and without virus manipulation. This work establishes a simple and effective platform to improve coronavirus pseudotyped particle systems by eliminating furin-mediated pre-activation, enabling more efficient and reliable production for downstream applications.

title: Precision Fermentation Gets a New Player: Genome Assembly and Genetic Transformation of a Novel Strain, Pichia hangzhouana, for Precision Fermentation of Food Ingredients
content: Precision fermentation leverages the metabolic pathways of microorganisms to produce valuable proteins and enzymes. Pichia hangzhouana, synonymous with Zygoascus hellenicus, is a non-conventional yeast with potential for food biotechnological applications. This study characterizes the CSIRO strain P. hangzhouana FRR5246, isolated from a tea beverage, to evaluate its suitability as a precision fermentation host for a variety of industrial, agricultural and food production applications. P. hangzhouana demonstrated robust growth across a range of carbon sources, with the highest optical density observed in media containing sucrose or sorbitol as sole carbon source. The yeast showed susceptibility to geneticin, hygromycin B, nourseothricin sulfate, and zeocin sulfate antibiotic agents. Successful genetic transformation was achieved, with the expression of a recombinant orange fluorescent protein (OFP) under the control of the native glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAP1) promoter. The secretome exhibited strong antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, indicating the presence of potent antimicrobial compounds. In addition, whole genome sequencing of P. hangzhouana FRR5246 provided genetic tools for recombinant expression of heterologous genes, insight into the genes, genetic architecture and regulatory mechanisms underlying phenotypic qualities, as well as confirming phylogenetic classification of this strain as clustering with the Dipodascomycetes, most closely related to species Zygoascus hellenicus. P. hangzhouana FRR5246 is a promising candidate for precision fermentation of food ingredients, capable of utilizing diverse carbon sources and producing recombinant proteins. In addition, production of antimicrobial compounds further enhances the potential for biotechnological exploitation. Future work will focus on optimizing growth conditions and exploring native inducible promoters for controlled gene expression.

title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics and Environmental Drivers of Maize Microbiome Structure across Diverse Agroecosystems in Georgia, USA
content: The understanding of how microbial communities differ across soils, environments, plant tissues, and developmental stages is key to the improvement of crop productivity and resilience. Here, we conducted a statewide survey of maize (Zea mays L.) microbiomes across 35 fields at 16 locations in Georgia, USA, sampling soil, rhizosphere, root interior, and stalk interior at two developmental stages (600 and 1400 growing degree days, GDD). More than 38000 ASVs were produced after amplicon sequencing of 16S rRNA genes. The phyla shown to be dominant are Proteobacteria, Actinobacteriota, Chloroflexi, Planctomycetota, and Acidobacteriota. Based on alpha and beta diversity analyses, the below-ground compartments (soil and rhizosphere) revealed higher diversity and stronger spatial structuring when compared to the above-ground sample types, whereas root and stalk interior microbiomes revealed marked shifts across growth stages. Amino acid metabolism, secondary metabolite biosynthesis, and energy-related pathways predictions (via PICRUSt2) show stage-dependent enrichment. Network analyses show persistent keystone taxa (Proteobacteria and Actinobacteriota) mediating microbial stability, coupled with an increase in modularity and connectivity as we move from early to late growth stages. Some environmental variables, such as temperature, humidity, soil potassium, and soil sodium, showed significant correlation with microbial diversity indicative of a compartment-specific environmental sensitivity. Collectively, our results show that in maize, microbial community composition, interaction, and potential functionality are both impacted by developmental stages and environmental heterogeneity. This study provides a fundamental framework for understanding the microbiome dynamics in field-grown maize across various agroecological conditions. It equally provides ecological insights relevant to microbiome-informed crop management.

title: Comparative landscape of extracellular vesicles across three pathogenic trematodes identifies a key conserved miRNA cargo involved in host liver fibrosis
content: Liver fibrosis caused by Schistosoma japonicum, Clonorchis sinensis, and Opisthorchis felineus represents a major global public health burden. Here, we systematically characterized extracellular vesicles (EVs) released by key stages of these parasites and uncovered, for the first time, a conserved repertoire of EV-derived miRNAs shared across all three species. By integrating animal models, single-cell RNA sequencing, and bioinformatic analyses, we comprehensively identified the targetome of miR-36-3p, a cross-species conserved miRNA cargo. Mechanistically, we found that miR-36-3p directly targets Atox1 in Kupffer cells, driving intracellular copper and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and thereby activating hepatic stellate cells. Strikingly, in vivo delivery of an AAV8-encoded miR-36-3p sponge markedly attenuated liver fibrosis across all three infection models. Collectively, these findings establish a conserved, parasite-derived EV miRNA cargo as a previously unrecognized driver of host liver pathology and identify it as a promising therapeutic target for preventing parasite-induced liver fibrosis.

title: A small molecule inhibits Neisseria gonorrhoeae pilus formation
content: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is becoming increasingly antimicrobial-resistant. N. gonorrhoeae requires the Type IV pilus (T4p) for pathogenesis, wherein the T4p promotes colonization through adherence to host cells and resistance to neutrophil killing. The pilus also is required for natural transformation and twitching motility. Collectively, these critical functions make the T4p an attractive drug target. Previously, we developed a high-throughput screen to identify compounds with activity against the zinc metalloprotease Mpg, which is involved in T4p biogenesis. Here, we identified a lead compound, SC144, that inhibits Mpg peptidoglycan-hydrolyzing activity in both N. gonorrhoeae and other bacteria encoding Mpg-like M23B metallopeptidase orthologs. Interestingly, SC144 targets Mpgs carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities. Importantly, SC144 inhibited N. gonorrhoeae colonization and prevented its survival in two primary human cell culture models of infection without toxic effects on these host cells. This work provides strong evidence that SC144 is a promising lead compound with anti-virulence activity against N. gonorrhoeae.

title: Two novel plant-derived yeast species in Thailandicola (Microbotryomycetes): comparative genomics and transformation
content: Plant tissues and surfaces are among the largest microbial habitats on Earth, and commensal yeasts are common members of these communities, where they can contribute to plant-microbe interactions including the biological control of plant diseases. Here, we describe two novel species of unpigmented, basidiomycete yeasts, in the class Microbotryomycetes from the plant phyllosphere (Thailandicola erigeronia and T. cardamina) represented by three isolates from leaves of multiple hosts. We characterize these taxa through analyses of metabolic requirements, tolerance to differences in osmolarity, pH, and temperature, and enzymatic activities. In parallel, we generate near-chromosome-scale hybrid genomes annotated with transcriptome data for these novel species and a congenic isolate. We employ whole-genome and multilocus phylogenetic approaches to infer the placement of these species within a monophyletic clade. We use comparative genomics to examine how the gene content of these yeasts differs from that of other members of the Microbotryomycetes, including an apparent proliferation of retrotransposons. We further demonstrate the genetic transformability of these taxa using Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation. The description of these new species, together with high-quality genome resources and a genetic transformation protocol, establishes a foundation for experimental studies of these novel plant-derived yeasts and their interactions with hosts and other microbes.

title: Individual symbiont strains can compensate for complex microbiome loss in the bull-headed dung beetle, Onthophagus taurus
content: Many animals and plants have evolved to rely on microbiome mediated interactions with their environment. Across diverse insect groups, many are incapable of either breaking down complex carbohydrates or synthesizing essential nutrients despite consuming diets which should require one, or both, functions. Onthophagus beetles are one such host, with recent work suggesting their ability to digest their dung diet, typically rich in tough to digest polysaccharides and poor in nutrients, is likely bolstered by heritable symbionts. Despite there being over 2,000 species of Onthophagus, and over 5,000 species of "true" dung beetles (Scarabaeinae), little is known about how the microbiomes of these beetles modulate their interactions with their dung diet. The work presented here assesses the possible significance of four individual microbiome members, present during Onthophagus taurus development. Results show that three of the four isolates tested partially recovered normative developmental outcomes in O. taurus. Specifically, inoculation with a strain of either Acinetobacter, Brucella, or Pseudomonas increased pupal size relative to beetles deprived of the maternal inoculate. This mirrors the effects of individuals receiving the full natural inoculate, which contains hundreds of bacterial species. Further, using whole genome sequencing, we form a hypothesis of what nutrients these isolates provide to benefit O. taurus development. The findings presented here further highlight Onthophagus dung beetles as powerful systems to study the complex ways in which microbiome function can interact with diet to influence developmental and evolutionary outcomes.

title: Towards a Generalized Imaging Spectroscopy Framework for Surface Soil Salinity Retrieval in Coastal Wetlands: Evaluating Transferability and Hydroperiod–Salinity Relationships
content:
Abstract
Coastal wetlands are threatened by changing climatic and hydrologic pressures that may salinize fresh‐brackish ecosystems, causing stress, transformation, or collapse. Monitoring soil salinity requires a generalizable remote sensing approach applicable across coastal environments. We collected in situ field spectrometer reflectance measurements and soil samples in California’s Carpinteria Salt Marsh Reserve (CSMR) to measure salt content. The first derivatives of these reflectances were used in a Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) model to predict soil salinity (n = 32, R2 = 0.90, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = 5.00 ppt). We applied the model to NASA's AVIRIS‐3 imaging spectroscopy data to map soil salinity in the CSMR (Validation: n = 32, R2 = 0.53, MAE = 9.22 ppt) and to AVIRIS‐NG data over South Africa’s Langebaan Lagoon to test model transferability (Validation: n = 11, R2 = 0.67, MAE = 14.11 ppt). Primary mapped retrievals and associated analyses were restricted to non‐submerged, soil‐dominated pixels with MESMA‐derived soil fractional cover ≥0.50. Reported retrieval performance therefore applies primarily to areas with substantial exposed soil. We used Sentinel‐1 Synthetic Aperture Radar time series to map the hydroperiod—the percentage of time a site was inundated over the data record—for comparison with the soil salinity maps. Soil salinity increased with hydroperiod at CSMR but decreased with hydroperiod at Langebaan Lagoon, consistent with differing hydrologic connectivity and inundation dynamics. These results demonstrate the potential for a transferable imaging spectroscopy framework for mapping surface soil salinity in coastal wetlands and for quantifying landscape‐scale hydro‐ecological controls on salinity patterns.

title: Early‐Life Thyroid Hormones Promote Telomere Elongation and Link Telomere Dynamics to Long‐Term Behaviour and Performance
content:
ABSTRACT
Telomeres are essential chromosomal structures that safeguard genome integrity. Telomere length (TL), which often shortens with age and stress exposure, is increasingly viewed as an index of life prospect. Within a pace‐of‐life framework, telomere dynamics can be defined as integrative markers of somatic state and expected lifespan, potentially linking early environments to later life‐history strategies. Because telomere dynamics can be tightly coupled to metabolic state—especially during early growth—thyroid hormones (THs), key promoters of growth and metabolism, are prime candidates for mediating these effects. Here, we test whether experimentally elevated early‐life thyroid hormone levels promote telomere maintenance during the main post‐hatching growth phase in zebra finch (Taeniopygia guttata) nestlings, and whether early‐life telomere dynamics predict adolescent and adult performance. By administering TH (T3) throughout the main growth phase until fledging, we analysed TL dynamics longitudinally at ‘adolescence’ (day 186 post‐hatching) and ‘adulthood’ (day 316 post‐hatching). We focused on TL distribution metrics, considering the shortest and the longest TL classes, as well as mean TL, calculated across all telomere length values. We then assessed the consequences of TH‐mediated TL dynamics for vertical escape flight and exploratory behaviour, two traits related with fitness and life‐history. Irrespective of the TH treatment, we observed (1) TL elongation during the main growth phase, driven by the longest TL, which challenges the prevalent notion that TL shortens in early life; (2) TL attrition only during adolescence and only in the shortest class of telomeres; (3) the TH treatment during early life led to TL elongation of the longest TL in adolescence; (4) this TL elongation, measured as the change in TL from fledgling to adolescence, was positively associated with exploratory behaviour and escape vertical flight in adulthood. Our findings indicate that early‐life THs can alter TL dynamics and that these telomere changes are associated with later behaviour and performance. They also highlight the importance of considering different classes of TL rather than relying solely on average TL measures, as short telomeres did not elongate whereas long telomeres changed in both directions and largely accounted for the patterns observed at the average TL level, raising questions about the biological meaning of variation among telomere classes.

title: Palaeoclimate Alone Fails to Explain the Asymmetry of the Great American Biotic Interchange
content:
Eco‐evolutionary simulations coupled with spatially‐explicit palaeoclimate reconstructions spanning the Americas for the last 5 million years yielded more South‐to‐North than North‐to‐South successful exchanges. These findings reveal that the asymmetry of the Great American Biotic Interchange (GABI), incontestably North‐to‐South, may not have emerged from palaeoclimate dynamics alone, challenging classical hypotheses to explain this macroecological enigma.

ABSTRACT
Asymmetric colonisation patterns often arise from large‐scale biotic exchanges involving two source areas. In the Pliocene, the closure of the isthmus of Panama facilitated the admixture between North and South American faunas, an event termed Great American Biotic Interchange (GABI). The ecological mechanisms underlying the asymmetry of the GABI, incontestably in favour of North American lineages, remain debated. Here, coupling a mechanistic eco‐evolutionary simulator with palaeoclimatic reconstructions, we test fundamental hypotheses relating this biogeographic imbalance to palaeoclimate dynamics. When climate is the only constraint to species' dispersal, our simulations yield more South‐to‐North than North‐to‐South dispersal events, mostly within the tropical biome. Also, our models fail to explain the migrant diversity desequilibrium between the two continents, as well as temperate specialists' over‐representation in the fossil record of successfully exchanged taxa. Hence, we argue that spatio‐temporal palaeoclimate dynamics alone cannot explain the asymmetry of the GABI, suggesting additional factors fashioned this macroecological enigma.

Macrophage signaling history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses to cytokine stimulation
content: Macrophages perform a wide array of distinct and crucial functions, and therefore tightly regulate their responses to external stimuli. These cells must integrate sequential signals over time to mount an appropriate response to their immunological niche. How prior cytokine stimulation shares macrophage responses to a subsequent stimulus remains poorly understood, yet has important implications for pathogen clearance as well as tissue repair and homeostasis. Here, we systematically characterize transcriptional responses to sequential cytokine stimulation in primary human macrophages, as well as demonstrate the effect of interactions with bacterial pathogens on macrophage transcriptional responses and plasticity. We find that prior stimulation history constrains subsequent transcriptional responses in a stimulus-specific and asymmetric manner. Across the cytokines we tested, we observe that IFN{beta} is a dominant regulator of subsequent responses to other cytokines. We observe that this plasticity restriction is concentration dependent, rapidly established, and persists after cytokine removal. Additionally, we show that endogenous IFN{beta} produced during infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis restricts subsequent cytokine responses in a manner that is dependent on the activity of the bacterial secretion system ESX-1. Taken together, these findings establish a hierarchical model of macrophage responses to cytokines that depends on cytokine identity and order.

title: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophile phenotyping by measuring metabolic byproduct formation in microplates
content: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophiles can support several low-pH biotechnologies, but their phenotyping remains limited by throughput and inconsistent methods. This study used an assay to monitor metabolic byproduct formation using absorbance indicators in static, oxic cultures in 96-well microplates. In abiotic experiments, ferric iron and/or pH measurements from 51 microplates containing simulant solutions span total iron concentrations of 0-1 M, pH 0.3-7.0, and incubation temperatures of 4-75 {degrees}C. Of these, 30 microplates tested different UV-transparency and gas-permeable membrane configurations. Another 12 microplates tested indicator compatibility with growth media containing ferrous iron and (in)soluble sulfur substrates. Biological experiments measured 438 microplates containing Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans ATCC 23270, Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans ATCC 19377, or Leptospirillum ferriphilum DSM 14647 with chemical additives across 1,400 concentration conditions, yielding 142,038 time-course points, including abiotic controls. Measurements of apparent substrate oxidation and/or growth from 96 culture tubes and 99 shake flasks provide context for microplate observations. The miniaturized assay and this dataset may be useful for microbiology, (critical-mineral) biotechnology development, and synthetic biology.
